selection_reason: With no prior experiments completed, the most critical uncertainty is the baseline performance of the simplest viable model. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration: a single-profile RNA model with the standard PCA representation and no aggregation or fusion steps. Running this first establishes a reference accuracy/F1 against which every subsequent design decision (multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders like scVI/scGPT, image modality, and multimodal fusion) can be meaningfully compared. It is also the fastest to train, giving quick signal under a limited budget. Without this anchor, any later experiment's performance would be uninterpretable—we could not tell whether a multimodal or multiprofile setup is genuinely adding information or merely adding complexity. This single experiment reduces the most fundamental uncertainty in the search space.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), we have almost no evidence about which design choices matter. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal at all, since RNA alone with PCA is barely above chance. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests this by holding profile setting constant (singleprofile) and using a standard, well-understood image encoder, making it a clean modality comparison against config_001. If image performs substantially better, the search should focus on image encoders and multimodal fusion; if it is also weak, the problem likely requires better RNA encoders or multimodal combination. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design axis (which modality is informative) before committing budget to more complex encoder, aggregation, or fusion choices.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 0.485 accuracy while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) achieves only 0.208, indicating RNA is the dominant signal and the primary lever for improvement. Uncertainty: PCA is a simple linear projection; it is unclear whether a pre-trained single-cell foundation model (scgpt) can capture richer biological structure and substantially improve classification. This experiment (config_007: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) isolates the effect of the RNA encoder by changing only the encoder while holding profile setting and architecture identical to config_001. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it directly tests the highest-impact design choice (representation quality of the dominant modality), (2) it is a clean single-variable comparison to the current best, (3) a positive result would justify investing further in advanced encoders and inform multimodal fusion choices, while a null result would redirect effort toward aggregation or fusion strategies.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the strongest baseline at 0.485 acc, while scgpt (config_007) underperforms at 0.411, confirming PCA as the preferred RNA encoder. Image-only (config_010) is very weak at 0.208, so multimodal gains will depend heavily on the RNA branch. Uncertainty: we have no evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves over singleprofile for the best RNA encoder, and this axis underpins all subsequent multimodal and scvi/scgpt experiments. This experiment (config_002) tests multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) while keeping the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) identical to config_001, cleanly isolating the profile-setting/aggregation effect without confounding. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends the strongest result, uses the least complex aggregation to avoid overfitting, and its outcome will guide whether to invest further in multiprofile + transformer or pivot to multimodal fusion with singleprofile.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large gain over config_001 (singleprofile, same encoder) at 0.485, confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. PCA also outperformed scGPT in singleprofile (0.485 vs 0.411), making pca_n2000 the strongest RNA encoder. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool for multiprofile with pca_n2000. This experiment (config_003) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002, isolating the effect of aggregation method (transformer vs avgpool) while holding model setting, profile setting, and encoder constant. If transformer helps, it reveals exploitable sequential structure across profiles and guides future multimodal designs; if not, avgpool is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget toward fusion or image modality. This is the highest-information next step because it builds directly on our strongest result and tests the one unexplored dimension within that configuration space.

Evidence: RNA-only multi-profile with PCA n2000 and avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, and avgpool clearly outperforms transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). PCA outperforms scGPT in single-profile (0.485 vs 0.411). However, scvi_n200 is completely untested across all settings, leaving a major gap in our understanding of RNA encoder choice. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multi-profile, avgpool) directly compares against config_002 by changing only the RNA encoder while holding the best-performing profile and aggregation settings fixed. This isolates the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: it tests an entirely unexplored encoder in the current best configuration, providing maximum new information per experiment. A positive result would immediately yield a stronger candidate; a negative result would confirm PCA's dominance and redirect effort toward multimodal fusion. Testing scGPT in multi-profile (config_008) would be less informative given the already strong prior that scGPT < PCA.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208 acc), raising the question of whether image features add any value when fused with a strong RNA signal. Uncertainty: We have no evidence on whether multimodal fusion improves or degrades performance relative to the best RNA-only setup. This experiment (config_031: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) tests whether adding image features to the known-best RNA configuration via weighted fusion provides complementary information. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it allows the model to down-weight the weak image signal (given the 0.208 image-only baseline), making this the safest multimodal test. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it answers the highest-level design question—whether the multimodal direction is worth pursuing at all—before committing further experiments to specific fusion or image-encoder variants. If it fails to beat 0.650, remaining budget can focus on RNA-only refinement; if it succeeds, a new promising direction opens.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is the best RNA-only setup, and for pca_n2000, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). However, scvi_n200 produces a learned latent representation that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation than a linear PCA projection. Uncertainty: We have not tested whether transformer aggregation could outperform avgpool specifically for scvi_n200. This experiment (config_006) isolates that single variable against config_005. If transformer wins, it signals that the current best multimodal config (config_031, avgpool) is not on the optimal aggregation track and config_033 becomes the priority. If avgpool wins, it confirms the aggregation choice and frees the next experiment to probe fusion strategy (concat vs weighted) or whether the image modality genuinely adds signal. This is the highest-information single-variable test available, directly informing the architecture of the top-performing configuration.

The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678), which improves modestly over the RNA-only equivalent config_005 (acc=0.650). The key uncertainty is whether the weighted fusion is genuinely contributing or whether a simpler concat fusion would perform comparably. config_030 is identical to config_031 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, making it a clean single-variable A/B test on the fusion mechanism. This is the most informative next step because: (1) it isolates the effect of fusion strategy in the highest-performing configuration, (2) if concat matches weighted, it simplifies the architecture and suggests the image contribution is robust regardless of fusion, and (3) if weighted clearly outperforms, it validates the more complex fusion and guides further multimodal exploration toward weighted designs. Under a limited budget, resolving this question before testing additional variables (e.g., transformer aggregation, ViT-L image encoder) ensures we build on the correct architectural foundation.

The current best configuration (config_031: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.678 acc, only modestly above the RNA-only baseline (config_005: 0.650). Image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality has untapped signal or is near its ceiling. Config_037 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (keeping scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fixed), directly isolating the effect of image encoder quality in the multimodal setting. If imagenet_vit_l yields a meaningful gain, it signals the image branch has more capacity to exploit and justifies further multimodal exploration; if it does not, it confirms the image contribution is inherently limited and the budget is better spent refining RNA-side choices. This single-variable comparison from the current best is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about the image modality's ceiling under the limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about the performance landscape. The most critical unknown is whether the basic RNA signal alone is informative for this task, which sets the floor against which all encoder, profile, aggregation, and fusion choices must be judged. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible RNA configuration—standard PCA dimensionality reduction, a single profile, no aggregation or fusion. It establishes the baseline RNA performance and confirms the pipeline works end-to-end. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the highest-value first measurement is the simplest reference point. Every subsequent RNA-based experiment (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile, multimodal) will be interpreted relative to this floor. Starting with a more complex configuration (e.g., multimodal or scgpt) would conflate multiple design choices and make it impossible to attribute performance gains to any single factor. A simple PCA baseline also carries minimal risk of implementation failure, ensuring the first budget slot yields clean, interpretable data.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have a single data point (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc). We know nothing about whether the image modality contributes useful signal, which is the central premise of a multimodal study. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean single-modality baseline for the image branch, directly answering whether spatial/morphological features are informative for this task. 3) Why best next: This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-leverage question. If image features are uninformative, the entire multimodal block (configs 016–051) is deprioritized and we should invest in RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. If they are informative, multimodal fusion becomes a promising exploitation direction. Using resnet50 (the same encoder in configs 016–021) and keeping singleprofile ensures a controlled comparison: later, config_016 vs config_010 vs config_001 will cleanly isolate the additive/fusion contribution of combining modalities. Changing only the modality (keeping profile setting identical) avoids confounding multiple design choices at once.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is only 0.208, making RNA the clearly dominant modality. With only two data points, the most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA representation quality can be improved. Question tested: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 (linear) to scvi_n200 (learned nonlinear) while keeping singleprofile constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_001. Why this is the best next step: If scvi_n200 meaningfully outperforms PCA, it establishes that learned representations matter and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal fusion with a stronger RNA backbone. If it does not improve, it tells us the encoder choice is less impactful than profile structure or fusion strategy, redirecting the search efficiently. This isolates one design axis without confounding changes, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.48–0.52) while image-only is weak (0.21), and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in singleprofile (0.520 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation improves upon the best singleprofile RNA result, and this is a key design axis before investing in multimodal fusion. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple average-pooling aggregation improve validation accuracy over the current best (config_004, scvi_n200 singleprofile, 0.520)? Why this is the best next experiment: It builds directly on our strongest encoder (scvi_n200), changes only the profile/aggregation axis (the minimal coupled change inherent to multiprofile), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to isolate whether multiple profiles add signal before introducing transformer complexity. A positive result justifies exploring transformer aggregation and multimodal extensions; a negative result tells us singleprofile suffices, redirecting budget toward encoder choice (scgpt) or multimodal fusion rather than aggregation architecture.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.650, F1=0.628), a large jump over config_004 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, acc=0.520). This confirms multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the strongest direction. However, we have no information about whether the aggregation method matters—avgpool is a simple baseline. Question: config_006 (same rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, but transformer aggregation) isolates the effect of aggregation while holding all other variables constant. Why best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, directly testing whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve on the already-strong multiprofile scvi result, or whether simple avgpool is sufficient. This informs whether future multimodal experiments should invest in transformer aggregation or whether avgpool is adequate, reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest direction (0.650-0.653 vs ~0.52 singleprofile), and transformer ≈ avgpool (0.3% gap, likely noise). The image modality is very weak (resnet50: 0.21), so multimodal gains are uncertain. Key uncertainty: whether the RNA encoder choice still matters within the multiprofile setting, and whether an alternative encoder (scgpt) can push past 0.65. Question tested: config_009 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding multiprofile + transformer fixed, isolating the encoder effect in the best-performing structural context. Why this is best: it is a single-variable extension of the current best (config_006), directly exploitative of the strongest signal, and simultaneously tells us whether scgpt is competitive or inferior—information that would guide all future encoder choices. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we gain a new best; if it lags, we confirm scvi_n200 is well-suited and can focus budget on other axes (e.g., multimodal fusion or image encoder quality).

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_006 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) at 0.653 acc, while image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208 acc. Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) is nearly irrelevant for RNA (0.650 vs 0.653). The critical open question is whether the image modality contributes any complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation, or whether it merely adds noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) directly extends config_006 by adding the image branch with the simplest standard fusion (concat), isolating the effect of the image modality while holding all other design choices constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it answers the highest-uncertainty architectural question—whether multimodal fusion is worth the added complexity—before committing further experiments to multimodal variants. If it fails to beat 0.653, we gain strong evidence to focus on RNA-only improvements; if it helps, it validates the multimodal direction for subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the best result so far at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, outperforming the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (config_006, 0.653) by ~3.5 points. However, we have only tested concat fusion in the multimodal setting; the weighted fusion alternative is completely unexplored. Question: Does the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) materially affect multimodal performance, or is the 3.5-point image gain robust to how modalities are combined? Why this experiment: config_033 changes exactly one variable (fusion: concat → weighted) relative to config_032, making it a clean A/B test that isolates the fusion mechanism. If weighted fusion improves performance, it reveals that modality importance is asymmetric and we should invest in tuning weights; if performance is similar, we can rule out fusion strategy as a bottleneck and redirect budget toward improving the image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or exploring other axes. Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment by directly extending our strongest result while resolving a fundamental design uncertainty that affects all future multimodal configurations.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration is config_033 (SCVI_n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1. Image-only ResNet50 is very weak (0.208), yet adding it to the multimodal pipeline yields a meaningful +0.06 gain over RNA-only (0.653→0.713). Weighted fusion clearly outperforms concat (0.713 vs 0.688), and transformer aggregation is the established choice. Uncertainty: We have only tested one image encoder (ResNet50). It is unknown whether a stronger pretrained encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) would extract more useful visual signal and further improve multimodal performance, or whether the image contribution is inherently limited. This experiment (config_039) changes exactly one variable—ResNet50→ViT-L—while holding the rest of the best configuration (SCVI_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) constant. It directly tests whether image encoder quality is a bottleneck, which is a critical architectural decision. If ViT-L improves performance, it validates investing in stronger visual representations; if not, it indicates the image modality's contribution is saturated and further effort should focus on RNA-side improvements. This single-variable comparison is the most informative next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_039 (SCVI_n200 + ViT-L, multi-profile, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc. With ResNet50, weighted fusion clearly outperformed concat (0.713 vs 0.688, config_033 vs config_032). Question: Does the weighted-fusion advantage over concat persist with the stronger ViT-L image encoder, or does the richer ViT-L representation make the fusion method less critical? This experiment isolates a single variable (fusion: concat vs weighted) against the current best, providing a clean A/B comparison. Why best next step: It is the most direct exploitation of the top-performing region while simultaneously testing whether a simpler fusion strategy (concat) would suffice, which has practical implications for model complexity. If concat performs comparably, it simplifies the architecture; if it degrades significantly, it confirms weighted fusion is a necessary component and we can confidently lock in config_039's design. No other untested configuration provides as clean a single-variable comparison to the current best.

No experiments have been completed yet, so the highest-priority need is to establish a clear performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: a single modality, single profile, and a linear (PCA) encoder with no aggregation or fusion. Running this first gives a well-defined performance floor against which every subsequent design choice—stronger RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image modality, and multimodal fusion—can be measured. It also isolates the contribution of the PCA representation before any other variable is introduced, so that later experiments can cleanly attribute performance changes to specific design decisions rather than conflating multiple factors. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the most minimal, interpretable baseline is the most information-efficient first step.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485). There is essentially zero evidence about whether the image modality carries any predictive signal for this task. This is the most fundamental design uncertainty: if image has no useful signal, the entire multimodal configuration space (~36 configs) becomes low-value, and budget should focus on RNA encoder/profile improvements. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the contribution of the image modality alone, keeping profile_setting identical to config_001 (singleprofile) so the comparison is clean—only the modality changes. ResNet50 is a standard, well-understood encoder, making this a fair first probe. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget with only one data point, the highest-information experiment is the one that partitions the configuration space most decisively. A strong image-only result would justify investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion strategies; a weak result would redirect all remaining budget toward RNA encoder and multiprofile exploration. No other single experiment reduces this level of uncertainty as efficiently, and it avoids simultaneously changing multiple design axes (unlike a multimodal config that would confound modality addition with fusion choice).

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA_n2000, single-profile) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50, single-profile) is very weak at 20.8%. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, so understanding what drives RNA performance is the highest-priority question. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the linear PCA representation is the bottleneck or whether a learned, biologically-informed encoder (scVI) captures non-linear gene-expression structure that improves classification. This experiment (config_004: RNA-only, scvi_n200, single-profile) isolates the effect of the RNA encoder by changing only that variable relative to config_001, keeping profile setting and all other hyperparameters constant. If scVI substantially outperforms PCA, it signals that representation quality is a key lever and justifies further investment in learned encoders (including scGPT) and in multimodal fusion with a stronger RNA backbone. If performance is similar, it tells us PCA is adequate and we should shift focus to profile/aggregation or image-side improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental representation question before branching into multiprofile, aggregation, or multimodal variants is the most information-efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly dominate (0.485–0.520) over image-only (0.208), and scvi_n200 is the best RNA encoder tested (0.520 vs 0.485 for pca_n2000). The critical open question is whether multiprofile representation improves over singleprofile, since this choice gates a large portion of the remaining search space. config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is the most direct extension of the best-performing config_004, isolating the effect of multiprofile + simple aggregation while holding the RNA encoder fixed. If multiprofile helps, it justifies investing further in aggregation variants and multimodal multiprofile configs; if it does not, we can deprioritize the entire multiprofile branch and focus budget on encoder selection or fusion strategy. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile, 0.520), confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether transformer aggregation captures inter-profile structure that simple averaging misses, or whether the profiles are homogeneous enough that avgpool already suffices. This experiment (config_006) isolates the aggregation variable by keeping model_setting, profile_setting, and rna_encoder identical to config_005 while switching from avgpool to transformer. It is the best next experiment because: (1) it is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best result, (2) the answer directly informs which aggregation to use in all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 018-051), and (3) if transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it reveals that profile ordering/interaction carries predictive signal, changing the design space for fusion strategies.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile (config_005/006) achieves ~0.65 acc, a large jump over singleprofile (0.52), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) makes negligible difference. The key remaining uncertainty within the RNA-only space is whether the scgpt encoder can outperform scvi_n200 in this multiprofile regime. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable swap from config_005, isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: the answer directly determines which RNA encoder to pair with image in all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 030-039 vs 042-051). Resolving encoder superiority before committing budget to multimodal runs avoids potentially running 8+ multimodal configs with a suboptimal encoder. It is the highest-leverage uncertainty to close given the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear best configuration so far (config_005/006: ~0.65 acc), with transformer and avgpool being nearly equivalent. Image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether adding image in a multimodal setting will help or dilute the strong RNA signal. Question: Does adding resnet50 image features (concat fusion) to the best RNA-only multiprofile scvi_n200 transformer configuration improve or degrade performance? This directly tests the value of multimodality against the current best baseline (config_006, 0.653) with only one variable changed (adding image + concat). Why best use of budget: All completed experiments are unimodal; the central open question is whether multimodal fusion adds value at all. Testing with the already-characterized resnet50 encoder and the simplest fusion (concat) isolates the multimodal question cleanly. If it helps, we can then explore better image encoders or fusion strategies; if it hurts, we save budget by not pursuing multimodal further.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) achieved the best accuracy so far (0.688), a ~3.5 pt gain over the best RNA-only model (config_006, 0.653). However, image-only resnet50 scored only 0.208, raising uncertainty about whether the image branch is contributing meaningful complementary signal or whether the modest multimodal gain is partly noise. Question: config_038 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while keeping all other settings identical to config_032. This isolates the effect of image representation quality. If imagenet_vit_l yields a substantial further improvement, it confirms the image modality carries extractable signal and justifies further investment in the image branch; if it yields little or no gain, it suggests the image modality contributes minimally regardless of encoder strength, and the small gain in config_032 may be within noise. Why best next: it is a clean single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly tests a critical design question (is the image branch worth keeping and investing in), and avoids the lower-priority question of fusion method (concat vs. weighted) which is less informative if the image signal itself is weak.

The current best configuration (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) achieves 0.721 accuracy. All multimodal results so far use 'concat' fusion; the 'weighted' fusion option is completely untested, leaving a key design dimension with zero evidence. Config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, providing a clean one-variable comparison that isolates the fusion mechanism. In rna_only, aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) showed negligible difference (~0.003), suggesting that how features are combined (fusion) may be a more impactful unexplored axis than aggregation. Under a limited budget, testing weighted fusion directly against the current best tells us whether the simple concatenation is suboptimal or whether the multimodal signal is already well-captured, reducing uncertainty about a core architectural choice before committing further experiments to the concat paradigm.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We know resnet50 image-only (single profile) is very weak (acc=0.208), and that ViT-L in the multimodal setting boosts performance from ~0.69 (resnet50) to ~0.72. However, we have zero data on whether ViT-L captures any standalone cellular phenotype signal. The image modality's role—purely complementary vs. having independent predictive power—remains untested. 2) What this tests: config_015 (image_only, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer) isolates the image modality with the best available encoder and matching multiprofile/transformer settings, directly measuring ViT-L's standalone contribution. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, this clean ablation is highly informative. If image-only ViT-L remains near 0.2–0.3, it confirms the image is purely complementary and future effort should focus on RNA-image interaction/fusion. If it reaches ~0.5+, the image has strong standalone signal and we should invest in image pipeline improvements. This single result fundamentally reshapes where to allocate remaining experiments, making it more decision-relevant than marginal fusion or aggregation tweaks that are already well-characterized.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy performs best. The most critical uncertainty is the absolute performance floor of the simplest reasonable model. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, least confounded configuration in the search space. It isolates the baseline contribution of raw RNA features reduced by a standard linear method, with no deep encoder, no multi-profile aggregation, and no fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Establishing this clean baseline first gives a reference point against which every subsequent experiment (image-only, multimodal, alternative encoders, multiprofile aggregation) can be meaningfully compared. It is also the cheapest to run (PCA is computationally trivial), preserving budget for more complex configurations later. Starting simple avoids conflating multiple design choices and lets me attribute any later performance gains or losses to specific variables.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality contributes any complementary signal beyond RNA. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal, most direct extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder and profile setting, and adds image with the simplest fusion (concat), isolating the effect of adding the image modality. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 0.485, we gain strong evidence to invest remaining budget in multimodal variants (better encoders, aggregation, fusion). If it does not improve, we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements, avoiding a large block of potentially unproductive multimodal experiments. This single experiment resolves the highest-impact design question while changing the fewest variables from our existing data point.

We have only two completed experiments: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile, acc=0.485) and multimodal (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat, singleprofile, acc=0.527). The ~4-point gain from adding image suggests a positive contribution, but we cannot yet tell whether image alone is a strong signal, whether RNA is the dominant modality, or whether the fusion is genuinely synergistic. Testing config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) completes the basic modality factorial and isolates the image contribution. This is the highest-information next step: if image alone is weak (~0.30), the multimodal gain is a small RNA-anchored boost and we should prioritize RNA encoders and fusion; if image alone is strong (~0.50+), the multimodal model may be underleveraging image and we should explore better image encoders or fusion strategies. Under a tight budget, resolving which modality drives performance is more foundational than tuning fusion or profile settings on top of an uncharacterized system.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, single profile, PCA) achieves 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, single profile, PCA+ResNet50, concat) achieves 0.527 acc, confirming that single-profile RNA is a reasonable baseline and that adding image helps modestly. However, we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile representations improve over single-profile. This is a fundamental architectural axis that, if positive, unlocks an entire branch of the search space (aggregation methods, multiprofile multimodal configs) and if negative, lets us discard roughly half the remaining configurations. config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool) is the cleanest possible test: it differs from config_001 only in profile setting (and the necessary aggregation), isolating the multiprofile effect without confounding with fusion, image encoder, or learned RNA encoders. It is also a simpler/faster model to train, making it budget-efficient. The result will directly inform whether subsequent experiments should prioritize multiprofile configurations (e.g., config_018, config_020) or remain in the single-profile regime.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc, showing multiprofile RNA is a strong direction. However, we only know multimodal helps in the singleprofile setting (config_016: 0.527 vs config_001: 0.485, +4.2 pts), and image-only is very weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image signal adds value or noise when combined with the already-strong multiprofile RNA. Question: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests whether adding the image modality improves upon the best-performing RNA-only multiprofile baseline, holding profile setting, RNA encoder, and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: it resolves the most consequential design decision—whether to invest further in multimodal configurations or focus on RNA-only improvements (aggregation, encoder choice). The result cleanly isolates the marginal contribution of the image modality in the multiprofile regime, and the answer will guide whether to explore the large multimodal configuration space (configs 019–051) or the smaller RNA-only space (configs 003–009) next.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc. Multiprofile with avgpool gave a large boost over single profile (+0.092), but we have no data on whether transformer aggregation (learned cross-profile attention) can further improve over simple averaging. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool in the best-performing multimodal/multiprofile setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_018), isolating the effect of aggregation without confounding RNA encoder, image encoder, or fusion changes. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests the most impactful remaining design choice in our current best configuration. If transformer helps, it opens a new optimization direction; if it doesn't, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder exploration. This reduces the most important uncertainty with minimal risk of confounding.

Evidence: The current best (config_018, acc 0.619) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and RNA is clearly the dominant signal (image_only acc 0.208 vs rna_only 0.485). All six completed experiments use pca_n2000, so we have zero evidence about whether a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) could extract a superior RNA representation. Question: config_030 changes exactly one variable from config_018—swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 while keeping multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, and concat fixed—directly isolating the effect of RNA representation quality in the best-performing pipeline. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA modality drives most of the predictive signal, so improving its encoder has the highest potential leverage. A single-variable A/B against the current best cleanly attributes any performance shift to the encoder choice, and the answer reshapes the entire remaining search (if scvi helps, we prioritize it across all subsequent configs; if it doesn't, we can rule it out and focus budget on image encoder or fusion strategy).

Evidence: The current best is config_030 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1. Multiprofile with avgpool aggregation is strongly supported (config_002→018, config_018→020), and scvi_n200 shows a modest edge over pca_n2000 (0.632 vs 0.619). However, the fusion method has never been varied—every completed multimodal experiment used concat. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation in the best-performing setting? config_031 changes only the fusion (concat→weighted) relative to config_030, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: Fusion strategy is a completely untested design axis that could have a larger effect than the ~0.013 encoder difference already observed. Testing it at the current best configuration maximizes information gain: if weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new exploitable direction; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward other untested axes (e.g., ViT-L image encoder or scgpt).

Evidence: The current best (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.678, a large jump from config_030 (same but concat fusion, 0.632, +0.046) and from config_018 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat, 0.619). The scvi→pca encoder swap (018 vs 030) gives only +0.013, while the concat→weighted fusion swap (030 vs 031) gives +0.046. Uncertainty: We cannot tell whether weighted fusion is broadly beneficial or only synergistic with scvi_n200. Question: config_019 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) isolates the fusion effect under the pca encoder, completing a 2×2 (encoder × fusion) comparison. If 019 ≈ 0.66–0.67, weighted fusion is the dominant driver and scvi adds little; if 019 ≈ 0.62–0.63, there is a strong encoder–fusion interaction and scvi is essential. Why best next: This single-variable change from the best config maximizes information per experiment, directly informs whether to invest in better RNA encoders (scgpt) or better image encoders (ViT-L) next, and avoids the risk of confounding multiple changes in a single run under a tight budget.

The current best configuration (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.678 accuracy, with consistent evidence that multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion, and scvi_n200 all contribute positively. The image-only baseline was very weak (0.208 with resnet50), yet adding image features to RNA still improved performance (0.591→0.678), suggesting the image modality contributes but may be limited by encoder quality. Config_037 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while keeping all other settings at their best-performing values. This isolates the effect of image encoder quality on the multimodal pipeline. If ViT-L improves performance, it identifies the image encoder as a bottleneck worth further investment; if not, it indicates the image contribution is inherently limited in this task, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt). This is the highest-expected-performance untested config and a clean single-variable exploitation of the best direction.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which design choices (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion) matter. The most fundamental uncertainty is what a simple baseline achieves, without which no subsequent comparison is interpretable. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest possible configuration—no deep encoder, no aggregation, no fusion. It establishes the lower-bound performance of the RNA modality with a linear representation and a single profile. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first run should be fast, unambiguous, and maximally informative as a reference. A PCA baseline is cheap to train, removes confounds from encoder choice and fusion strategy, and provides a concrete number against which every later experiment (deeper RNA encoders, image-only, multimodal, multiprofile, various aggregations/fusions) can be directly compared. Starting here avoids overcommitting to any complex design decision before we know what the data can support.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), so virtually all design dimensions—modality, encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion—are unexplored. The most critical uncertainty right now is whether the image modality carries any useful signal for this task at all; without knowing that, we cannot rationally invest in multimodal fusion experiments. Question: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests whether image features alone are informative, using the same profile setting and the same level of architectural simplicity as config_001, so the only variable that changes is the modality. Why this is the best next experiment: It provides a clean, single-variable comparison (RNA vs. image) that calibrates our expectations for every downstream multimodal experiment. If image-only is strong, multimodal fusion becomes a high-value direction; if it is weak, we can focus budget on RNA-side improvements (encoder, profile, aggregation) rather than spending experiments on fusion strategies that may add little. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, singleprofile, PCA n2000) achieves 0.485 acc / 0.464 F1, while config_010 (Image, singleprofile, ResNet50) achieves only 0.208 acc / 0.172 F1. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, and the multiprofile/aggregation axis is entirely untested. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve the RNA representation, holding the encoder (PCA n2000) constant? This isolates the profile+aggregation effect as a single-axis change from our best baseline. Why this is the best next experiment: With only two completed runs, the most informative next step is to determine whether multiprofile aggregation can push the already-best modality higher. The answer directly gates whether the many multiprofile multimodal configurations (config_018–051) are worth pursuing, and it keeps the comparison clean by changing only profile setting and aggregation relative to config_001. Avgpool is chosen over transformer as the simpler, more interpretable first test of aggregation.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a substantial +10.6% improvement over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), establishing that multiprofile aggregation is a strong lever. Image alone (config_010, 0.208) is weak, so the current promising direction is RNA with multiprofile. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer) matters, or whether the gain is simply from having multiple profiles regardless of how they are pooled. Question tested: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and encoder identical to config_002, cleanly isolating the effect of aggregation strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a minimal, controlled extension of the strongest result, directly informs whether we should use transformer aggregation in all future multiprofile and multimodal configurations, and avoids the risk of confounding by simultaneously changing encoder or modality. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it reshapes the design space; if not, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can pivot to testing alternative RNA encoders or multimodal fusion with confidence.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, which substantially outperforms singleprofile RNA (0.485) and image-only (0.208). However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA), leaving the representation choice as a major unresolved variable. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly tests whether a learned nonlinear representation (SCVI) outperforms linear PCA under the identical multiprofile+avgpool setting, isolating the encoder as the sole changed variable. Why this is best: It is the cleanest single-factor comparison against our current best, it reduces uncertainty about whether representation quality is a bottleneck before investing in multimodal fusion experiments, and the result will inform which RNA encoder to pair with image fusion in subsequent experiments. If SCVI matches or beats PCA, it reshapes the multimodal search space; if PCA is already near-optimal, we can confidently move to fusion testing.

The current best is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool; acc 0.650). The strongest evidence so far is that encoder choice and profile/aggregation settings matter: scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 (+6 pts), multiprofile > singleprofile (+10 pts), and avgpool > transformer (+7 pts with pca). The key untested question is whether scgpt—a pretrained single-cell foundation model—outperforms the VAE-based scvi_n200 representation. config_008 changes only the encoder (scvi_n200 → scgpt) while holding the best-known multiprofile + avgpool settings fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. This is the best use of the next budget slot because (1) it directly tests whether a fundamentally different representation paradigm (pretrained generative model vs. VAE) can push performance beyond 0.650, (2) the answer will determine which encoder to pair with image modalities in subsequent multimodal experiments, and (3) unlike re-testing aggregation (config_006), where the prior from pca strongly favors avgpool, the encoder question is genuinely uncertain—pretrained models can either help or hurt depending on task alignment, as the weak resnet50 image result already hints.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc, while the image-only model (config_010, resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208 acc. We have strong evidence about which RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation work best, but zero evidence on whether the image modality adds any value when fused with a strong RNA representation. Question: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests whether adding resnet50 image features via the simplest fusion (concat) to the best-known RNA pipeline improves or degrades performance. Why best: This is the central hypothesis of a multimodal cellular profiling study. The answer determines whether the remaining budget should be spent exploring multimodal variants (weighted fusion, ViT, transformer aggregation) or focused on refining the RNA-only pipeline. It uses the best-validated RNA settings, so any performance change can be attributed to the addition of the image modality and fusion, making it a clean, high-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best RNA-only config (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA/image/aggregation but concat fusion) achieves 0.632 acc — slightly worse. This single data point suggests the image modality (resnet50) may be adding noise rather than signal, but the difference is small (~1.8%) and could reflect the fusion method rather than the modality itself. Question: config_031 isolates the fusion method (weighted vs. concat) while holding all other design choices identical to config_030. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds config_005's performance, the image modality has latent value and is worth further investment (e.g., better image encoders). If it does not, we gain strong evidence to redirect the remaining budget toward RNA-only optimization. Why this is best: it is the most controlled, single-variable comparison available that directly resolves the strategic question of whether to pursue multimodal or focus on RNA-only, making the most efficient use of a limited experiment slot.

Evidence: The current best is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. RNA-only with scvi_n200+avgpool is 0.650, so image adds ~2.8 pts only with weighted fusion. However, image-only with resnet50 was very weak (0.208), raising the question of whether the image modality's contribution is bottlenecked by encoder capacity. Uncertainty: We have only tested resnet50 as the image encoder; it is unclear whether a stronger pretrained encoder (imagenet_vit_l) would meaningfully improve the image signal and thus the multimodal result. This experiment (config_037) changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other parameters at their best-known values (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted), giving a clean single-variable comparison to config_031. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly tests whether the image modality can contribute more signal, which determines whether further multimodal experiments should invest in image quality or whether we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side improvements.

The current best configuration (config_037: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.7062 accuracy. In RNA-only experiments, avgpool consistently outperformed transformer aggregation (0.5907 vs 0.5191 with pca_n2000), but this was tested without image features. config_039 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping all other settings at their best-known values (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). This isolates the effect of aggregation in the multimodal context where image features may interact differently with profile-level aggregation. If transformer aggregation helps here, it could push performance beyond 0.7062; if not, it confirms avgpool as the correct choice and directs remaining budget toward other design axes. This is a minimal single-variable extension of the strongest evidence, making it the most efficient use of the next experiment.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a reliable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration: a single modality with a standard linear encoder and no aggregation or fusion complexity. It isolates the raw RNA signal and provides a reference performance against which every subsequent design choice (alternative encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion strategy) can be meaningfully compared. Starting here minimizes confounding, is computationally cheap, and if it performs poorly, immediately flags a data-quality or task-difficulty issue before investing in more complex configurations. This is the highest-information first experiment under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000, acc≈0.485), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. If it does not, the entire multimodal branch (configs 016–051) becomes low-value and the search should focus on RNA representation and profile settings. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-axis test: it mirrors the simplicity of config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation) while introducing only the image modality with a standard encoder. The result will (a) establish whether image features are informative for this task, (b) provide a per-modality baseline to later decompose multimodal gains, and (c) partition the remaining search space, making every subsequent experiment more targeted under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA) achieves 0.485 accuracy while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) achieves only 0.208, a large gap that creates critical uncertainty about whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative for this task or whether ResNet50 is simply a poor encoder. Question: config_013 (image-only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable change from config_010, isolating the effect of the image encoder. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it validates the image modality and justifies investing in multimodal fusion configs (016-051). If it also performs poorly, we can eliminate the majority of multimodal configurations from consideration and redirect budget toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) and profile/aggregation settings. Why best next experiment: With only 2 data points, the most consequential uncertainty is whether the image modality can contribute at all. Resolving this gates decisions on ~36 multimodal configs and determines whether to focus remaining budget on RNA improvements or multimodal fusion, making it the highest-information-value single experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) is clearly the dominant modality at 0.485 acc, while both image encoders are weak (~0.21-0.23). We have no data on whether multiprofile + aggregation can improve the RNA baseline. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with average-pool aggregation improve RNA classification, holding the encoder fixed at pca_n2000? Why this is best: config_002 is a minimal, controlled extension of config_001 (same encoder, same modality) that isolates the effect of the profile/aggregation design axis. Using avgpool (simpler) before transformer avoids confounding complexity. The result directly tells us whether multiprofile aggregation is a productive direction for the dominant modality, reducing uncertainty before committing budget to more complex multimodal or encoder-variant experiments.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best performance so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), a ~10.6% gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, acc=0.485). Image-only models are weak (0.21-0.23), confirming RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have only tested avgpool as the multiprofile aggregation method; it is unknown whether a transformer-based aggregation would better capture inter-profile interactions and further improve performance. This experiment (config_003) isolates the aggregation variable by changing only avgpool→transformer while keeping rna_only, multiprofile, and pca_n2000 fixed, making it a clean A/B comparison against config_002. It is the best next step because it directly exploits the current best direction with a minimal, interpretable change; the result will inform whether more complex aggregation is warranted before investing compute in multimodal fusion experiments, and it reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice that would propagate into all future multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.591) while image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227). Within RNA, multi-profile + avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591) clearly outperforms single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). However, only PCA n2000 has been tested as the RNA encoder. Question: Does a learned encoder (scvi_n200) improve over PCA in the best-known multi-profile + avgpool setup? config_005 isolates exactly one variable (RNA encoder: PCA→scvi) against config_002, giving a clean representation comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing in multimodal fusion (where the weak image signal may not help) or further aggregation variants, we need to know whether the RNA representation itself is the bottleneck. The result directly determines which encoder to carry forward into all subsequent multimodal experiments, making this the highest-information-per-budget choice.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. We also know that for PCA, avgpool (0.591) substantially outperformed transformer (0.519) in the multiprofile setting, suggesting aggregation choice is important. However, we have no evidence on whether this aggregation preference is encoder-dependent. Question: Does transformer aggregation help or hurt with the scvi_n200 encoder specifically? This tests the interaction between encoder and aggregation while holding all other variables constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, single-variable change from the current best config, directly exploiting the strongest evidence while reducing uncertainty about whether transformer aggregation should be ruled out for the best encoder. If transformer also underperforms, we can confidently eliminate it and redirect remaining budget toward encoder comparison (scgpt) or multimodal fusion. If it helps, we immediately identify a better configuration.

Evidence: RNA-only models substantially outperform image-only models (best RNA ~0.653 vs best image ~0.227), scvi_n200 with multiprofile is the strongest RNA setup, and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has minimal impact for scvi. The critical open question is whether the weak image modality provides any complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment (config_033) pairs our best RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with resnet50 and weighted fusion, directly comparable to config_006 (0.653). Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can learn to downweight the much weaker image signal, giving the fairest test of whether image adds value. If this matches or beats 0.653, multimodal fusion is worth further exploration; if it falls short, we can confidently focus the remaining budget on RNA-only improvements (e.g., scgpt encoder) and skip the 30+ multimodal configurations. This single experiment resolves the highest-impact design decision under budget constraints.

Evidence: config_033 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, multi-profile, transformer, weighted) achieved 0.713 acc, a substantial +6% jump over the best RNA-only result (config_006, 0.653). However, this is our only multimodal data point, and we cannot yet determine whether the gain comes from the image features themselves or from the specific 'weighted' fusion mechanism. Question: config_032 is identical to config_033 except fusion changes from 'weighted' to 'concat'. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy. If concat performs comparably, the gain is driven by incorporating image features broadly; if it drops significantly, the weighted fusion is a critical design choice that must be preserved. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison to our current best, directly addressing the largest source of uncertainty (is the multimodal gain robust to fusion choice?), and it avoids changing multiple factors simultaneously. Under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the fusion mechanism before scaling to other image encoders or profile settings is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) achieves the best validation accuracy (0.713) and F1 (0.695), substantially outperforming the best RNA-only model (config_005/006 at ~0.65), confirming that the image modality contributes complementary information in fusion. However, image-only models are very weak (0.21-0.23), so it is unclear whether the image encoder quality limits the multimodal gain or whether the current resnet50 features are already sufficient. Question: Does replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l in the multimodal fusion pipeline further improve performance? config_039 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l relative to config_033, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest configuration while resolving a key uncertainty about the image representation's contribution. If imagenet_vit_l helps, it identifies a clear path to push performance higher; if it does not, it confirms that the image signal is inherently limited and we should focus on RNA-side improvements (e.g., scgpt encoder or aggregation changes) instead. This is more informative than, e.g., testing avgpool vs. transformer aggregation (which showed little difference in RNA-only scvi_n200) or testing scgpt (which adds a new, untested variable on the RNA side).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about task difficulty, the relative contribution of RNA vs. image modalities, or whether multiprofile/complex encoders add value. The single most important unknown is the performance floor of a simple, well-understood baseline. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration—no image branch, no multiprofile aggregation, no learned encoder beyond PCA. It establishes a clean, fast, interpretable baseline accuracy/F1 against which every subsequent design choice (adding image, switching to scvi/scgpt, moving to multiprofile, adding fusion) can be measured. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first run should minimize confounds and maximize interpretability. A PCA-based RNA-only single-profile model trains quickly, has no pretraining or hyperparameter sensitivity, and gives an unambiguous reference point. If it performs well, it tells us the task is tractable and that added complexity must clear a meaningful bar; if it performs poorly, it signals that the representation or modality choice is the critical lever to explore next. Starting here avoids the risk of attributing performance to the wrong factor in a more complex configuration.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any useful signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the image-modality baseline under the same simple singleprofile setting, enabling a clean modality comparison against config_001. This is the highest-information next step: if image-only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, multimodal fusion (configs 016+) becomes a promising direction worth investing in; if image-only is weak, we can deprioritize multimodal and image-encoder variants and focus budget on RNA encoder and multiprofile improvements. Testing this before any multimodal or multiprofile variant avoids committing budget to complex combinations whose value depends on the untested premise that both modalities contribute signal.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while config_010 (image, resnet50) achieves only 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA data point, so we cannot yet assess whether the RNA encoder choice (PCA vs. learned representations) is a meaningful design lever. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile, rna_only) changes exactly one variable from config_001—the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI—while holding profile setting and all other factors constant. This cleanly isolates the effect of a learned, biologically-informed representation versus a linear dimensionality reduction. Why this is the best next experiment: With only 2 completed runs, the highest-value uncertainty to resolve is whether the RNA encoder matters at all. If scVI substantially outperforms PCA, it justifies investing subsequent budget in scgpt and in multiprofile/aggregation variants built on the stronger encoder. If it does not, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward profile setting, aggregation, or multimodal fusion. A single-variable comparison is the most efficient use of a limited experiment slot.

Evidence: RNA-only models substantially outperform image-only (0.485-0.520 vs 0.208), and scvi_n200 beats pca_n2000 (0.520 vs 0.485), establishing scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder so far. The critical unresolved question is whether multiprofile representation (with aggregation) adds value over singleprofile. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile) by changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It isolates the multiprofile effect without confounding with a more complex aggregation (transformer) or a new encoder (scgpt). If multiprofile+avgpool improves over 0.520, it validates the multiprofile axis and justifies testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not, a large portion of the search space (all multiprofile configs) can be deprioritized, saving budget for the more promising multimodal or encoder-comparison directions. This is the highest-information single step under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.520/0.498), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever so far. scvi_n200 also outperformed pca_n2000 in singleprofile (0.520 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation mechanism matters—i.e., whether a transformer aggregator can capture inter-profile dependencies beyond simple averaging. This experiment (config_006) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding the best-performing encoder (scvi_n200) and multiprofile setting fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it exploits the strongest evidence (multiprofile + scvi_n200) while resolving a critical design choice (aggregation type) that will directly inform which aggregation to pair with multimodal fusion in later experiments, without introducing additional confounds.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile (config_005/006) achieves ~0.65 acc, a large jump over its single-profile version (0.52), while pca_n2000 single-profile is 0.485. Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) appears negligible (~0.003 gap). The key open question is whether the RNA encoder still matters in the multiprofile regime or whether the multiprofile structure largely subsumes encoder differences. Question tested: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Why best next: We already have single-profile baselines for both encoders, so this directly extends that comparison to the multiprofile setting. If pca_n2000 multiprofile is close to scvi_n200 multiprofile, it tells us the multiprofile structure is the dominant driver and we can focus budget on fusion/multimodal questions. If it lags substantially, it confirms encoder quality remains critical and motivates testing scgpt next. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about where to invest remaining experiments, making this the highest-information single step under budget constraints.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 (config_005, avgpool: 0.650; config_006, transformer: 0.653) is the strongest configuration so far, and the aggregation choice appears to have minimal impact (~0.003 difference). Image-only is very weak (0.208), suggesting the image modality may not contribute much. Uncertainty: We have no data on the scgpt encoder, which could represent a fundamentally different (and potentially superior) RNA representation compared to scvi_n200 or pca_n2000. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting? Config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) directly parallels config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the encoder as the only changed variable. Why this is the best next experiment: Resolving the encoder question is foundational—it determines which RNA backbone to build multimodal experiments on. Testing scgpt now avoids wasting budget on multimodal configs built on a suboptimal encoder, and the clean comparison (same profile, same aggregation) maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear best (0.653 acc), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208 acc). This raises a critical uncertainty: is the weak image performance due to the resnet50 encoder being inadequate, or is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task? This question gates whether any of the 30+ multimodal configurations are worth testing. config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_010 (same setup but resnet50), isolating the effect of image encoder quality. If ViT-L is also weak, we can confidently allocate remaining budget to RNA-only refinements and skip all multimodal configs. If ViT-L substantially improves, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion with ViT-L. This is the highest-information single experiment because it resolves a binary design decision (pursue multimodal or not) that would otherwise require multiple multimodal trials to infer indirectly.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 + transformer (config_006) achieves 0.653 acc, establishing a strong RNA baseline. Image-only models are very weak (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227), raising the critical question of whether adding image to the dominant RNA signal helps, is neutral, or hurts. No multimodal configuration has been tested yet, so we have zero evidence on fusion utility. This experiment (config_039: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) directly tests whether the image modality provides complementary information to the best RNA configuration. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because the image signal is ~3x weaker; weighted allows the model to downweight uninformative image features rather than forcing equal representation. If config_039 exceeds 0.653, image adds value and we should explore fusion strategies; if it falls below, image is detrimental and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the single largest open design question (multimodal vs. unimodal) while building on the strongest validated RNA settings.

Evidence: config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.725) and F1 (0.685), a substantial jump over the best RNA-only multiprofile result (0.653, config_006). However, we have only a single multimodal data point, so we cannot yet determine which design choices in that configuration are responsible for the gain. The most critical untested variable within that exact setup is the fusion strategy: we have only tested 'weighted' fusion. Question: config_038 is identical to config_039 except fusion is changed from weighted to concat, isolating the effect of fusion strategy while holding all other factors (RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, aggregation) constant. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean single-variable A/B comparison against our best result, maximizing information per experiment. (2) If concat performs comparably, fusion strategy is not a critical design axis and we can simplify the search; if weighted is clearly better, we confirm an important design choice before scaling to other encoders or profile settings. (3) It exploits the strongest evidence (the 0.725 result) while reducing uncertainty about a key architectural decision, which is more informative than, e.g., swapping the image encoder (whose standalone contribution is negligible at ~0.22 accuracy) or changing aggregation (which showed near-zero difference in RNA-only: 0.650 vs 0.653).

With no prior experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: it uses the most standard and well-understood RNA encoder (PCA), the simplest profile setting (single), and a single modality. This minimizes confounding design decisions. It serves as the reference point against which I can subsequently isolate the effect of multiprofile aggregation (config_002/003), alternative RNA encoders (config_004/007), the image modality (config_010/013), and multimodal fusion (config_016/017). Starting here maximizes the information gained per experiment by anchoring all future comparisons to a well-defined, minimal baseline.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc, 46.4% F1), which is a weak baseline. We have zero information about whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. This is the most critical unknown: if image features are uninformative, the entire multimodal branch (~36 configs) is low-value, and we should focus on improving the RNA side. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest possible probe of image-modality informativeness. It uses a standard, well-validated encoder (ResNet-50) in the simplest profile setting, so any performance difference from config_001 can be attributed to the modality/encoder rather than confounding complexity from aggregation or fusion. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, resolving whether the second modality is useful at all is the highest-leverage question. A strong image-only result would justify investing in multimodal fusion configs; a weak result would redirect effort toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. It also establishes a second single-modality baseline, making future multimodal comparisons interpretable (does fusion beat the best single modality?). Changing only the modality from RNA to image keeps the comparison maximally informative with minimal confounds.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, PCA-2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while config_010 (image, ResNet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality by a wide margin. With only two data points, the key uncertainty is whether the RNA representation itself is the bottleneck—PCA is a linear, unsupervised projection, and a learned encoder (scVI) may capture nonlinear structure that PCA misses. Question tested: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while keeping model_setting=rna_only, profile_setting=singleprofile, and no aggregation, making it a clean single-variable comparison against config_001. Why this is the best next experiment: it isolates the effect of representation learning on the strongest modality. If scVI substantially improves over PCA, it signals that learned encoders are a high-value design axis and justifies further investment in scgpt/multimodal variants. If it does not, PCA is likely near the ceiling for this task and effort is better spent on profile/aggregation or fusion. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design choice before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only singleprofile experiments show scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) by ~3.5%, while image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208). We have not yet tested the third RNA encoder (scgpt) in any setting. Question: Does scgpt provide a meaningfully different (better or worse) representation than scvi_n200 in the simplest controlled setting? Why this experiment: config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_004—only the encoder changes.
