Resolving the encoder ranking before layering on multiprofile, aggregation, or fusion avoids committing multiple future experiments to a suboptimal encoder and maximizes information gain per experiment under the tight budget.

Evidence: Among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 is the clear winner (acc 0.520, F1 0.498) over pca_n2000 (0.485) and scgpt (0.411), and image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), indicating RNA dominates. All four completed experiments are singleprofile, so the effect of multiprofile is entirely untested. Question: Does multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve upon singleprofile when paired with the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200)? This directly compares to config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile), isolating the profile-setting/aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It builds on the strongest evidence (scvi_n200), tests the single most important unexplored design axis (multiprofile vs singleprofile), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to avoid confounding. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, it justifies investing in transformer aggregation and multimodal fusion; if it doesn't, it saves budget by ruling out an entire branch of configurations before committing to more complex multimodal setups.

The strongest finding so far is the large multiprofile boost: scvi_n200 goes from 0.520 (singleprofile, config_004) to 0.650 (multiprofile+avgpool, config_005), a +0.13 gain. However, we have only one multiprofile data point, so it is unclear whether this benefit is general across encoders or specific to scvi_n200. config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_001 (pca_n2000, singleprofile) by changing only the profile setting while holding encoder and aggregation fixed. If multiprofile also lifts pca_n2000, it validates multiprofile as a broadly beneficial design axis and justifies further investment (e.g., transformer aggregation in config_006). If it does not, it reveals an encoder×profile interaction that reshapes the search. This single-variable comparison is the most informative next step under a limited budget because it clarifies the scope of the largest effect observed before committing to more complex or expensive extensions.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is the strongest result at 0.650 acc, showing that multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the best RNA direction. The aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer) is a critical but untested design choice under this best encoder setting. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for scvi_n200 multiprofile? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest evidence while testing one important design decision. The result directly informs whether transformer aggregation is worth adopting in later multimodal experiments (where aggregation interacts with fusion), and it avoids the risk of jumping to multimodal settings while the RNA-side design space is not yet well characterized. It is more informative than testing scgpt multiprofile (config_008) because scgpt was already the weakest encoder in singleprofile, making it a lower-priority question.

1) Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 + transformer (config_006, acc 0.653) is the current best, and multiprofile + scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA pipeline. However, image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), leaving open the critical question of whether image features add complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. 2) Question tested: Does concatenating resnet50 image features to the best RNA multiprofile transformer model (config_006) improve validation accuracy, or does the weak image signal dilute the RNA representation? This isolates the effect of adding the image modality as a single conceptual change (image + fusion) on top of the best known RNA baseline. 3) Why best use of budget: The answer determines the entire direction of the remaining search—pursuing multimodal configs (032-051) or focusing on RNA-only refinements. Without this result, spending experiments on more complex multimodal variants risks wasting budget on a modality that may not contribute. It is the highest-information experiment available because it directly tests the core multimodal hypothesis with minimal confounds.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.688) and F1 (0.659), outperforming the best RNA-only multiprofile model (config_006, 0.653/0.628) by ~3.5 pp. However, the image-only model (config_010, resnet50) was very weak (0.208), suggesting the image modality contributes only a small complementary signal. Question: config_033 is identical to config_032 except fusion changes from concat to weighted. This isolates the fusion strategy and tests whether the image contribution is best captured by equal-weight concatenation or by learned per-modality weighting. If weighted fusion matches or exceeds concat, it indicates the image signal is small and benefits from down-weighting; if concat is clearly better, the modalities are more complementary than the weak image-only score suggests. Why best next experiment: it is a single-variable comparison directly extending the current best result, requiring no new assumptions, and it reduces uncertainty about whether the modest multimodal gain is robust to a different (and potentially more adaptive) fusion mechanism before investing budget in larger changes like a different image encoder.

Evidence: config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) is our current best at 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1, beating the best RNA-only model (config_006, 0.653) by ~6 points. However, the image modality alone with resnet50 was very weak (config_010: 0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image branch is contributing meaningful signal or merely adding noise. Question: Does a substantially stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs. resnet50) improve the multimodal model, or is the image modality's contribution limited regardless of encoder quality? config_039 changes only the image encoder relative to config_033, isolating this single variable. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean one-variable extension of our best configuration, directly tests whether the image modality has untapped representational capacity, and the answer will determine whether future budget should invest in image-encoder variants or pivot to other design axes (RNA encoder, aggregation). A large gain would validate the multimodal direction and guide further image-side exploration; a small or null gain would indicate the image modality's ceiling is low, redirecting effort to RNA-side or fusion improvements.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most important. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 is the simplest possible configuration—RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000) with no aggregation or fusion. It establishes a minimal performance floor and tells us whether the basic linear structure in the RNA data is already informative for the task. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Starting with the simplest, fastest, and most interpretable baseline is the most information-efficient use of the first budget slot. It gives a clear reference point against which every subsequent configuration (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be compared. If PCA-single-profile already performs well, we know the task is relatively easy and can focus budget on marginal gains; if it performs poorly, we know we must invest in richer representations. Choosing a more complex first experiment (e.g., scGPT or multimodal) would confound multiple design choices at once and make it harder to attribute performance to specific decisions. A cheap, simple baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 at ~48.5% accuracy), evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal at all, which determines the entire direction of the search (RNA-focused vs. image-focused vs. multimodal). config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001: it changes only the modality while keeping the profile setting (singleprofile) and architecture simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion) identical. If image-only substantially outperforms RNA-only, we should prioritize image encoders and multimodal fusion; if it underperforms, RNA is the dominant signal and we should focus on RNA encoder and profile choices. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc / 46.4% F1, while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8% acc. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, so improving its representation is the highest-priority question. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether a learned, domain-specific encoder (scvi_n200) can outperform a simple linear PCA projection, or whether PCA already captures the relevant signal. This experiment (config_004) is a clean single-variable change from config_001—only the RNA encoder changes (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200), keeping singleprofile and no aggregation/fusion—so any performance difference can be attributed to the representation choice. If scvi substantially beats PCA, it justifies investing further in learned encoders and multimodal fusion with a stronger RNA backbone; if it does not, it tells us PCA is sufficient and we should redirect budget toward profile settings, image encoders, or fusion strategies. Under the limited budget, isolating the representation effect on our strongest modality is the most informative next step before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.520) far outperform image-only (0.208), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Within RNA singleprofile, scvi_n200 (0.520) beats pca_n2000 (0.485), suggesting a learned latent representation is preferable. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile, which is a fundamental architectural decision that gates an entire branch of the search space. Question tested: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a near-minimal change from config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile), isolating the effect of multiprofile + simple average-pool aggregation. Why best next: It directly compares against the current best (config_004) with only one design axis changed, giving a clean read on whether multiprofile is worth the added complexity. If multiprofile helps, the next step is to test transformer aggregation (config_006); if it does not, we can prune the multiprofile branch and focus budget on encoder or fusion questions. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scVI_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 accuracy, a large jump over config_004 (scVI_n200, singleprofile) at 0.520, confirming that multi-profile with aggregation is highly beneficial. However, we only have one data point on aggregation (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) further improves over simple average pooling, or whether avgpool already captures most of the multi-profile benefit. This experiment (config_006: scVI_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005—only the aggregation changes. It directly isolates the effect of aggregation method while holding encoder and profile setting fixed. Under a limited budget, resolving whether transformer aggregation adds value over avgpool is critical because the answer propagates to every future multimodal or multiprofile experiment, making this the highest-information next step.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the clear winner so far (config_005/006 at ~0.65), and the multiprofile effect is large (~0.13 gain over singleprofile). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) makes negligible difference. The image modality appears weak (resnet50 image-only at 0.208). Uncertainty: We have not tested whether scgpt, a more specialized RNA foundation-model encoder, can outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) by changing only the RNA encoder, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next: This is a single-variable, high-information experiment in the most promising region. If scgpt improves, we gain a new best and a direction to extend into multimodal; if it matches or lags, we confirm scvi_n200 is near-optimal and can redirect budget toward testing whether a better image encoder (ViT-L) or multimodal fusion adds value on top of the RNA signal. It avoids the risk of spending a run on a multimodal config that adds complexity while the RNA encoder question remains open.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear current best (0.653 acc, config_006), with aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) making negligible difference. Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208), raising the question of whether image features can add complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. The biggest open uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion can push beyond the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. This experiment tests that directly: it pairs the best-validated RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with the already-characterized resnet50 image encoder and uses simple concat fusion. By holding the image encoder to resnet50 (the only one we've seen), we isolate the fusion question without confounding with an untested image backbone. If multimodal helps, the next step is to try ViT-L; if it does not, we learn that image features (at least at this quality level) are not complementary to the RNA signal, redirecting effort toward RNA-side improvements. This is the highest-information next experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the current best at 0.688 acc, outperforming the best RNA-only config_006 (0.653) by ~3.5 points, confirming the image modality adds value. However, we have only tested concat fusion; weighted fusion remains entirely untested. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform concat in the multimodal setting, or is concat already near-optimal? This experiment changes exactly one variable (fusion: concat→weighted) relative to config_032, giving a clean A/B comparison that isolates the fusion method effect. Why this is the best next step: Under a limited budget, testing the fusion strategy at the current best configuration is the most efficient way to either (a) find a free improvement that lifts the ceiling for all future multimodal experiments, or (b) confirm concat is sufficient and redirect effort toward other levers (image encoder, aggregation). It avoids the risk of changing multiple variables simultaneously and directly reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice before scaling to more complex configurations.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (scVI + ResNet50 + multiprofile + transformer + weighted) at 0.713 acc. The image modality is very weak alone (ResNet50 single: 0.208) yet adds ~6 points in the multimodal setting, suggesting it carries complementary signal. Key uncertainty: is the image encoder quality (ResNet50) the bottleneck limiting how much the image contributes, or is the signal inherently limited? Question: config_039 is identical to config_033 except the image encoder is swapped from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L, isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why best next: It is a clean single-variable extension of the best-performing configuration, directly testing whether a stronger image encoder unlocks more multimodal gain. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it confirms the image modality has untapped signal and justifies further image-encoder investment; if not, it tells us the image contribution is near its ceiling and effort should shift to RNA-side improvements or fusion strategy. This is more informative than testing aggregation (avgpool vs transformer showed negligible difference in RNA-only) or fusion (weighted already beats concat by ~2.5 pts).

Evidence: The current best is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725). We have strong evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat in multimodal (config_033: 0.713 vs config_032: 0.688 with resnet50, a ~2.5% gap). However, we have not tested whether this fusion advantage holds with the VIT image encoder, which produces a different representation geometry. Question: config_038 (identical to config_039 except fusion=concat) isolates the single variable of fusion type under the best-performing image encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean one-variable comparison with the current best, directly testing whether the weighted-fusion advantage generalizes across image encoders. If concat approaches weighted with VIT, it suggests the VIT representation is more naturally aligned and a simpler fusion suffices (practical simplification). If the gap persists or widens, it confirms weighted fusion is a robust, encoder-independent design choice and we can confidently exploit it in all future multimodal configurations. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces uncertainty about a key architectural decision without changing multiple factors simultaneously.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit; the priority is to establish a reliable performance baseline at minimal cost. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: it uses a standard linear dimensionality reduction, a single profile, and no learned encoder, making it fast to train and interpret. Running this first gives us a reference accuracy/F1 against which every subsequent design choice (multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders like scVI or scGPT, image modality, and fusion strategy) can be measured for marginal benefit. Because the budget is limited, starting from the cheapest baseline maximizes the number of informative comparisons we can still afford, and it lets us later isolate the effect of each added component (e.g., comparing config_001 vs config_002 to isolate multiprofile+avgpool, or config_001 vs config_016 to isolate adding an image modality with concat fusion) without confounding multiple changes.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), giving us a weak RNA-only baseline and essentially no information about whether the image modality is informative. Uncertainty: The most critical open question is whether image features carry complementary or superior signal relative to RNA. Question tested: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the modality effect by matching config_001 on profile_setting (singleprofile) while switching to the simplest image encoder (resnet50). This is a clean single-variable comparison (RNA vs. image modality). Why this is the best next step: Under a tight budget, knowing whether image is a viable modality determines the entire downstream search strategy—if image is strong, we prioritize image/multimodal configs; if weak, we focus on RNA encoder and profile improvements. Testing a multimodal config now would confound modality, fusion, and aggregation effects, making the result harder to interpret. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-leverage design decision.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no evidence on whether the profile/aggregation axis (single vs. multiprofile with pooling) improves performance. This experiment (config_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly compares to config_001 by changing only the profile setting and adding avgpool aggregation, isolating the effect of multi-profile representation with a simple, interpretable aggregator. It is the best next step because (1) it keeps the encoder fixed (pca_n2000) for a clean single-axis comparison, (2) the multiprofile+aggregation decision is a structural prerequisite that gates all downstream multimodal multiprofile experiments (configs 018–021, 030–033, etc.), so resolving it early maximizes information value for the remaining budget, and (3) avgpool is the simplest aggregation, giving a conservative baseline before testing transformer aggregation.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, the best result so far, substantially outperforming the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). However, the singleprofile→multiprofile jump also introduced an aggregation step, so we cannot yet tell whether the gain comes from the multiprofile representation itself or from the aggregation mechanism. Question: config_003 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, transformer) directly compares transformer aggregation against avgpool while holding all other factors constant, isolating the effect of the aggregation method. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-variable comparison against our current best, requires no new encoders or modalities, and tells us whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) is worth the added complexity before we invest budget in learned encoders (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion. If transformer significantly beats avgpool, it signals that richer aggregation is a key design lever; if not, we can focus budget on encoder choice and multimodal combinations with confidence that simple averaging suffices.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile+avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best so far, while image-only ResNet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak. The critical open question is whether the image modality provides complementary information when fused with the strong RNA signal, or whether it merely adds noise. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the minimal extension of config_002: it holds RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical and introduces only the image branch and concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding the image modality. If it fails to beat 0.591, we learn that ResNet50 image features are not complementary and can redirect budget toward better RNA encoders or a stronger image encoder (ViT-L). If it does help, it confirms the multimodal direction and justifies further fusion-architecture exploration. Under a tight budget, resolving whether multimodal is worthwhile at all is the highest-value single experiment.

Evidence: RNA (PCA n2000) dominates over image (ResNet50) by a wide margin (0.591 vs 0.208), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~0.028). The best RNA-only config (config_002: multi-profile, avgpool) achieves 0.591, but we have no evidence yet about whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) can capture nonlinear structure that PCA misses. Question: Does scvi_n200 improve over PCA n2000 in the same RNA-only, multi-profile, avgpool setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002, isolating the RNA encoder effect without confounding from image or fusion choices. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA is the dominant signal source, so understanding whether a learned encoder can push RNA-only performance above 0.591 is the highest-leverage question. If scvi helps here, it will likely compound in the multimodal setting; if it does not, we can rule out RNA encoder complexity as a bottleneck and focus budget on image or fusion improvements. This avoids the risk of changing the RNA encoder in the already-complex multimodal setting where a small effect could be masked by other factors.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, showing that scvi_n200 with avgpool aggregation is the strongest RNA configuration. Separately, config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 shows a modest boost over its RNA-only counterpart config_002 (0.591), suggesting image adds ~3 pts with a weaker RNA encoder. Uncertainty: We do not know whether adding ResNet50 image still helps when the RNA side is already strong (scvi_n200), or whether the weak image signal (image-only acc only 0.208) becomes irrelevant or even detrimental. Question tested: Does the multimodal fusion of scvi_n200 (best RNA) + ResNet50 (best tested image) with avgpool and concat outperform the RNA-only scvi_n200 baseline? This is a single-variable extension of config_005 (adding the image modality), isolating the marginal contribution of image given an optimal RNA pipeline. Why best use of budget: The answer directly determines whether to invest remaining experiments in multimodal variants (configs 031-051) or to focus on RNA-only encoder/aggregation refinements. It is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the central design question—does multimodality add value on top of the best unimodal model—before committing to a large family of multimodal configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder (config_005: 0.650 acc vs config_002: 0.591 for pca_n2000), avgpool beats transformer for aggregation, and multiprofile beats singleprofile. Surprisingly, adding resnet50 image with concat fusion to the scvi_n200 multimodal model (config_030: 0.632) slightly underperforms the RNA-only version (config_005: 0.650), whereas with pca_n2000 the multimodal concat helped (config_018: 0.619 > config_002: 0.591). This suggests the concat fusion may be the bottleneck when the RNA signal is already strong. Question: Does weighted fusion resolve the multimodal underperformance with scvi_n200? config_031 changes only the fusion strategy (concat→weighted) relative to config_030, giving a clean A/B test of fusion. Why this is best: it isolates a single design variable, directly addresses the most surprising finding (multimodal < unimodal with the best encoder), and determines whether the image modality is salvageable with better fusion or fundamentally unhelpful—critical information before investing further experiments in multimodal variants.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (scvi_n200 rna_only: 0.650 vs image_only resnet50: 0.208), and within RNA, scvi_n200 with avgpool aggregation is the best tested encoder (0.650 vs pca_n2000's 0.591). However, scgpt has been completely untested, leaving a major uncertainty about whether a different RNA representation could outperform scvi_n200. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (same setup but scvi_n200), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA is the primary signal source, so the encoder choice is the highest-leverage design decision. Resolving whether scgpt is competitive with or superior to scvi_n200 before committing further experiments to multimodal scgpt variants (configs 042-051) avoids wasting budget on a potentially inferior encoder. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new high-value direction; if not, we can confidently focus remaining experiments on optimizing the scvi_n200 pipeline (e.g., testing imagenet_vit_l as image encoder in the multimodal setting).

Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, resnet50) at 0.678 acc. A critical unknown remains: we have only tested resnet50 as the image encoder, and image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208), suggesting the image features may be a bottleneck. The ViT-L encoder is completely untested. Question: config_037 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l relative to config_031, providing a clean single-variable test of whether a stronger image representation improves the best-known multimodal configuration. Why best next: This is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve. If ViT-L substantially improves performance, it opens a new promising direction; if it does not, it tells us the image modality is inherently limited and we should focus optimization on the RNA side. Either outcome significantly reduces uncertainty about the most important remaining design axis (image encoder quality) while staying in the most promising region of the search space.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about baseline performance for any modality, encoder, or profile setting. The most critical uncertainty is the absolute performance scale of the primary modality (RNA) under the simplest, most standard configuration. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000) establishes the simplest possible RNA baseline. It isolates the contribution of the RNA modality with a fast, well-understood linear representation and no aggregation or fusion complexity, giving a clean reference point against which all later RNA-encoder choices (scvi, scgpt), profile settings (multiprofile + aggregation), and multimodal fusion can be measured. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first run should be the fastest to execute and the most informative as a calibration anchor. PCA-2000 with a single profile is computationally cheap, minimizes confounding variables, and directly answers 'how well does the primary modality perform at baseline?'—information needed before investing in more expensive image or multimodal runs. It also serves as the control for every subsequent RNA-encoder comparison (configs 004, 007) and profile-setting comparison (configs 002, 003), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice at this stage.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical open question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-axis comparison: it mirrors config_001's simplicity (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion) while swapping the modality. This establishes the image-only baseline, which is essential before interpreting any multimodal result—without it, we cannot tell whether a multimodal configuration is genuinely benefiting from fusion or simply performing at the RNA-only level. It also isolates the effect of the image encoder (ResNet50) without confounding from aggregation or fusion choices. Under a tight budget, securing both unimodal baselines before testing fusion is the highest-information-per-experiment strategy.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA-2000) achieves 48.5% acc / 46.4% F1, while config_010 (image-only, singleprofile, ResNet50) is very weak at 20.8% acc. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, and the PCA encoder is a simple linear baseline. Uncertainty: We do not know whether a learned nonlinear RNA encoder (scVI, 200-dim latent) can meaningfully improve over PCA, which is a fundamental representation question that will affect all downstream multimodal decisions. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates exactly one variable—RNA encoder—against the config_001 baseline, keeping profile setting and modality identical. If scVI substantially outperforms PCA, it justifies investing budget in scVI-based multimodal configs; if not, PCA remains the efficient choice and we can redirect exploration toward profile/aggregation or image-side improvements. Under a tight budget, this clean A/B comparison on the strongest modality maximizes information gained per experiment.

Evidence: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieved 0.520 acc vs config_001 (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 0.485, showing learned RNA representations beat linear ones. config_010 (resnet50 image-only) at 0.208 confirms image is currently weak. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested scgpt, a third learned RNA encoder, and the encoder choice is foundational for all subsequent multiprofile and multimodal experiments. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the same singleprofile, rna_only setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only the RNA encoder changes from config_004). Why this is best: Completing the encoder ranking (pca < scvi vs scgpt) before introducing additional variables (multiprofile, aggregation, fusion) ensures that all future experiments build on the best-known RNA representation. If scgpt is substantially better, it reshapes the entire search strategy; if comparable, it confirms scvi_n200 as the default and we can next isolate the multiprofile/aggregation question with confidence.

Evidence: Among single-profile RNA encoders, scvi_n200 is the clear best (acc=0.520, F1=0.498), outperforming pca_n2000 (0.485) and scgpt (0.411). Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208), making multimodal fusion with resnet50 risky. We have zero data on multiprofile or aggregation effects. Question: Does moving from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve upon the best single-profile RNA result (scvi_n200)? This directly extends our strongest configuration along the profile/aggregation axis while holding the encoder fixed. Why this is best: It isolates the effect of multiprofile+aggregation on the best-known encoder, uses the simplest aggregation as a conservative baseline, and the outcome will gate whether the entire multiprofile branch (including multimodal multiprofile configs) is worth further budget. Testing multimodal now would confound the image-modality weakness with the profile/aggregation question.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder (0.520 singleprofile vs 0.485 pca, 0.411 scgpt), and switching to multiprofile+avgpool produced a large jump to 0.650 acc (config_005), the best result so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether transformer aggregation could further improve (or degrade) performance. This experiment (config_006: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) isolates the aggregation variable while holding the best-performing encoder and profile setting constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because (1) it directly extends the strongest evidence by testing a logical single-variable change, (2) the answer will inform whether avgpool or transformer should be used in all subsequent multimodal experiments, and (3) it avoids confounding by not changing encoder, profile, or modality simultaneously.

Evidence: The largest gain so far comes from switching to multi-profile with scVI_n200 (0.520→0.650, +13 pts), while PCA_n2000 single-profile scores 0.485 and scGPT single-profile scores 0.411. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference with scVI. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multi-profile gain is a general property of having more biological profiles (i.e., more information per cell) or is specific to scVI's learned latent representation. This experiment (PCA_n2000, multi-profile, avgpool) fills in the encoder×profile 2×2 grid: if PCA also jumps substantially, the gain is profile-driven and any encoder benefits; if PCA shows little improvement, the gain is representation-specific to scVI. This cleanly isolates one variable (encoder) against the already-established multi-profile setting, making it the most informative single experiment under budget constraints before committing to multimodal or alternative encoders.

Evidence: RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile + transformer (config_006) is our best result at 0.653 acc, while image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. The critical open question is whether multimodal fusion adds value or merely injects noise from the weak image branch. Config_032 takes our best-validated RNA pipeline (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) and adds the simplest image component (resnet50, concat fusion), directly testing whether complementary image signal improves over the RNA-only ceiling. If accuracy exceeds ~0.653, multimodal is a promising direction and we can then optimize the image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion strategy. If it drops below 0.653, it indicates resnet50 image features are net noise, prompting a test of ViT-L before further multimodal investment. This is the highest-information single experiment because it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty—whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all—while exploiting our strongest RNA evidence rather than re-testing lower-priority questions like aggregation for PCA or scgpt in multiprofile.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.688 acc, a ~3.5% gain over RNA-only multiprofile (0.653). However, image-only with resnet50 is very poor (0.208 acc), raising the question of whether resnet50 is a bottleneck limiting the image's contribution in fusion. Question: config_038 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings identical to config_032, cleanly isolating the effect of image encoder quality on multimodal performance. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable comparison to our current best, tests a high-impact design decision (whether a stronger image representation unlocks substantially more complementary signal), and the answer will determine whether further investment in image encoder quality is worthwhile or whether the image modality's contribution is fundamentally limited regardless of encoder choice. This is more informative than testing minor architectural variants (e.g., concat vs. weighted fusion) under the current budget constraints.

Evidence: config_038 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + concat, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.7207 acc, and all multimodal results so far use concat fusion. We have no data on whether weighted fusion could improve or degrade performance relative to concat under the best-known representation settings. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the fusion-strategy effect with a single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (best RNA encoder, best image encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) while testing the one untested design axis at that operating point. A clear win or loss on fusion method will either yield an immediate performance gain or confirm concat suffices, freeing the next budget slot to probe aggregation or image-encoder contribution. This is more informative than, e.g., testing avgpool (already near-equivalent to transformer in RNA-only) or a weaker RNA encoder, both of which have lower expected information gain per experiment.

No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence and maximum uncertainty across all design axes (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion). The most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000). This establishes a clear performance floor with the least number of learned or architectural parameters (PCA is a fixed linear projection, no image branch, no aggregation, no fusion). It isolates the raw RNA signal quality and gives a reference against which every subsequent experiment—adding an image modality, switching to scVI/scGPT, enabling multiprofile with aggregation, or introducing fusion—can be directly compared. Choosing this minimal baseline first avoids confounding: if later multimodal or multiprofile configurations outperform it, we can attribute the gain to the added complexity rather than to an untested encoder choice. It is the best use of the first budget slot because it maximizes the interpretability of all future comparisons.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, PCA, singleprofile → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean, single-variable test: it holds profile setting constant (singleprofile) and swaps the modality from RNA to image, using a standard pretrained encoder. If image features yield substantially higher accuracy, it strongly motivates exploring the multimodal branch (configs 016–051) and justifies budget there. If image features perform comparably or worse, it indicates the bottleneck is representation quality within a single modality, redirecting budget toward better RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the single highest-level design decision (modality contribution) before committing budget to more complex fusion/aggregation choices.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while config_010 (image, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8%, a ~28-point gap. This leaves major uncertainty about whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative or simply poorly encoded by resnet50. Question: config_013 swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a larger, ViT-based architecture), keeping everything else identical to config_010. This isolates the effect of image representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion (configs 016-051) or multiprofile/aggregation strategies, we need to know whether the image modality can be made competitive. If imagenet_vit_l substantially closes the gap, multimodal experiments become high-value and we should prioritize them. If it does not, we can deprioritize image and multimodal paths and focus budget on RNA encoder improvements (scvi_n200, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. This single-variable change maximally reduces strategic uncertainty with one experiment.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 acc, far exceeding both image-only baselines (~0.21-0.23), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA) in one profile setting, leaving it unclear whether the 0.485 ceiling is due to the linear PCA representation or is inherent to the RNA signal. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the effect of the RNA encoder (learned nonlinear latent representation vs. linear PCA) while holding profile setting constant. Why this is best: The encoder choice is the most fundamental design decision—it will influence every downstream multimodal and multiprofile experiment. If scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, it signals that learned representations are critical and justifies investing in scgpt and multimodal variants with better encoders. If it performs similarly or worse, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects the search toward profile/aggregation/fusion. This single experiment reduces the most consequential uncertainty with minimal confounding, making it the highest-information next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.520) dominate image-only models (0.208–0.227) by a wide margin, and scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) by ~3.5 acc points. All completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile axis is entirely unexplored. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve on the best singleprofile RNA configuration (config_004, scvi_n200, 0.520)? Why this is the best next step: config_005 changes exactly one variable (singleprofile→multiprofile with avgpool) from the current best configuration, isolating the profile-setting effect while holding the RNA encoder at its proven-best value. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, a follow-up can test transformer aggregation; if it does not, we avoid spending budget on more complex aggregation schemes. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk experiment given the current evidence.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, 0.520), confirming multiprofile + scvi_n200 as the strongest direction. However, only avgpool aggregation has been tested; transformer aggregation is unexplored. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for combining multiple RNA profiles with the scvi_n200 encoder? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005), isolating the effect of aggregation strategy. Why best next: (1) It directly extends the current best configuration along the most important untested design axis within the proven RNA-multiprofile regime. (2) The aggregation choice will propagate to all future multimodal experiments, so resolving it now reduces uncertainty for the entire remaining search. (3) It avoids the risk of simultaneously introducing image modality (which is currently very weak at ~0.21-0.23) and fusion, which would confound interpretation. (4) It is a high-information experiment: if transformer >> avgpool, we gain a clear upgrade path; if they are similar, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can confidently move to multimodal with avgpool.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 yields the best results (0.650-0.653), a large jump over singleprofile scvi (0.520) and singleprofile pca (0.485). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) is negligible (~0.3%). Uncertainty: We do not know whether the multiprofile gain is a general property of multi-view profiling or is specifically enabled by the learned scvi representation. This experiment (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool) directly isolates the encoder effect in the multiprofile regime by holding profile setting and aggregation fixed while swapping scvi→pca. If pca+multiprofile approaches 0.65, the encoder is secondary and simpler pipelines suffice; if it drops substantially, learned encoders are essential for multiprofile to work. This is the highest-information single comparison available: it clarifies the encoder×profile interaction in the performance-critical regime before investing budget in multimodal or scgpt variants that build on an untested assumption about which encoder to use.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, with config_006 (transformer aggregation) essentially matching it at 0.653. Image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227), and the scvi_n200 encoder clearly outperforms pca_n2000 in both single- and multi-profile settings. However, the scgpt encoder has not been tested at all, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of which RNA representation is best. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005—the only difference is the RNA encoder (scgpt vs. scvi_n200), while profile setting and aggregation are held at their best-known values. This directly tests whether scgpt is competitive with or superior to scvi_n200 in the multiprofile regime where gains are largest. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It resolves a major uncertainty about encoder choice before committing budget to multimodal or further aggregation experiments, since the encoder decision will affect all downstream multimodal configurations. (2) It follows the principle of isolating one variable: only the encoder changes relative to the current best. (3) If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising branch; if it falls well short, we can confidently rule it out and focus remaining budget on multimodal fusion with scvi_n200. (4) Given that avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly equivalent for scvi_n200, using avgpool here avoids confounding the encoder question with the aggregation choice.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: config_006, scvi_n200/multiprofile/transformer at 0.653), while image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23), suggesting image features carry little standalone signal. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the image modality provides any complementary information when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment (config_039) directly tests that question by combining the best-known RNA setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with the best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) using weighted fusion, which is appropriate given the large modality strength imbalance. If it exceeds 0.653, multimodal fusion is worthwhile and we can explore fusion strategies; if it does not, we can confidently focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the central design question (is multimodality useful here?) with the strongest available components, rather than testing a weaker combination that would be harder to interpret.

The best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted fusion, acc=0.7250), which shows a substantial ~7-point gain over the best RNA-only multi-profile model (0.6530). However, we have no direct comparison of fusion strategy in the multimodal setting. Config_038 is identical to config_039 except it uses concat instead of weighted fusion, isolating exactly one variable. This tells us whether the multimodal gain requires learned cross-modal weighting or whether a simple concatenation suffices. Understanding this is critical: if concat performs comparably, the design space simplifies considerably; if weighted fusion is clearly superior, it indicates the two modalities contribute non-uniformly and the interaction is informative. Under a limited budget, this single-variable A/B test against the current best configuration is the highest-information-per-experiment choice, directly informing whether to invest further in fusion complexity or shift attention to other design axes (e.g., image encoder choice).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero prior information about any design axis (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion). The most critical unknown is whether the basic RNA signal alone provides any useful classification performance, and what magnitude of accuracy to expect. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable baseline. It isolates the question 'does a linear 2000-dim PCA reduction of single-profile RNA data yield meaningful signal?' without confounding from learned encoders, image data, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Establishing this minimal baseline is the standard and most information-efficient first step in sequential design. It is computationally cheap (PCA is fast, no image pipeline), provides a reference point against which every subsequent experiment (learned encoders, multiprofile, image, multimodal) can be compared, and helps calibrate the performance landscape before investing budget in more complex configurations. Without this anchor, later comparisons would lack a clear attribution of where gains (or losses) originate.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries meaningful signal for this task at all. This is the most consequential design decision: it determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and which branch of the configuration space to prioritize. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001—same profile setting, same structural simplicity (no aggregation/fusion needed)—isolating the effect of modality. If image-only substantially outperforms RNA-only, multimodal fusion configs become high-priority; if it underperforms, we should invest in RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) instead. ResNet50 is a standard, well-calibrated image encoder appropriate for a first modality probe. Under a tight budget, resolving which modality is stronger before committing to complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations is the highest-information-value next step.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8% acc, making RNA the clearly dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA encoder tested (linear PCA). Question: Does a learned, biologically-informed RNA representation (scvi_n200) outperform linear PCA in capturing task-relevant structure? This is a clean single-variable change from config_001 (same model_setting, same profile_setting, only encoder differs), isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why best next experiment: Since RNA is the stronger modality, improving its representation has the highest expected payoff. If scvi_n200 improves over PCA, it validates learned representations and makes the many multimodal scvi configurations (config_028-039) high-value follow-ups. If it does not improve, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward multiprofile/aggregation or fusion design. This single experiment reduces the largest current uncertainty about the most impactful design axis.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520) clearly outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) for single-profile RNA, and image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), suggesting RNA is the dominant signal. The multiprofile design axis is completely untested. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (with simple avgpool) improve upon the best single-profile RNA result (config_004, scvi_n200, 0.520)? This isolates the multiprofile effect using the strongest encoder identified so far and the simplest aggregation, avoiding confounds from transformer aggregation or a weaker encoder. Why best next: Multiprofile is the largest untested structural axis; resolving whether it adds value (or not) with a clean, minimal change from config_004 will either open a promising direction for further exploitation (aggregation type, fusion) or allow us to deprioritize it and focus budget on encoder improvements or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: The strongest signal so far is the large jump from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_005: 0.650 vs config_004: 0.520, +13 pp), and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is sufficient or whether a transformer-based aggregation can further exploit the multiprofile structure. Question: config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, changing only the aggregation method. This isolates the effect of aggregation while holding the best-performing encoder and profile setting fixed. Rationale: Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because (a) it directly exploits the strongest observed direction (multiprofile + scvi), (b) it tests whether the current best can be improved along the aggregation axis, and (c) the answer determines whether all subsequent multiprofile experiments (including any multimodal ones) should use avgpool or transformer, saving future compute and guiding the search efficiently.

We now have three of four cells in a critical 2×2 factorial (encoder × profile): pca-single (0.485), scvi-single (0.520), and scvi-multiprofile (0.650–0.653). The missing cell is pca-multiprofile (config_002). This experiment directly tests whether the large multiprofile gain (~13 pts) is a general property of multi-profile aggregation or is specifically enabled by scvi_n200's learned latent representation. If pca-multiprofile also reaches ~0.65, the profile setting dominates and encoder choice becomes secondary; if it stays near ~0.50, the interaction between encoder and profile is the key driver, and future experiments should prioritize encoder selection. Resolving this interaction is the highest-information next step because it determines whether subsequent budget should be spent exploring new encoders (scgpt) in multiprofile, exploring multimodal fusion, or other directions. It also avoids changing multiple factors at once (only encoder differs from the best config_005, with aggregation held at avgpool where the transformer gain was negligible).

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile models dominate (0.59–0.65), with scvi_n200 consistently outperforming pca_n2000, and image-only models are very weak (0.21). Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has minimal impact (~0.003). Uncertainty: We have not tested scgpt, the third available RNA encoder, and it is unclear whether it can match or exceed scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting. This experiment (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, acc=0.650), isolating the encoder effect while holding profile and aggregation constant. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, it opens a new high-performing direction for subsequent multimodal experiments; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the best encoder and can redirect budget toward testing whether multimodal fusion or a stronger image encoder (ViT) adds value. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves a key untested design axis at the current performance frontier without conflating multiple changes.

Evidence: RNA-only experiments clearly establish that scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the best RNA configuration (config_006: 0.653 acc, transformer aggregation; config_005: 0.650, avgpool). The image modality is unexplored beyond a weak resnet50 baseline (config_010: 0.208 acc). The biggest remaining design uncertainty is whether adding image features via fusion can complement the strong RNA signal or will only add noise. This experiment (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) directly tests that question by pairing the best RNA setup with a stronger image encoder (ViT-L vs. the weak ResNet50) and a simple concat fusion. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it resolves the highest-impact unknown—whether multimodal fusion adds value at all—before committing further experiments to the multimodal space; (2) it uses a direct comparison to config_006 (same RNA encoder, profile, and aggregation) so the effect of adding image is isolated; (3) choosing ViT-L over ResNet50 avoids confounding a negative result with a known-weak image encoder, making the outcome more interpretable; and (4) the result will inform whether to invest remaining budget in tuning fusion strategy, image encoder, or aggregation in the multimodal setting.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI_n200, ViT_L, transformer, concat) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.721) so far, a ~7-point gain over the best RNA-only config (0.653). However, we have no evidence about whether the concat fusion is optimal or whether the two modalities have asymmetric information content that a weighted fusion could exploit. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of fusion strategy. This tells us whether the modalities contribute equally (concat sufficient) or unequally (weighted better), which is a fundamental design decision for all future multimodal experiments. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a minimal single-variable change from the current best configuration, directly comparable to config_038, and resolves an important uncertainty about how to combine modalities before investing further experiments in other design axes (aggregation, image encoder choice, or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, this clean A/B comparison maximizes information per experiment.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The multimodal configs (038/039) show a large jump from the best RNA-only result (0.653) to ~0.725, but we have only one image-only data point (ResNet50, single-profile, 0.208), which tells us almost nothing about how well the ViT-L encoder captures useful signal. We cannot yet decompose whether the multimodal gain comes from genuinely complementary image information or merely from a larger model. 2) What this tests: config_015 (image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer) isolates the image modality with the same strong encoder used in the top multimodal configs, directly measuring how much predictive signal the image carries independently. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, this single-variable test reduces the largest remaining uncertainty—whether the image branch is contributing real information or is a dead weight. If ViT-L image-only is strong (>0.5), the multimodal gain is partly additive image information and we should invest in image-side improvements; if it remains weak, the multimodal gain likely comes from cross-modal interaction, guiding us toward fusion/aggregation refinements. This knowledge is prerequisite for making informed exploitation decisions in subsequent experiments, making it more informative than marginal tweaks (e.g., concat vs weighted) that show only ~0.4% differences.

No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. The most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 (config_001). This establishes a performance floor using a fast, reliable linear encoder and a single profile, with no aggregation or fusion complexity. It serves as the reference against which all subsequent experiments can be compared to isolate the marginal contribution of multiprofile, learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), the image modality, aggregation strategies, and fusion methods. Starting here minimizes the risk of a failed or confounded first run and maximizes the interpretability of every later comparison, making it the best use of the first budget slot under complete uncertainty.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most fundamental uncertainty in a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this: it matches config_001 in profile setting (singleprofile) and overall simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion), changing only the modality from RNA to image. If image-only accuracy is close to or exceeds 48.5%, it confirms that image features are a viable signal source and justifies investing budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If it is substantially lower, we learn that RNA is the dominant modality and can focus subsequent experiments on RNA encoder/aggregation choices rather than fusion strategies. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-level design axis (modality) before committing budget to more granular questions like encoder choice, aggregation, or fusion type.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant signal, while config_010 (image-only, resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, indicating the image modality is currently a weak or uninformative source. This leaves the RNA-side design choices as the highest-leverage area to explore. Question: config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly tests whether moving from a single profile to multiple profiles with average-pool aggregation improves RNA classification, while holding the encoder (pca_n2000) constant. This isolates the profile/aggregation effect in a clean A/B comparison against config_001. Why this is the best next step: Under a tight budget, understanding whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile is a prerequisite for interpreting all downstream multimodal and multiprofile configurations (configs 018-051). If multiprofile does not help the RNA baseline, many complex configurations can be deprioritized; if it does, we gain a strong prior for which aggregation strategies to pair with fusion. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty about a design axis that affects the majority of remaining configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a substantial +10.6 pt gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). This strongly indicates that multiprofile aggregation is the key lever for RNA performance. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for the same encoder and profile setting. Question tested: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and rna_encoder identical to config_002, cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it is a single-variable comparison extending the strongest finding, (2) the answer directly determines which aggregation to carry into all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 020/021, 026/027, etc.), (3) it is low-risk since RNA already performs well, and (4) under a limited budget, resolving the aggregation choice before adding modality complexity avoids confounding multiple design decisions simultaneously.

Evidence: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.591, F1 0.573), substantially outperforming the single-profile baseline (config_001, 0.485) and the transformer aggregation (config_003, 0.519). Image-only models are very weak (0.208). The only RNA encoder tested is PCA (linear, 2000-dim). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the RNA representation itself is a meaningful design lever, or whether the profile/aggregation choices dominate. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable change from config_002, swapping the linear PCA encoder for a learned non-linear variational representation at 200 dimensions. This isolates the effect of RNA encoder while holding the best-known profile and aggregation fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: If scvi_n200 matches or beats PCA, it reveals that learned representations add value and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal combinations. If it underperforms PCA, it strongly suggests the linear structure is sufficient, allowing us to rule out an entire family of configurations (005–009 and their multimodal counterparts) and redirect budget toward fusion or image-encoder questions. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core design axis with a single experiment.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.650) while image-only with ResNet50 is very weak (0.208). Within RNA, multiprofile+avgpool is the best profile/aggregation combo, and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 by ~6% (0.650 vs 0.591) under identical settings. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested the third RNA encoder (scGPT) under the same favorable conditions, so we do not know whether scGPT could surpass scvi_n200 or whether scvi_n200 is already near the encoder ceiling. Question tested: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) isolates the encoder variable while holding profile and aggregation fixed, giving a direct scGPT-vs-scvi_n200 comparison. Why best next: The RNA encoder is the highest-leverage design choice given RNA's dominance; resolving it before investing in multimodal or image-encoder experiments prevents committing budget to a suboptimal base representation. A clean single-variable comparison also yields the most interpretable evidence for all downstream fusion decisions.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multi-profile + avgpool (config_005, 0.650) is the clear current best, and with PCA-2000, avgpool beat transformer by ~7 points (0.591 vs 0.519). However, scvi_n200 produces a learned nonlinear latent representation, so the aggregation interaction may differ. Question: Does the avgpool-over-transformer advantage hold for scvi_n200, or does the richer learned representation benefit from transformer-based aggregation? This is a clean single-variable comparison (config_005 vs config_006, only aggregation changes). Why best next: It definitively resolves the aggregation choice for the top-performing encoder, which will inform every subsequent experiment (including multimodal fusion). If avgpool remains superior, we can lock in that design and focus remaining budget on the more impactful question of whether multimodal fusion adds value. If transformer surprisingly helps, it opens a new promising direction. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision with minimal confounding.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.48–0.65) vastly outperform image-only (0.21), and the best RNA config is scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (0.650). The critical open question is whether adding the image modality via fusion can complement the strong RNA signal or will dilute it. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests that question with the simplest fusion (concat) and the same image encoder (resnet50) already characterized in isolation. If it beats 0.650, multimodal fusion is a promising direction and we can then explore better image encoders (ViT-L) and weighted fusion. If it underperforms, we learn that the weak image features (0.208 standalone) do not contribute useful complementary signal, saving budget from exploring the many multimodal variants. This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design decision (modality combination) before committing budget to finer-grained fusion/encoder variations.

Evidence: config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored 0.632, which is notably below the RNA-only scvi_n200 baselines (config_005: 0.650, config_006: 0.653), suggesting that naive concat fusion of a weak image modality (image-only resnet50: 0.208) actively hurts performance. Question: Does weighted fusion, which can down-weight the weaker image branch, recover the RNA-only performance or even exceed it? config_031 is identical to config_030 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating fusion as the sole variable. Why this is the best next step: It is the cleanest single-variable comparison available to determine whether resnet50 image carries any salvageable signal in a multimodal setting. If weighted fusion still underperforms RNA-only, we can confidently deprioritize resnet50-based multimodal configs and redirect budget toward RNA-only refinement or a stronger image encoder (ViT-L). If it recovers to ~0.65+, it justifies further multimodal exploration with resnet50. This single experiment resolves a critical fork in the search strategy under limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_031 (multimodal, scVI_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. However, the image-only ResNet50 baseline was extremely weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality is contributing meaningful signal or merely adding noise that the weighted fusion partially compensates for. Question: config_037 isolates a single variable—upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L—while keeping the rest of the pipeline identical to config_031 (scVI_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether a stronger visual representation unlocks additional signal from the image modality. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean one-factor comparison against our current best, so any performance change can be attributed to image encoder quality. (2) The answer has high strategic value: if ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, the image modality is a genuine contributor and further multimodal exploration is warranted; if it does not, we can conclude the image channel is not informative and redirect budget toward RNA-side improvements. (3) It avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously (unlike config_039, which would also change aggregation), preserving interpretability under a tight budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or fusion strategy contributes most to validation accuracy. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration—single modality, single profile, linear PCA encoder with no aggregation or fusion. It establishes a clean performance floor for the RNA signal alone, with no confounding from image features, learned encoders, multi-profile aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first experiment should be fast, interpretable, and set a reference against which every subsequent design choice can be measured. PCA is computationally trivial, singleprofile avoids aggregation complexity, and rna_only isolates one modality. This baseline lets me attribute any future gain unambiguously to adding image features, a learned encoder, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion. It also minimizes risk of a failed or ambiguous run, preserving budget for more informative follow-up comparisons (e.g., config_010 for image-only, or config_016 for the first multimodal test).

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), leaving virtually no information about whether the image modality carries any discriminative signal. The majority of the remaining search space (configs 016–051) is multimodal, so the value of that entire branch hinges on whether image features are informative at all. Question: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the image modality with a standard, well-understood encoder, giving a clean baseline for image performance without confounding from fusion, aggregation, or multiprofile. Why this is the best use of the next budget: If image_only substantially exceeds or falls below the RNA-only baseline, it immediately reshapes strategy—validating or deprioritizing the entire multimodal branch and guiding whether to invest subsequent experiments in fusion/aggregation or in improving the RNA side. No other single experiment reduces uncertainty across such a large portion of the search space.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8%, suggesting the image modality is currently very weak. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether this poor image performance is due to the weak resnet50 encoder or because the image modality simply lacks discriminative signal for this task. This experiment (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the effect of image encoder quality by swapping resnet50 for a much stronger ViT-L while keeping everything else identical to config_010. Why it is the best next step: the result directly determines whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all. If ViT-L substantially improves image accuracy, multimodal fusion experiments become promising and worth the budget. If it remains poor, we can eliminate ~36 multimodal configurations and focus remaining budget on improving the RNA signal (multiprofile, better encoders). This single experiment maximally reduces strategic uncertainty before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile designs.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while both image-only baselines (config_010, config_013) are far weaker at ~21-23%, indicating RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile representation with aggregation improves over singleprofile, and no data on any aggregation method. This experiment (config_002) directly extends config_001 by switching to multiprofile + avgpool while keeping the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), cleanly isolating the effect of profile structure and aggregation. Choosing avgpool over transformer first is the simpler, more conservative test: if multiprofile+avgpool helps, we can then test transformer as a refinement; if it does not, the multiprofile structure itself is ruled out as the bottleneck, redirecting attention to encoder choice. Under a tight budget, this single-variable change from the best existing baseline maximizes information gained per experiment.

The strongest result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a clear ~10.6 pp improvement over single-profile (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multi-profile aggregation is beneficial. The key remaining question within this proven design axis is whether the aggregation method itself matters: does a transformer aggregator outperform simple average pooling? config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding encoder (PCA n2000), profile setting (multi), and modality (RNA-only) constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. This is preferred over switching the RNA encoder (e.g., scvi) because it first resolves whether the aggregation architecture is a meaningful design lever; if transformer adds little over avgpool, we can rule out that dimension and focus budget on encoder choice next. Image-only results (0.208–0.227) are far below RNA, making multimodal fusion premature until the RNA pipeline is better characterized.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, while image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227). Avgpool aggregation clearly outperforms transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). The critical open question is whether adding the image modality to the strong RNA signal provides any benefit, or whether the weak image features will dilute the RNA signal. Question tested: config_018 directly extends config_002 by adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion, keeping all other design choices identical (multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool). This isolates the effect of introducing the image modality. Why best next experiment: It is the single most informative comparison under budget constraints—a clean A/B test of 'best RNA setup' vs 'best RNA setup + image.' The result will determine whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal fusion strategies (weighted, better image encoders) or to focus on improving the RNA-only pipeline (e.g., scvi/scgpt encoders). Concat is the simplest fusion, making it the appropriate first probe before committing to more complex fusion variants.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc, but only marginally (~2.8%) above the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (config_002, 0.591).
