Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) achieves only 20.8%, strongly indicating RNA is the dominant informative modality. This makes the choice of RNA representation the highest-leverage design decision. Uncertainty: We have only tested a linear PCA encoder (n2000). It is unknown whether a learned, nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) captures biologically meaningful structure that PCA misses, which could substantially shift the performance ceiling. Question tested: config_004 is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001 (same rna_only model, same singleprofile setting; only the encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200), directly isolating the effect of representation quality. Why best next step: Under a tight budget, establishing whether a purpose-built single-cell encoder outperforms PCA determines whether to invest further in encoder choice or instead focus on profile/aggregation/fusion dimensions. If scvi improves accuracy meaningfully, it reshapes the multimodal strategy; if not, PCA suffices and we can redirect budget toward multiprofile or fusion experiments.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) at 0.520 acc, and image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208, confirming RNA is the dominant signal. However, we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile (with aggregation) improves over singleprofile—this is the largest untested design axis, affecting half the configuration space. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance when using the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200)? config_005 is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_004 (same encoder, same modality; only profile setting and aggregation change). Why this is best: It isolates the multiprofile effect with the simplest aggregation, reducing uncertainty about a high-impact design choice before committing budget to more complex multiprofile variants (transformer, scgpt, or multimodal multiprofile). If multiprofile+avgpool shows no gain, we can deprioritize most multiprofile configs; if it shows gain, we can then test transformer aggregation and multimodal extensions with confidence.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a large jump over config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile: 0.520). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is a major design lever. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) further improves performance, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this encoder. Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding rna_only, multiprofile, and scvi_n200 fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. Why best next step: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (best-performing config) to isolate the effect of aggregation, a design choice that will propagate to every future multimodal experiment. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, we gain a better aggregation for all downstream fusion experiments; if it does not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget toward encoder or modality questions. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 yields a large jump (~13 pts) over singleprofile (0.520→0.650), while aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) makes almost no difference (0.650 vs 0.653). Image-only is very weak (0.208). Key uncertainty: Is the multiprofile benefit specific to scvi_n200's learned latent representation, or is it a general property of aggregating multiple profiles regardless of encoder? This experiment (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool) directly tests that interaction by changing only the profile setting relative to config_001 (pca_n2000 singleprofile, 0.485). If pca_n2000 also jumps substantially, multiprofile is a universal design win and we can focus budget on encoder choice and fusion. If it does not, the benefit is tied to scvi's representation, guiding us toward learned encoders. This is a clean single-variable comparison, more informative than jumping to multimodal (where the weak image modality muddies interpretation) or testing scgpt (which introduces two untested variables at once), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA multiprofile with scvi_n200 + avgpool (config_005, acc=0.650) and pca_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) show that the RNA encoder choice contributes ~6 points of accuracy in the multiprofile setting. Aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer) has negligible effect (0.650 vs 0.653). scgpt is the only untested RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as an RNA encoder in the best-performing multiprofile setting? config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating encoder quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal or image-encoder experiments, we need to know the ceiling of the RNA-only pipeline. If scgpt substantially beats scvi_n200, it changes which RNA encoder to pair with image in multimodal configs; if it underperforms, we can confidently anchor multimodal experiments on scvi_n200. This reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis (representation) with minimal confounds.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear winner (acc 0.653), and we've mapped the RNA encoder ranking (scvi > pca > scgpt) and confirmed aggregation barely matters. However, the image modality is essentially unexplored—config_010 (resnet50, singleprofile) scored only 0.208, near chance. The critical uncertainty is whether a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) can extract any useful signal from the images, or whether the image modality is simply uninformative for this task. Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010 (only the image encoder changes from resnet50 to ViT-L), isolating the effect of representation quality on image signal. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing limited budget in multimodal fusion experiments (configs 016-051), we need to know whether image carries any discriminative information at all. If ViT-L image remains near chance, we can rule out the image modality entirely and focus remaining budget on RNA refinements. If it shows meaningful signal, multimodal fusion becomes a high-value direction. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design decision (include image or not) with a minimal, interpretable comparison.

Evidence: Multi-profile RNA with scvi_n200 is the strongest setup (config_005: 0.650 acc, config_006: 0.653 acc), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has negligible impact (~0.3% difference). Image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23 acc), raising the question of whether image adds any value when fused with the strong RNA signal. Question: Does adding the image modality (resnet50) to the best RNA multi-profile configuration (scvi_n200, avgpool) improve validation accuracy over the RNA-only baseline of ~0.650, or does it dilute the signal? This is the minimal multimodal extension of config_005—only adding image_encoder and fusion (concat, the simplest option)—so it cleanly isolates the contribution of the image modality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in optimizing fusion type, image encoder, or aggregation within the multimodal space, we need to know whether image contributes at all. If config_030 matches or beats 0.650, we have a strong direction to exploit; if it underperforms, we save budget by ruling out the image modality and focusing on RNA-only refinements. Starting with the simpler resnet50 and concat fusion keeps the experiment interpretable.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200/multiprofile achieves 0.650–0.653, while the sole multimodal experiment (config_030: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) underperforms at 0.632. Image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227), suggesting the image modality may be adding noise. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the multimodal deficit is due to the relatively weak resnet50 image encoder or a fundamental lack of image signal for this task. Question tested: config_036 swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (the stronger encoder, which was also better in image-only: 0.227 vs 0.208) while holding all other settings identical to config_030. This isolates the effect of image representation quality. Why best next experiment: If even the best available image encoder cannot lift the multimodal model above the RNA-only baseline, we can confidently conclude the image modality is uninformative for this task and redirect remaining budget to RNA-only optimization. If it does help, it reveals that image encoder quality is the bottleneck and justifies further multimodal exploration. This single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

With no completed experiments, the most informative first step is to establish the simplest, most interpretable baseline: RNA-only with PCA (2000 components) and a single profile. This configuration isolates the raw RNA signal without confounding from learned encoders, aggregation, image data, or fusion. It provides the reference performance against which we can later measure the incremental value of (a) learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), (b) multiprofile aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer), (c) adding image data, and (d) fusion strategy. PCA is computationally cheap and well-understood, minimizing the risk of the first experiment being dominated by training instability or hyperparameter sensitivity. Establishing this anchor first ensures that every subsequent experiment can be interpreted as a controlled perturbation of a known quantity, maximizing the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), leaving the most critical design question unresolved—whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task. Question tested: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest image-only model and serves as a direct, single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the effect of modality while holding profile setting (single) and model complexity (no aggregation, no fusion) constant. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget with only one data point, the highest-priority uncertainty is whether image information is worth integrating at all. If image_only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, it justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion designs; if it performs substantially worse, it redirects effort toward improving the RNA pipeline (encoder choice, multiprofile aggregation). This experiment reduces the largest single source of uncertainty about the design space and avoids committing budget to multimodal or multiprofile variants before confirming the value of the second modality.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, indicating RNA is the dominant modality and the key design decisions lie on the RNA side. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether multiprofile (multiple profiles per cell with aggregation) improves over singleprofile for RNA. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly extends config_001 by adding multiprofile with simple average-pool aggregation, isolating the effect of profile setting while keeping the encoder identical. This is the best next experiment because it is the minimal, cleanest change from our strongest baseline, resolves whether multiprofile is worth pursuing (which gates many downstream experiments on aggregation and encoder choice), and avoids jumping to multimodal fusion or a new encoder before establishing whether the profile axis matters.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a substantial +10.6 pt gain over config_001 (singleprofile, same encoder, 0.485 acc), confirming that multiprofile + aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. Image-only resnet50 (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so multimodal fusion with resnet50 is not yet justified. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method itself matters—i.e., whether a transformer aggregator can further improve over simple average pooling. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and encoder identical to config_002, giving a clean single-variable comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it isolates the aggregation effect within the currently strongest modality, and the result will directly inform which aggregation to carry into all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 018–051), reducing uncertainty across a large portion of the remaining search space.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and image-only ResNet50 (0.208). Avgpool clearly beats transformer for RNA aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). The key remaining uncertainty within the RNA pipeline is whether the linear PCA representation is a bottleneck or already near-optimal. Question: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 while holding the proven-best multi-profile + avgpool setting fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. Why best next: it isolates the representation effect without introducing confounds from fusion or image modality; if scvi improves on PCA, it signals that learned cell-relationship encodings matter and justifies further encoder exploration; if it does not, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward multimodal fusion or better image encoders. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice given the limited budget.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc, showing that (a) multiprofile with avgpool outperforms singleprofile and transformer aggregation, and (b) upgrading the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI yielded a meaningful +0.059 gain. However, we have no data on the scGPT encoder, leaving open whether a different learned representation could further improve performance. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the encoder effect under the same profile and aggregation settings that produced the best result, giving a clean three-way encoder comparison (PCA vs scVI vs scGPT) at the strongest configuration. Why this is the best next step: It tests a single variable (encoder) while holding the two most important settings (multiprofile, avgpool) fixed, directly informing whether the scVI representation is near-optimal or whether scGPT offers a further gain. This knowledge is critical before committing budget to multimodal fusion experiments, which would otherwise confound encoder choice with fusion strategy.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multi-profile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, and we know avgpool > transformer for PCA (config_002 vs 003). However, it is untested whether this aggregation preference holds for scvi_n200, whose learned latent representations may interact differently with transformer attention vs. simple averaging. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve or degrade performance when paired with the strongest RNA encoder (scvi_n200)? This is a single-variable change from the current best (config_005 → config_006), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why best next: It reduces uncertainty about a design choice that directly informs every future multimodal experiment (configs 032/033 use scvi_n200 + transformer, configs 030/031 use avgpool). Resolving this before committing budget to multimodal fusion ensures we build on the correct RNA-side foundation, and it is lower-risk than jumping to a multimodal config where the weak image signal (ResNet50 at 0.208) could confound the interpretation.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieves 0.653 accuracy, while the only image-only test (resnet50, singleprofile) yields a very low 0.208 accuracy. This single data point is insufficient to determine whether the image modality carries any useful signal or whether resnet50 is simply a poor encoder for this task. Question: Does a stronger, ImageNet-pretrained encoder (ViT-L) reveal any meaningful image signal? This is a single-variable change (encoder only) from config_010, isolating the effect of representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before committing limited budget to any of the 36 multimodal configurations, we must establish whether image features are informative at all. If ViT-L also performs near-chance, we can confidently abandon multimodal fusion and focus remaining experiments on refining the RNA-only pipeline (e.g., scvi_n200 singleprofile, scgpt+transformer). If ViT-L substantially improves over resnet50, it justifies investing in multimodal fusion with the stronger encoder. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design decision (include image or not) with minimal confounding.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile achieves the best performance (0.653 acc, 0.628 F1), while image-only models are extremely weak (0.208–0.227 acc) regardless of encoder. The critical unresolved question is whether adding the image modality via fusion can improve upon the strong RNA-only baseline, or whether the weak image signal is simply noise that will degrade performance. This experiment tests multimodal fusion (weighted) with the proven best RNA setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) and resnet50. Weighted fusion is the most informative choice here because it can downweight the weak image channel, making it the fairest test of whether image carries any complementary signal. If config_031 fails to exceed 0.653, it provides strong evidence that the image modality is uninformative for this task and the search should focus on RNA-only refinements; if it does exceed it, it justifies further multimodal exploration. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the central design question (is multimodality worth pursuing?) before committing budget to the many remaining multimodal variants.

The only multimodal experiment so far (config_031: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.678 acc, ~2.5pp above the best RNA-only (config_006: 0.653). This is promising but based on a single data point, and we cannot yet tell whether the gain is robust or an artifact of the weighted fusion choice. Config_030 is identical to config_031 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, making it a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the effect of fusion strategy. If concat yields similar performance, the multimodal gain is confirmed as robust and we can confidently build on it; if it degrades substantially, weighted fusion is identified as a critical design choice. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most promising direction (multimodal + scvi_n200 + multiprofile) before committing further experiments to variations on that path.

With no prior experiments completed, there is no evidence to guide exploitation; the priority is establishing a clear, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest viable configuration: a single modality, a single profile, and the most straightforward linear encoder (PCA). It carries minimal implementation risk and isolates the core classification task without confounding from fusion, aggregation, or learned encoders. This baseline performance will serve as the reference floor against which we can measure the incremental contribution of each design axis (profile setting, encoder choice, image modality, aggregation, fusion) in subsequent experiments. Starting at the simplest corner of the design space allows each follow-up to change one dimension at a time, maximizing the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is complete, yielding ~48.5% accuracy and ~46.4% F1, establishing a weak RNA-only baseline. The largest unresolved design question is whether adding image information provides complementary signal. Question tested: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal-change extension of config_001—identical RNA encoder and profile setting, with only the addition of a ResNet50 image branch and simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) model_setting (unimodal vs. multimodal) is the highest-level design decision; resolving it can eliminate or prioritize ~36 of the remaining 50 configs. (2) It is a clean A/B comparison to config_001, changing only the addition of image, so any performance difference can be attributed to the image branch. (3) If multimodal significantly outperforms RNA-only, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal variants (better encoders, aggregation, fusion). If it does not, the search can focus on improving the RNA representation (scvi, scgpt) or profile/aggregation strategies within the unimodal space, avoiding wasted experiments on a modality that adds no value.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA, single) scored 0.485 acc and config_016 (multimodal, PCA+ResNet50, concat, single) scored 0.527 acc, showing a ~4.2% gain from adding the image modality. However, we lack the image-only baseline, so we cannot determine whether the multimodal gain reflects genuine cross-modal synergy or simply that the image carries stronger independent signal than RNA. Question: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50) completes the {RNA, Image, Both} comparison triangle under identical profile and encoder conditions, isolating the image's standalone contribution. Why this is the best next step: Without this baseline, we cannot judge whether the multimodal result is truly additive/synergistic or whether a simpler image-only model would suffice. This single clean comparison (removing only the RNA branch from config_016) reduces the most critical uncertainty before investing further experiments in more complex multimodal variants (multiprofile, alternative encoders, weighted fusion). It is the highest-information experiment per unit budget at this stage.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear ~4-point gain over RNA-only (config_001: 0.485/0.464), confirming that multimodal fusion with these encoders is beneficial. Image alone (config_010: 0.208) is weak, so the gain comes from complementary information. Uncertainty: We have only tested concat fusion; weighted fusion is untested and could redistribute modality contributions more effectively (especially given the large performance gap between RNA and image). This experiment (config_017) changes exactly one variable—fusion from concat to weighted—while holding model setting, profile setting, RNA encoder, and image encoder identical to config_016. This clean A/B comparison isolates the effect of fusion strategy. If weighted outperforms concat, it identifies a low-cost improvement to carry forward into all future multimodal experiments (multiprofile, alternative encoders). If they are comparable, we can deprioritize fusion and redirect budget toward the larger unexplored dimensions (multiprofile, scvi/scgpt encoders, ViT image encoder). Under a limited budget, this single-variable test maximizes information per experiment.

Evidence: Our best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) at 52.7% accuracy, showing a modest ~4pp gain over RNA-only (48.5%) and a negligible difference between concat and weighted fusion. The single most important unexplored design dimension is profile setting (single vs. multi), which has not been tested in any completed experiment. Question: config_018 is a clean single-variable extension of config_016—identical model setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion—changing only the profile setting from single to multi (necessitating avgpool aggregation). This directly tests whether multiprofile + avgpool aggregation improves upon the current best configuration. Why best next experiment: If multiprofile helps, it opens a high-value direction across many downstream configs (different encoders, fusion methods, aggregation strategies). If it does not help, we can efficiently prune the entire multiprofile branch and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder or image encoder choices within singleprofile. This one experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about a major architectural axis while building directly on our strongest evidence.

The strongest result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc, a large jump over the single-profile multimodal baseline (config_016, 0.527). However, this comparison conflates three changes: adding a second modality (already tested), switching to multiprofile, and introducing avgpool aggregation. The critical open question is whether the multiprofile+avgpool benefit is inherent to the RNA representation or requires the multimodal interaction. config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable extension of config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile) that isolates the multiprofile/aggregation effect on the RNA side alone. If RNA multiprofile alone yields a substantial gain (e.g., >0.55), the benefit is in the RNA profile representation and we should prioritize multiprofile RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) next. If it stays near 0.485, the gain is synergistic and we should focus on the multimodal aggregation design (e.g., transformer in config_020). This ablation is the highest-information experiment under the budget because it disambiguates the mechanism behind the largest observed effect and directly guides the next 2-3 experiments.

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study came from switching to multiprofile (config_018: 0.619 vs config_016: 0.527 for multimodal; config_002: 0.591 vs config_001: 0.485 for RNA-only), and the only aggregation tested so far is avgpool. Fusion method (concat vs weighted) showed negligible difference in singleprofile (0.527 vs 0.523), so it is lower priority. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for combining multiple profiles, given that the multiprofile gain is the dominant source of accuracy? This experiment (config_020) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other parameters at their current best values (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why best next: It is a single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly tests whether a more expressive aggregation can further exploit the multiprofile signal, and the result will inform whether transformer aggregation is worth exploring across other encoder/fusion combinations under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal (image-only acc=0.208; RNA-only multiprofile avgpool=0.591 is close to the best multimodal result of 0.619), and multiprofile+avgpool is the strongest setting so far. However, we have only tested PCA-2000 as the RNA encoder—a linear projection—across all 7 completed experiments. The RNA encoder is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design axis remaining. Question: config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (same setting but PCA-2000), isolating whether a learned generative representation (scvi) captures more predictive structure than PCA. Why this is the best use of the next experiment: it directly tests the most consequential unexplored axis (RNA representation quality) without confounding from image modality, fusion, or aggregation changes. If scvi_n200 improves RNA-only performance, we gain a strong prior for deploying it in the multimodal multiprofile setting; if not, PCA remains validated and we can redirect budget toward image encoder or other axes. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA n2000 in the RNA-only multi-profile setting (0.650 vs 0.591, config_005 vs config_002), and the best multimodal config so far (config_018: PCA, multi, avgpool, concat, ResNet50) achieves 0.619. Question: Does the scvi_n200 encoder improvement transfer to the multimodal setting? config_030 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 relative to config_018 (keeping multi-profile, avgpool, concat, ResNet50), cleanly isolating the encoder effect in the multimodal context. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest single finding (scvi > PCA) in the most promising model architecture, uses a single-variable change to maintain interpretability, and if it succeeds, establishes scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder for further exploration (e.g., with ViT or transformer aggregation). If it fails, it tells us the scvi benefit is specific to RNA-only and the image modality interacts differently with the learned representation.

Evidence: The RNA encoder is the most impactful design axis so far — switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multiprofile RNA-only setting improved accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (+0.06), the largest single-factor gain observed. However, scgpt has not been tested at all, leaving a major uncertainty about whether a third, potentially stronger RNA representation exists. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (same settings but scvi_n200), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly tests the most consequential unexplored axis before committing budget to multimodal or image-encoder variants built on top of it. (2) If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi, it reopens the multimodal search with a stronger RNA backbone; if it underperforms, we can confidently focus remaining budget on scvi-based configurations. (3) It changes only one factor relative to config_005, avoiding the confound of simultaneously altering encoder, modality, or aggregation. This maximizes information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With zero completed experiments, the most informative first step is to establish a clean, minimal baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: one modality, one profile, a linear and well-understood encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. This isolates the 'floor' performance of the pipeline. Every subsequent experiment—adding image modality, switching to learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), moving to multiprofile, or introducing fusion—can be directly compared against this reference to attribute performance gains or losses to specific design choices. Starting with the simplest model also reduces the risk of confounding: if a more complex configuration underperforms, we can rule out pipeline issues more easily. Under a tight budget, this single experiment maximizes the information gained per run by anchoring the entire search space to a known reference point.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), we have essentially no information about whether the image modality carries useful signal. The most impactful uncertainty is whether image features are informative at all, since a negative answer would eliminate ~36 multimodal configurations from further consideration. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest possible image experiment—no aggregation, no fusion—so it cleanly isolates the information content of the image channel. Paired with the existing RNA baseline, it gives us two single-modality reference points, enabling us to interpret any future multimodal result as a measure of complementarity rather than conflating modality value with fusion/aggregation effects. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the current sparse evidence.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% acc, far outperforming image-only ResNet50 (config_010, 20.8% acc), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether the profile setting (single vs. multi) matters for RNA, which is a fundamental architectural choice affecting all downstream configurations. This experiment (config_002) tests multiprofile + avgpool aggregation with the same PCA encoder as config_001, isolating the effect of profile setting while keeping the encoder fixed. If multiprofile improves performance, it validates a design axis that applies universally across encoders and fusion strategies; if it does not, we can rule out that axis and focus budget on encoder choice (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion. This is the most informative single-variable extension of our best result and the best use of the next experiment under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA-2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 accuracy, a large jump over config_001 (single-profile, 0.485), confirming that multi-profile aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the gain comes primarily from having multiple profiles or from the aggregation method itself—specifically, whether a transformer aggregator can further improve over simple average pooling. This experiment (config_003) changes exactly one variable from config_002 (avgpool → transformer) while holding encoder, profile setting, and modality fixed, giving a clean A/B comparison. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it justifies the added complexity in all downstream multimodal experiments; if it does not, avgpool is confirmed as sufficient and we can rule out transformer across the remaining search space, saving budget. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice because it directly extends the strongest result with a single-variable change.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485), transformer aggregation (0.519), and image-only ResNet50 (0.208). This establishes multi-profile + avgpool as the strongest RNA configuration and suggests the image modality (ResNet50) is currently a weak signal. Uncertainty: whether PCA_n2000 is the best RNA representation, or whether a purpose-built learned encoder (scvi) could further improve performance in this optimal multi-profile/avgpool setup. Question tested: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 while keeping multi-profile and avgpool fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison to config_002. Why best next step: It directly exploits the strongest known direction (multi-profile + avgpool) while probing the most impactful remaining design choice (RNA encoder quality). The result will determine whether to invest further in RNA encoder upgrades or pivot to multimodal/fusion experiments, and it avoids the low-information risk of adding a weak image modality before confirming the RNA backbone is well-optimized.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, outperforming config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.591. This confirms multiprofile+avgpool is the right structural choice and that encoder quality matters (~6% gain). Uncertainty: we have not yet tested whether scgpt, the third available encoder, surpasses scvi_n200 under identical conditions. Question tested: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) provides a clean A/B comparison of scgpt vs scvi_n200 while holding profile setting and aggregation constant, isolating the encoder/representation effect. Why best next step: Before investing limited budget in multimodal fusion experiments (where image-only performance is very weak at 0.21), we need to confirm which RNA encoder is optimal. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it changes the foundation for all downstream multimodal configs; if it does not, we lock in scvi_n200 and can confidently move to multimodal testing. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful remaining design choice within the RNA-only space.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005) is the best configuration so far (acc 0.650), and for PCA_n2000 the aggregation choice showed a clear gap (avgpool 0.591 vs transformer 0.519). However, that comparison was made with a linear PCA representation; scvi_n200 produces a learned, potentially higher-dimensional latent space where attention-based (transformer) aggregation could behave differently. Question: Does the avgpool-over-transformer advantage generalize to the scvi_n200 encoder, or does the richer learned representation benefit from transformer aggregation? This experiment (config_006) changes exactly one variable—aggregation—from the current best config, making it a clean controlled comparison. Why it is the best next use of budget: it directly resolves whether transformer aggregation is viable for the top encoder before committing remaining experiments to multimodal/fusion configurations. If avgpool wins again, we can confidently lock in the aggregation choice and direct all subsequent budget toward the higher-impact multimodal fusion question; if transformer unexpectedly wins, that changes the entire downstream search strategy. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core design axis with a single, well-isolated experiment.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005, acc=0.650) is the best result so far, and image-only with resnet50 is very weak (config_010, acc=0.208). The critical untested question is whether the image modality, despite its poor standalone performance, provides any complementary signal when fused with the strongest RNA representation. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests that question by taking the best RNA-only configuration and adding image via the simplest fusion (concat). It changes only one design axis (adding image + fusion) relative to config_005, isolating the marginal contribution of the image modality. If config_030 does not meaningfully exceed 0.650, it strongly indicates resnet50 features are uninformative here and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side improvements or a stronger image encoder. If it does exceed, it justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and ViT-based image encoders. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it resolves the go/no-go decision for the entire multimodal branch.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, config_006) achieves 0.653 acc, but adding resnet50 image features via concat fusion (config_030) drops performance to 0.632. This is surprising and suggests either the fusion strategy or the weak image signal (image_only resnet50 was only 0.208) is the bottleneck. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding all other factors (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) identical to config_030. This isolates whether the performance drop is due to the fusion mechanism (concat giving equal weight to a weak image signal) or the image representation itself. Why best: It is a single-variable, directly controlled comparison against config_030, making the result maximally interpretable. If weighted fusion recovers to ~0.65+, the issue is fusion strategy and we can exploit multimodal with resnet50. If it remains ~0.63, the image encoder is the bottleneck and the next experiment should test imagenet_vit_l. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about which design axis to pursue next, making this the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_031 (multimodal, multi-profile, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. The image-only ResNet50 model was very weak (0.208), yet weighted fusion still boosted multimodal performance over RNA-only (0.678 vs 0.650), suggesting the image modality contributes complementary signal but is limited by encoder quality. ViT-L has not yet been tested in any configuration. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L improve multimodal performance when all other settings (scvi_n200, multi-profile, avgpool, weighted) are held at their best-known values? Why this is the best next experiment: config_037 is a single-variable change from the current best (config_031), cleanly isolating the effect of image encoder quality. If ViT-L helps, it identifies a promising direction for further exploitation; if it does not, it confirms that the image modality's contribution is bounded regardless of encoder, redirecting effort toward RNA-side improvements. This is more informative than testing aggregation (transformer ≈ avgpool already shown for scvi_n200) or other encoders (scgpt already underperforms).

With no completed experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, minimal baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: it uses the least complex RNA encoder (PCA), a single profile (no aggregation needed), and no image or fusion components. This isolates the fundamental RNA signal quality without confounding from learned encoders, multi-profile aggregation, or cross-modal fusion. It will tell us the performance floor for RNA alone, which is essential context for interpreting whether richer encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or multimodal fusion actually add value. Starting from this null model ensures that every later experiment can be interpreted as a controlled addition of one design axis, maximizing the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether image features carry any discriminative signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this question: it changes only the modality (RNA → image) while holding profile setting (singleprofile) constant, enabling a direct 1-variable comparison against the baseline. If image-only performs comparably or better, it justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion; if it performs substantially worse, we can deprioritize image-dependent configurations and focus budget on RNA encoder and profile/aggregation variants. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because the modality decision gates an entire branch of the search space.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA n2000, single profile) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant modality, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) is very weak at 20.8%. We have no information yet on whether the multiprofile axis adds value. Question: config_002 (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the effect of switching from single to multiprofile while holding the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and modality constant. Using avgpool (the simplest aggregation) keeps the comparison clean. Why this is the best next step: (1) It is a single-variable comparison directly from our best baseline, so any performance change can be attributed to the profile setting. (2) The multiprofile axis is a major design decision that underpins many downstream multimodal configs (config_018–051); knowing whether it helps with the base encoder tells us whether to invest in multiprofile+fusion or focus on single-profile improvements. (3) If multiprofile+avgpool does not improve over single-profile PCA, it signals that the profile axis may not be the bottleneck, redirecting budget toward encoder quality or fusion strategy. (4) It avoids the confound of simultaneously changing encoder, dimensionality, and profile as in config_004/005.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.591) so far, a substantial +0.106 improvement over singleprofile RNA (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is beneficial. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool). Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform simple average pooling for combining multiple RNA profiles? This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly that variable—same model setting, same profile setting, same RNA encoder, only aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer. Why best next step: It is a clean single-variable comparison extending our strongest result, directly informing whether the added complexity of a transformer aggregator is warranted before we invest budget in multimodal configurations where aggregation design will be even more critical. A positive result would justify transformer in multimodal settings; a null or negative result would steer us toward simpler, more robust aggregation strategies.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591) is clearly the best configuration so far, outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and vastly outperforming image-only (0.208). Avgpool also beats transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). However, all RNA results used PCA n2000; we have no evidence about whether a learned biological representation (scvi) improves over a linear one. Question: Does replacing PCA with scvi_n200 under the same multi-profile + avgpool setup improve the RNA representation and validation accuracy? Why this is the best next experiment: config_005 changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder) relative to our best result (config_002), cleanly isolating the effect of representation while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed. This is the highest-information single experiment: if scvi helps, we know learned representations matter and should extend to scgpt and multimodal; if it doesn't, PCA is sufficient and we can pivot budget toward testing whether the weak image modality adds value in a multimodal setting. Either outcome meaningfully narrows the search space under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.650) over image-only (0.208). Within RNA, multiprofile+avgpool consistently outperforms singleprofile or transformer aggregation (config_002: 0.591 > config_001: 0.485; config_002: 0.591 > config_003: 0.519). The encoder swap from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_005 vs config_002) yielded the largest single gain (+5.9 pp to 0.650), making encoder choice the most impactful design axis. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested scgpt, the third available RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 under the same multiprofile+avgpool setting? config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the encoder effect. Why best next: The encoder is the highest-leverage choice identified so far, and resolving whether scgpt beats scvi_n200 will (a) establish the best RNA backbone, (b) inform which encoder to pair with image in any future multimodal experiments, and (c) avoid committing multiple future experiments to a suboptimal encoder. Testing transformer aggregation with scvi_n200 (config_006) is lower priority since avgpool already showed a consistent advantage over transformer with pca_n2000.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool (config_005) is the current best at 0.650 acc, and image-only with resnet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the image modality contributes complementary information when fused with the strong RNA signal, or whether it will dilute performance. This experiment (config_030) tests multimodal fusion by adding resnet50 image features via concat to the best-validated RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), changing only the modality and fusion while holding all RNA-side settings at their proven optimum. It is the best use of the next experiment because it answers the single most consequential design question—whether a multimodal strategy is worth pursuing at all—before committing budget to more complex fusion variants or alternative image encoders. If it beats 0.650, we justify exploring ViT-L and weighted fusion; if it underperforms, we can redirect budget to RNA-only refinements or a stronger image encoder.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool; config_005) achieves 0.650 acc, while adding resnet50 image with concat fusion (config_030) slightly *decreases* performance to 0.632. Image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208). This raises the question of whether the slight multimodal drop is due to concat diluting the weak image signal or whether the image simply adds no useful information. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted (keeping scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, multiprofile identical to config_030), isolating the fusion mechanism. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds 0.650, it indicates the image carries signal that concat fails to leverage; if it remains near 0.632, it strongly suggests resnet50 features are not informative for this task and we should pivot to testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L). Why best: It is a single-variable, controlled follow-up to the most recent multimodal result, directly resolving the key uncertainty about whether image fusion is the bottleneck before committing budget to larger architectural changes.

Evidence: The current best is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. We know avgpool > transformer for PCA multiprofile (0.591 vs 0.519), but we have not tested whether this aggregation preference holds for the superior scvi_n200 encoder. Uncertainty: It is possible that transformer aggregation, which captures inter-profile relationships, synergizes better with the richer scvi_n200 representations even though it underperformed for PCA. This experiment (config_033) is a single-variable change from the current best (avgpool → transformer, weighted fusion retained), directly testing whether aggregation can further improve the top configuration. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it is the most natural exploitation step from the current best, isolates the aggregation effect cleanly, and the outcome is informative either way: a gain identifies a new best, while a loss confirms avgpool as the correct aggregation for scvi_n200 and redirects effort toward the untested image-encoder axis (ViT-L).

Evidence: config_033 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) is the best result so far at 0.7131 acc / 0.6945 F1, and the pattern across configs 030→031→033 shows that transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the strongest combination. However, the image-only resnet50 baseline (config_010) is very weak (0.2079), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality is contributing meaningfully or whether a stronger image encoder is needed. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve the best-performing multimodal configuration? This is a single-variable change (image encoder only) from config_033, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest evidence (best config) along the one untested dimension, and the answer has high downstream value—if ViT-L helps substantially, it confirms image features are a bottleneck and justifies further image-encoder exploration; if it does not, it confirms the current configuration is near its ceiling and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., RNA-only transformer via config_006 or fusion ablation via config_032).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about baseline performance, data quality, or which design axes matter. The most critical unknown is whether a simple RNA-only model with a standard PCA embedding achieves reasonable validation accuracy, establishing the performance floor for the entire search. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration in the space. It isolates the contribution of a basic RNA representation without confounding factors from multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders, image modalities, or fusion strategies. It answers: 'What is the performance ceiling of the simplest viable model?' 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Establishing this baseline is a prerequisite for interpreting every subsequent experiment. Without it, a multimodal or multiprofile result cannot be attributed to the added complexity versus the data itself. PCA is also computationally cheap, reducing the risk of wasting budget on a pipeline failure. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the starting point and provides a concrete reference against which all later gains (from scvi/scgpt encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, or fusion) can be measured.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, acc≈0.485), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most fundamental question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality provides any signal beyond the RNA baseline. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the cleanest logical extension of config_001: it keeps the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical, and introduces only the image modality with the simplest reasonable choices (resnet50, concat fusion). This isolates the effect of adding image information. If config_016 substantially exceeds 0.485, it confirms image is a useful modality and justifies further investment in image encoder and fusion choices. If it does not, it tells us the image signal is weak or poorly captured by resnet50, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. Under a limited budget, answering 'does the second modality help at all?' before exploring encoder variants, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion strategies is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc vs config_001 (rna_only, pca_n2000) at 0.485 acc, a ~4.2 pp gain from adding the image modality. However, we cannot yet decompose how much of that gain comes from the image signal independently versus a synergistic interaction with RNA. Question: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the image modality's standalone contribution. If image_only ≈ 0.50+, the image is a strong independent signal and we should prioritize better image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and fusion strategies. If image_only ≈ 0.45 or lower, the multimodal gain is largely additive/synergistic with RNA, and we should focus on RNA encoder quality and fusion design instead. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-axis comparison (removing RNA while keeping resnet50 identical to config_016), directly resolves the most fundamental uncertainty about modality contribution, and will guide whether subsequent budget is better spent exploring image encoder upgrades, fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, concat fusion) achieves 0.527 acc, clearly above rna_only (0.485) and far above image_only (0.208), suggesting the multimodal direction is promising and that the image modality contributes complementary signal. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether the modest gain from adding image is sensitive to how the two modalities are combined; weighted fusion could better balance the strong RNA signal against the weaker image signal. This experiment (config_017) is a clean single-variable change from config_016—only fusion switches from concat to weighted—so any accuracy/F1 difference can be attributed to the fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step: it either confirms concat is sufficient (freeing us to explore profile/encoder/image-encoder changes) or reveals that weighted fusion is materially better, which would redirect all subsequent multimodal experiments. It avoids introducing multiple new variables (profile, aggregation, new encoders) simultaneously.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) at 0.527 acc, modestly above RNA-only (0.485) and far above image-only (0.208). Fusion strategy (concat vs weighted) shows negligible difference. The single most important untested design axis is whether multiprofile + aggregation provides additional signal beyond a single profile. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance in the current best multimodal setup? config_018 is a direct, minimal extension of config_016—same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), same image encoder (resnet50), same fusion (concat)—changing only the profile/aggregation dimension. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation cleanly. Why best next: With only 4 experiments completed, understanding whether multiprofile aggregation is beneficial is foundational before investing budget in alternative RNA encoders or image encoders. If multiprofile helps, it opens a productive direction (configs 019-027); if it does not, we can focus budget on encoder choices instead.

Evidence: The largest performance jump so far came from switching to multiprofile + avgpool in the multimodal setting (config_016→config_018: 0.527→0.619 acc). However, it is unclear whether this gain is driven by the multiprofile representation itself (more information from multiple profiles) or by a specific interaction between multiprofile aggregation and multimodal fusion. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly isolates the profile/aggregation effect by applying the same multiprofile + avgpool pipeline to RNA data alone, holding the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) constant relative to config_001. Why this is the best next experiment: The result is a critical diagnostic that reshapes the entire search strategy. If multiprofile substantially improves RNA-only performance, the benefit is in the profile representation, and subsequent experiments should explore alternative RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) with multiprofile. If it does not help RNA alone, the gain is specific to multimodal fusion with multiprofile, and we should focus on optimizing the image encoder and fusion strategy in the multimodal setting. This single experiment reduces the most important structural uncertainty in the design space and is more informative than, e.g., testing transformer aggregation (config_020), which only explores a narrow variation within the already-promising multimodal+avgpool region.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation provides a large boost over singleprofile (+0.092 vs config_016). However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) for multiprofile, leaving open whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) could further improve performance. Question: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model setting, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion constant relative to config_018. This isolates the effect of aggregation method in the highest-performing regime. Why best: It is a clean single-variable extension of our current best, directly answers whether avgpool is sufficient or whether attention-based profile combination adds value, and the result will inform the aggregation choice for all subsequent multiprofile experiments (across RNA encoders and image encoders), making it the most information-dense next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc. Across all 7 completed experiments, only pca_n2000 has been used as the RNA encoder, leaving the RNA representation axis entirely unexplored. RNA is the dominant signal (RNA-only multiprofile: 0.591 vs image-only: 0.208), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~0.028), suggesting the RNA representation may be a bottleneck. Question: Does replacing linear PCA with a learned autoencoder (scvi_n200) improve the RNA representation enough to lift performance in the best-known multimodal multiprofile setup? config_030 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200) while holding model setting, profile, image encoder, aggregation, and fusion fixed, isolating the encoder effect. This is the highest-information next step because the RNA encoder is the single largest untested design axis, and a positive result would redirect the search toward learned representations, while a null/negative result would confirm PCA is sufficient and shift focus to the image encoder or fusion strategy.

Evidence: The current best is config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 acc. All completed multimodal experiments used resnet50 as the image encoder; imagenet_vit_l has never been tested. Image-only performance is low (0.208), but in the multimodal setting the image modality adds ~0.03-0.04 over RNA-only, and it is unclear whether a stronger, larger image encoder (ViT-L) could extract more complementary signal. Question: config_036 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while holding all other settings at their best-known values (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), cleanly isolating the image-encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It resolves a major untested design dimension with a single-variable comparison to the current best. If ViT-L improves performance, it signals the image modality is underutilized and further image-side investment is warranted; if it does not, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects budget toward RNA-encoder or fusion choices. This is higher-information than testing weighted fusion (nearly resolved by singleprofile evidence) or transformer aggregation (already shown inferior to avgpool).

Evidence: The current best (config_036, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, acc=0.715) shows that image encoder choice is the dominant factor, and avgpool outperformed transformer by 0.040 in the earlier pca_n2000+resnet50 multiprofile comparison (config_018 vs config_020). However, that aggregation comparison was made with weaker encoders. Question: Does avgpool still dominate transformer when paired with the strongest encoders (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l), or might the richer VIT features interact differently with transformer-based aggregation? Config_038 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer relative to config_036, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next: It directly tests whether the aggregation finding generalizes to the top-performing setting, isolating one design decision. If transformer remains inferior, we can lock in avgpool and redirect budget to other levers (e.g., fusion or RNA encoder exploration); if it improves, it reveals a non-obvious interaction that would change the search trajectory. This is a minimal, high-information experiment that exploits the current best direction while reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no prior information about which modalities, encoders, or profile settings contribute meaningfully to validation accuracy. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA n2000) establishes the simplest, most standard RNA baseline—using a well-understood linear encoder and no aggregation or fusion complexity. It anchors the performance floor for the RNA modality and provides a clean reference against which every other design axis (image modality, multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders like scVI/scGPT, and fusion strategies) can be incrementally compared. 3) Why it is the best use of the first experiment: With a limited budget, the first run should minimize confounds and maximize interpretability. Starting from the most parsimonious configuration ensures that any future gain (or lack thereof) can be attributed to a single added design choice rather than a bundle of changes. It also avoids the risk of over-investing early in complex multimodal or multiprofile settings whose value is entirely unvalidated. This baseline will inform whether to prioritize exploring image modality, better RNA encoders, or multiprofile aggregation next.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the largest uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. We have zero image-only data points, making it impossible to judge whether the low RNA-only performance reflects a genuinely hard task, a poor PCA representation, or a modality mismatch. Config_010 (image_only, resnet50, singleprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison: same task, same simple profile setting, but the image modality with a standard pretrained encoder. If image-only accuracy is substantially higher, the search should pivot toward image-centric or multimodal configurations; if it is similarly low, the task is inherently difficult and we should focus on improving representations (scvi/scgpt) or aggregation. This experiment isolates the modality question without confounding encoder, profile, or fusion choices, making it the highest-information-use next step under a limited budget.

With only two completed experiments, evidence is sparse. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) was poor at 20.8%. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the RNA representation itself is the bottleneck: does a learned encoder (scvi_n200) meaningfully outperform a linear one (pca_n2000)? config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from config_001, providing a clean single-variable comparison. If scvi_n200 substantially improves accuracy, it signals that representation quality is a key lever and justifies investing in learned encoders for all downstream (multiprofile, multimodal) experiments. If it does not, we know the representation is not the limiting factor and should prioritize testing profile setting, aggregation, or modality fusion instead. This is the highest-information next step under a tight budget because it isolates one critical design axis before committing to more complex configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520 acc) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485 acc) in singleprofile RNA, establishing scvi_n200 as the stronger RNA encoder. Image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208 acc). Uncertainty: We have no multiprofile results yet, and this is a critical design axis that affects all downstream multimodal and aggregation choices. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) by changing only the profile setting and adding a simple avgpool aggregation, cleanly isolating the multiprofile effect. It uses the best RNA encoder identified so far and the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to avoid confounding with a complex transformer. If multiprofile helps, it justifies investing further in transformer aggregation and multimodal multiprofile configs; if it doesn't, we can prune a large portion of the search space and focus on singleprofile or encoder improvements. This is the highest-information experiment given the current evidence.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (scvi_n200, single, 0.520), showing multiprofile is highly beneficial. However, we cannot yet tell whether the gain comes from having multiple profiles per se or from the avgpool aggregation specifically. Question: config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a single-variable comparison against config_005, isolating the aggregation method (transformer vs avgpool) while holding encoder and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly tests the most impactful design axis identified so far—aggregation—under the strongest configuration. (2) The answer immediately informs whether transformer aggregation should be adopted for all subsequent multimodal experiments, reducing uncertainty across the entire remaining search space. (3) It changes only one variable relative to the best result, making the comparison clean and interpretable, which is critical under a limited budget. (4) If transformer outperforms avgpool, it signals that learned cross-profile interactions matter; if they are comparable, it confirms that the multiprofile gain is primarily from profile redundancy rather than aggregation sophistication, guiding where to invest remaining experiments.

Evidence: The largest performance gain so far comes from switching to multiprofile with scvi_n200 (0.520→0.650, +13 pts), while the image modality is very weak (0.208). However, we cannot yet tell whether the multiprofile benefit is a general property of the data or an interaction specific to scvi_n200. Question: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) changes only the profile setting from config_001, isolating the multiprofile effect for the PCA encoder and completing a 2×2 (encoder × profile) comparison at the avgpool aggregation. Why best next: If pca+multi also jumps substantially, multiprofile is the dominant design lever and we should exploit it with scgpt or multimodal next; if it does not, the scvi+multi interaction is critical and we should prioritize encoder choice. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design decision before committing budget to more complex multimodal or new-encoder configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.653) while image-only is very weak (0.208). Within RNA, multiprofile gives a large boost (~+13% over singleprofile) and scvi_n200 beats pca_n2000 by ~6% in the multiprofile setting. Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) makes negligible difference (0.650 vs 0.653). The current best is config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, 0.653). Uncertainty: We have no data on scgpt, a fundamentally different RNA encoder (generative single-cell model), and it is unclear whether it can surpass scvi_n200. Question: config_009 (scgpt, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable swap from config_006, isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly tests whether a different learned representation can beat the current best, informing whether representation quality is a further lever or whether we've saturated the RNA-only ceiling. (2) The result will determine which RNA encoder to pair with any future multimodal fusion experiments, making it a prerequisite for informed multimodal design. (3) It avoids the risk of prematurely jumping to multimodal fusion when the image modality is so weak that its added value is uncertain, and it changes only one variable, keeping the comparison interpretable under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer (config_006, acc 0.653) is the clear best so far, and image-only with resnet50 is very weak (config_010, acc 0.208). The aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference, and scgpt/pca are clearly inferior to scvi_n200. The major unexplored question is whether adding image features provides complementary signal on top of the strong RNA representation. This experiment (config_032) takes the best RNA configuration and adds resnet50 image features with concat fusion, isolating the effect of multimodal fusion while holding all other design choices at their best-known values. It is the minimal, controlled extension of our current best: if accuracy exceeds 0.653, image adds value and we should explore ViT and weighted fusion; if it does not, we know resnet50 image features are not complementary and should pivot to testing imagenet_vit_l in a multimodal setting. This is the highest-information single experiment under the budget because it directly answers whether the multimodal direction is worth further investment.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.688 acc, only ~0.035 above the best RNA-only (config_006, 0.653). We have no data on fusion strategy—concat is the only method tested. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining the scvi_n200 RNA features with ResNet50 image features? config_033 changes only the fusion method (concat→weighted) relative to config_032, making it a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests an important, unexplored design axis (fusion) with minimal confounding. If weighted fusion helps, it reveals that modality interaction is a meaningful lever; if it does not, we can rule out fusion as a bottleneck and redirect effort toward image encoder quality (ViT-L) or RNA-side improvements. Under a limited budget, this controlled 1-variable test maximizes information per experiment.

The current best configuration (config_033: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.713 accuracy, a clear improvement over the best RNA-only multiprofile (config_006: 0.653). However, the image-only baseline (config_010, resnet50) is very weak at 0.208, raising the question of whether the image modality's contribution in the multimodal model is being bottlenecked by the relatively weak ResNet50 encoder. Config_039 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_033. This directly tests whether a stronger visual representation can unlock additional signal from the image modality. If ViT-L substantially improves performance, it indicates the image channel has untapped potential and future experiments should prioritize image representation quality. If the gain is marginal, it confirms that the image contribution is inherently limited and effort should shift to other design axes (e.g., aggregation, fusion strategy, or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, resolving this uncertainty about the image encoder's ceiling is more informative than testing aggregation variants (which showed negligible effect in RNA-only) or weaker modalities.

No experiments have been completed yet, so there is no evidence to exploit. The most critical first step is to establish a performance baseline that calibrates all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: a single modality, a single profile, and the most basic linear encoder (PCA). Running this first gives us a reference accuracy/F1 floor against which we can measure the marginal contribution of every other design axis—adding a second modality, using multiple profiles, switching to learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), or changing aggregation/fusion. Without this anchor, later experiments cannot tell us whether added complexity is genuinely helpful or merely overfitting. It is the lowest-cost, highest-information experiment to run first under a limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only completed experiment (config_001, rna_only + PCA) yields a low validation accuracy of ~48.5%, which is near chance for a multi-class task. This tells us almost nothing about whether the image modality carries independent signal for this task, or whether a learned RNA encoder would help. The fundamental question—does image carry discriminative information here?—is completely unanswered. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50) establishes a clean unimodal image baseline. It changes only the modality relative to config_001 (same singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion), isolating the effect of switching from RNA to image. 3) Why it is the best next step: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or learned encoders, we need to know whether the image channel has signal at all. If image_only performs well, multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction; if it also performs poorly, the task may require a better RNA encoder or a different representation strategy. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) and directly informs which of the ~50 remaining configurations are worth pursuing under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image, singleprofile, resnet50) is very weak at 20.8%. With only two data points, the highest-priority uncertainty is whether the RNA baseline can be improved, since RNA is clearly the dominant modality and most downstream multimodal configs depend on a strong RNA representation. Question tested: config_002 (RNA, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the minimal extension of config_001, isolating the effect of using multiple profiles with average-pooling aggregation while holding the encoder constant. This tells us whether the multiprofile+aggregation axis—required for nearly all multimodal configurations—adds value over a single profile. Why best next step: It is a clean, single-concept comparison to our best result, reduces uncertainty about a design axis that gates the entire multimodal search space, and if it improves on 48.5%, it validates the multiprofile direction before investing budget in more complex multimodal or encoder variants.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best performance so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), a substantial +10.6% improvement over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, acc=0.485). Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002, exploiting the strongest evidence while reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice. If transformer aggregation helps, it validates a more expressive fusion path for later multimodal experiments; if it does not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget toward encoder choice or multimodal fusion.
