Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, showing multiprofile+avgpool is the strongest RNA configuration. Under a limited budget, resolving whether representation learning matters is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. With PCA, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519, config_002 vs config_003), but that comparison was made with a simpler linear representation. Evidence: scVI with multi-profile and avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is the best RNA-only configuration so far, and multi-profile + avgpool is the dominant setting. However, scGPT has not been tested at all, and the RNA encoder choice is a fundamental representation decision that will govern all downstream multimodal experiments. The existing evidence shows a strong RNA-only baseline (scvi_n200 + multiprofile at ~0.65) but the only image-only test (config_010: resnet50, singleprofile) yielded a very weak 0.208 accuracy—essentially at chance level. This creates major uncertainty about whether the image modality contains any useful signal for this task. Config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010, isolating the effect of a much stronger pretrained image encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50). If ViT-L substantially improves image-only performance, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If it remains near chance, it strongly suggests image features are not informative for this task, allowing us to redirect budget toward refining the RNA pipeline (e.g., scgpt+transformer, or singleprofile scvi_n200) rather than exploring 30+ multimodal configurations that would likely underperform the 0.65 RNA baseline. This is the highest-uncertainty-reduction experiment available under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the strongest configuration (~0.65 acc), while image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23 acc for both resnet50 and ViT-L). The critical open question is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal yields any complementary benefit, or whether it merely adds noise. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the most direct logical extension of the best RNA-only result, adding the simplest image encoder (resnet50, already characterized) and simplest fusion (concat). It isolates the single question 'does image add value when combined with the best RNA representation?' without confounding changes to encoder, aggregation, or fusion strategy. If it fails to exceed 0.65, it strongly argues against pursuing multimodal configurations and redirects budget to RNA-only refinements; if it succeeds, it justifies further fusion and image-encoder exploration.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile+avgpool is the best RNA-only model (0.6501 acc, config_005). The sole multimodal experiment (config_030: scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) scored 0.6315, actually worse than RNA-only, suggesting concat fusion with a weak image encoder (~0.21 alone) introduces noise. Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), so the image signal is marginal. Question: Does weighted fusion allow the model to downweight the noisy image channel and recover (or exceed) RNA-only performance? This is a minimal change from config_030 (only concat→weighted), isolating the fusion mechanism. Why best next experiment: It directly diagnoses whether the multimodal underperformance is a fusion artifact or a fundamental lack of complementary image information. If weighted recovers to ~0.65, the image adds no value but is harmless; if it exceeds 0.65, there is hidden complementary signal; if it stays at ~0.63, the image is actively harmful regardless of fusion. This single result sharply narrows the remaining multimodal search space and is more informative than swapping the image encoder (which is weak either way) or testing transformer aggregation (already shown ≈ avgpool for scvi_n200).

With zero completed experiments, the highest-priority question is establishing a performance baseline against which all added complexity (multiprofile, learned encoders, image modality, fusion) can be measured. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration in the search space: a standard PCA dimensionality reduction on a single RNA profile with no learned encoder, no image, no aggregation, and no fusion. It serves as the 'null model' floor. Every subsequent experiment—whether it adds a learned RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt), a second profile with aggregation, an image branch, or a multimodal fusion—can be directly compared to this baseline to isolate the marginal contribution of each design choice. Starting with the minimal configuration also avoids confounding multiple design decisions at once and gives the cleanest reference point for the limited experiment budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. Before investing in multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative encoders, I need a second unimodal baseline. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest possible comparison: it matches config_001 in simplicity (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion) and isolates the modality variable. If image accuracy substantially exceeds 48.5%, I know the image channel is the stronger signal and should prioritize image-centric and multimodal configurations. If it is comparable or lower, the problem is intrinsically difficult and I should focus on representation quality (encoder choice) rather than modality or fusion complexity. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about which modality to build upon, making it the highest-information next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the stronger modality, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is very weak at 20.8%. The key uncertainty is whether moving from a single profile to multiple profiles with aggregation improves the RNA representation. config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the minimal extension of config_001—it changes only the profile setting and adds avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA encoder. Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a strong +0.106 improvement over config_001 (single-profile, 0.485), confirming multi-profile aggregation is highly beneficial for RNA. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so multimodal fusion is premature. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for multi-profile RNA. Establishing the optimal aggregation strategy for RNA before layering on additional modalities or encoders is the highest-information next step under a limited budget, because the aggregation choice will propagate into all subsequent multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the best result so far (acc 0.591, F1 0.573), clearly outperforming singleprofile PCA (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). This establishes multiprofile + avgpool as the strongest profile/aggregation combination. If scvi improves on PCA, it justifies further encoder exploration; if not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects effort toward multimodal fusion or other design axes. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, and for PCA the same comparison showed avgpool (0.591) clearly outperforming transformer (0.519). Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest single performance lever identified so far (pca_n2000→scvi_n200 in multiprofile/avgpool: 0.591→0.650, ~6 pp). scgpt is the only encoder completely untested. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean one-variable comparison against config_005 (same settings, scvi_n200, acc 0.650), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile, aggregation, and modality constant. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it reshapes the entire search strategy; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the best encoder and can confidently build multimodal experiments on top of it. This single experiment reduces the most critical remaining uncertainty about representation quality at minimal cost.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only image-only result so far (config_010, resnet50 singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208 accuracy, while RNA-only models range from 0.48 to 0.65. We have no data on whether a stronger pretrained image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) provides any meaningful signal for this task. 2) What this tests: config_013 isolates the effect of image encoder quality (ViT-L vs. ResNet50) in the simplest possible setting (singleprofile, image-only), directly answering whether the image modality carries useful discriminative information at all. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: This single-variable test gates an entire branch of the search space. If ViT-L singleprofile remains very weak (<0.30), we can confidently deprioritize all 36 multimodal configurations and redirect limited budget toward refining the RNA pipeline (e.g., confirming scvi_n200 multiprofile as the best RNA setup, or testing scgpt+transformer). If ViT-L shows substantially better performance, multimodal fusion with scvi_n200 becomes a high-value direction. Under a tight budget, this experiment maximizes information gain by resolving the most consequential open question—whether the image modality is worth integrating at all—before committing to any multimodal configuration.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile achieves the best performance (0.650-0.653), while image-only models are near chance (~0.21-0.23), indicating image is a very weak signal. The critical open question is whether fusing this weak image modality with the strong RNA signal can improve upon the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. This experiment (config_031: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) directly tests that question using the best-known RNA encoder and profile setting. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can learn to downweight the weak image features, making it the more robust fusion strategy when modality strengths are highly asymmetric. If this does not exceed ~0.653, we can confidently conclude image adds no value and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement; if it does, we gain evidence that multimodal fusion is worthwhile and should explore further.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.678) so far, only modestly above the RNA-only scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool baseline (config_005, 0.650). Image-only models are very weak (~0.21–0.23), so it is unclear how much the image branch is truly contributing versus adding noise. The only multimodal fusion tested so far is 'weighted'; we have no evidence on whether 'concat' fusion would perform comparably or differently. Question: config_030 is identical to config_031 except fusion=concat, giving a clean single-variable A/B test of the fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, isolating one design choice (fusion method) at the current best-performing configuration maximizes information gain. If concat ≈ weighted, the fusion choice is not a bottleneck and we can pivot to testing image encoder quality (ViT-L) or aggregation. If concat is substantially worse, we confirm weighted fusion is critical and should lock it in before exploring other axes. This avoids confounding multiple changes and directly informs whether the modest multimodal gain over RNA-only is robust to fusion design.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no baseline performance to reference. The most critical uncertainty is the performance floor of the simplest RNA-only model, which will calibrate whether more complex design choices (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, multimodal fusion) actually add value. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space—a standard PCA reduction with no learned encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. It establishes the baseline accuracy/F1 for RNA-based classification under the most minimal pipeline. 3) Why it is the best use of the first experiment: Starting with the simplest baseline is the highest-information first step because it anchors all subsequent comparisons. With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any useful signal for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001: it holds profile setting (singleprofile) and structural simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion) constant while switching modality from RNA to image. If image accuracy is substantially higher, it justifies investing further experiments in multimodal fusion and ViT encoders; if it is comparable or lower, it suggests RNA is the primary signal and the search should focus on RNA encoder and profile/aggregation choices. Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) only reaches 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. With only two data points, the largest uncertainty is whether a learned RNA representation can substantially improve over the PCA baseline. Question: config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001—only the RNA encoder changes. scgpt is a pretrained generative model for single-cell data that may capture richer biological structure than linear PCA. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It isolates the effect of representation quality on the dominant modality without confounding with profile, aggregation, or fusion changes. (2) The outcome directly guides all subsequent experiments—if scgpt substantially improves, we exploit that encoder across profile/fusion settings; if it does not, PCA is competitive and we pivot to testing multiprofile/aggregation or multimodal fusion. Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the best result so far at 0.485 acc, while scgpt (config_007, 0.411) underperforms and image-only resnet50 (config_010, 0.208) is very weak. The profile setting (single vs multi) is a critical, untested design axis that affects a large portion of the configuration space. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve upon the best singleprofile RNA result, while keeping the proven pca_n2000 encoder fixed? Why this is best: config_002 is a minimal, controlled change from config_001 (only profile setting and aggregation change), isolating the effect of multiprofile. Starting with avgpool (simpler aggregation) before transformer avoids confounding two new variables. The outcome directly informs whether to invest further experiments in multiprofile + transformer, multimodal multiprofile, or to abandon multiprofile altogether—making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA_n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, showing a large ~10.6% gain over single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.485). This strongly suggests multi-profile aggregation is a key design lever. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple avgpool in the multi-profile setting, or whether avgpool already captures most of the benefit. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model setting, profile setting, and encoder fixed to the best-known combination, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Evidence: Multi-profile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, a clear ~10-point gain over single-profile PCA (0.485), and avgpool beats transformer (0.519). However, scVI is completely untested across all experiments, leaving a major gap in encoder knowledge. It will clarify whether a learned variational encoder can match or exceed the simple PCA baseline in the strongest RNA configuration. This is the best next step because it reduces uncertainty about a critical, unexplored design axis with a clean single-variable comparison before investing budget in more complex multimodal experiments where encoder choice would be confounded with fusion effects.

The current best result is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. If avgpool wins again, we can confidently lock in avgpool for all future multimodal experiments and pivot to testing fusion strategies; if transformer wins, we learn that scvi_n200's structured latent space benefits from attention, which would change our aggregation choice for every downstream configuration. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile achieves ~0.65 acc (configs 005/006), far exceeding pca_n2000 singleprofile (0.485) and scgpt singleprofile (0.411). For pca_n2000, multiprofile+avgpool gave a ~0.106 boost over singleprofile, but we have no data on whether scvi_n200 benefits similarly from multiprofile or is already strong in singleprofile. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) isolates the profile-setting effect for the best-performing RNA encoder with only one variable changed relative to configs 005/006. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean single-factor comparison that directly tests whether the multiprofile gain is encoder-dependent or universal. (2) The result determines whether future multimodal experiments should use multiprofile or singleprofile for scvi_n200, saving budget by avoiding redundant variants. Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the clear best pipeline (acc ~0.65), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (acc 0.208). If performance drops or stays flat, we can eliminate the large multimodal search space and focus budget on refining the RNA pipeline. Evidence: The best RNA-only model (config_005/006, scvi_n200 multiprofile) achieves ~0.650-0.653 accuracy, while the only multimodal experiment (config_030, scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) scores 0.632 — actually below the RNA-only baseline. This suggests concat fusion may be diluting the strong RNA signal with weak image features (resnet50 alone is only 0.208). If weighted fusion recovers to ≥0.650, it confirms the image carries marginal signal that needs proper weighting; if it remains below 0.650, we gain strong evidence that resnet50 image features are unhelpful and should pivot to ViT-L (config_036/037). This is the most budget-efficient next step because it directly resolves whether the current multimodal setup is salvageable before committing experiments to a different image encoder.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about whether the data contains usable signal, how strong a simple baseline is, or which design axes (modality, profile, encoder, aggregation, fusion) will matter. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration—single modality, single profile, a lightweight linear encoder, no aggregation or fusion. With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest parallel baseline: same profile setting, same simplicity level, but swapping the modality. If image-only performs comparably to RNA-only (~48%), multimodal fusion is unlikely to add much; if it substantially outperforms, the image channel is a strong signal source and multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction; if it underperforms, RNA remains the dominant modality and effort should focus on improving RNA representations (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile). Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant signal modality. This experiment (config_002: rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable extension of config_001—only the profile setting changes from single to multi, with the simplest aggregation (avgpool)—isolating the effect of multi-profile aggregation on RNA performance. Evidence: The strongest result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, a ~10.6% improvement over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is highly beneficial. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether a transformer-based aggregation would further improve over simple average pooling, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this setup. Evidence: RNA dominates over image (0.485 vs 0.208), and within RNA, multi-profile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc 0.591) is clearly the best setup, beating both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). However, PCA is the only RNA encoder tested, so we cannot yet tell whether the learned representation quality is a bottleneck or whether the profile/aggregation design is the primary driver. Question: Does replacing PCA with the learned SCVI encoder (200-dim) improve performance when holding profile (multi) and aggregation (avgpool) fixed at their best-performing values? This isolates the encoder effect with a single-variable change from config_002. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether a more expressive RNA representation can push past the 0.591 ceiling, which determines whether subsequent multimodal experiments should pair a stronger encoder with image fusion. If SCVI matches or beats PCA, it justifies investing budget in multimodal configs with learned encoders; if it underperforms, PCA is sufficient and budget is better spent exploring fusion strategies. This is more informative than jumping to multimodal (where image's weakness confounds the fusion question) or testing image improvements (which seem unlikely to close the 0.38 gap to RNA).

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, showing that learned encoders substantially outperform PCA (0.591) under the same profile/aggregation settings, and avgpool outperforms transformer for aggregation. Uncertainty: SCGPT is a completely untested encoder—we have zero data on how its learned representations compare to SCVI. Question tested: Does scgpt under the best-known settings (multiprofile, avgpool) match or exceed scvi_n200? This is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005 (only the RNA encoder changes). Why best next experiment: It reduces the most uncertainty by probing an entirely new encoder dimension under controlled conditions. The result directly determines which learned encoder to carry forward into any future multimodal or profile-setting experiments, making it more informative than re-testing aggregation (already strong evidence for avgpool) or jumping to multimodal (multiple simultaneous changes, and image alone was very weak at 0.208).

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is our strongest result, and for pca_n2000 multiprofile, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519, config_002 vs config_003). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different (learned, nonlinear) representation than PCA, so the aggregation interaction may differ. Question: Does transformer aggregation help or hurt when paired with the scvi_n200 encoder, or does avgpool remain superior? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison (aggregation only) that directly extends our best-performing configuration. The answer will determine the optimal aggregation strategy for all subsequent multimodal experiments involving scvi_n200, making it a high-information, low-risk choice that reduces uncertainty about a critical design axis before we commit budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200/multiprofile/transformer is the current best (~0.653), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). The critical uncertainty is whether the image modality has any useful signal at all, or whether the poor resnet50 result reflects a fundamental lack of image informativeness. config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L) isolates the image encoder question by swapping resnet50 for a much stronger pretrained ViT-L while keeping everything else identical to config_010. This is a single-variable comparison that directly tells us whether image carries discriminative signal. If ViT-L is also weak, we can confidently rule out image and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement. If ViT-L is competitive, it justifies investing in multimodal fusion experiments (e.g., config_036/037). Without this prerequisite, any multimodal result would be confounded by not knowing whether the image branch contributes or dilutes the RNA signal.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool/transformer at ~0.65), while image-only models are very weak (ResNet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227). The critical open question is whether the weak image signal provides any complementary information when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment pairs the best-validated RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) with the simplest image encoder (ResNet50) and simplest fusion (concat), forming a clean comparison against config_005 (0.650) and config_006 (0.653). If config_030 fails to exceed ~0.65, it strongly suggests image adds no value and we can eliminate all 36 multimodal configs, redirecting budget to RNA-only refinement. If it does exceed, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion and motivates testing weighted fusion and ViT-L. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the single most consequential design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) with minimal confounding changes.

The key finding from config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 0.6315) is that the multimodal model underperforms the RNA-only counterpart (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool → 0.6501). This is surprising and suggests the image modality or the fusion strategy is harmful. Config_031 is a clean single-variable comparison with config_030, changing only the fusion from concat to weighted. This directly tests whether the way modalities are combined is the bottleneck. If weighted fusion recovers the gap, the issue is feature interaction and we should explore fusion strategies further. If it does not, we gain strong evidence that resnet50 image features are net-negative for this task, redirecting the remaining budget toward optimizing the RNA-only pipeline (e.g., transformer aggregation with scvi_n200) rather than multimodal variants. Given the limited budget, isolating this one variable is more informative than jumping to a different image encoder or aggregation, which would confound multiple factors.

With no prior experiments, the most informative first step is to establish a simple, well-understood baseline that will serve as a reference for all future comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the minimal configuration: a single modality, a single profile, and a linear (PCA) encoder with no learned components. This establishes the performance floor and eliminates confounding from encoder training dynamics, aggregation, or fusion. Subsequent experiments can then cleanly isolate the marginal contribution of each design axis—e.g., switching the RNA encoder to scVI or scGPT (configs 004/007), adding multiprofile + aggregation (configs 002/003), adding an image modality (configs 010/013), or combining modalities (configs 016+). Starting from the simplest reference point maximizes the information gained per experiment under a limited budget, because every future result can be interpreted as a delta from this anchor rather than as an absolute number with no context.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse and the most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries signal comparable to or stronger than RNA. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001: same profile setting (singleprofile), same simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion), differing only in modality/encoder. This isolates the question 'which modality is the stronger signal?' without confounding changes in profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. The answer is critical for all subsequent decisions: if image substantially outperforms RNA, we should prioritize image encoder and multimodal fusion experiments; if RNA is stronger, we focus on RNA encoder improvements; if both are weak, multimodal fusion becomes more appealing. No other single experiment reduces this top-level uncertainty as efficiently.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is weak at 20.8%. We have very sparse evidence and haven't yet tested whether the profile/aggregation dimension matters for the stronger modality. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the most direct extension of config_001, changing only the profile setting from single to multi (with the necessary avgpool aggregation), while keeping the same encoder. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation on RNA representation. Why best next: It builds on the strongest existing signal with a minimal, interpretable change. If multiprofile+avgpool improves over singleprofile, it validates the aggregation dimension and informs multimodal design (configs 018-027). If it does not improve, it tells us singleprofile suffices and we should focus budget on encoder quality or fusion strategy instead. This reduces the most critical uncertainty before committing experiments to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a substantial ~10.6% improvement over config_001 (same encoder, singleprofile, 0.485 acc), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is a high-impact design choice. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool). Question: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, isolating whether a learned, attention-based aggregation of profiles can further improve over simple averaging. Why best next experiment: This is a clean single-variable comparison on the strongest RNA configuration identified so far, directly testing whether the aggregation mechanism (a core architectural decision) can extract more signal from the multiprofile structure. The result will tell us whether to invest remaining budget in more complex aggregation/fusion designs or whether simple averaging already captures most of the multiprofile benefit, thereby guiding all subsequent multimodal and encoder choices.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, showing that multiprofile+avgpool substantially outperforms singleprofile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). However, PCA is the only RNA encoder tested, leaving a major uncertainty: whether a learned representation (scvi_n200) can improve upon PCA in the same multiprofile+avgpool setting. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares to config_002 by changing only the RNA encoder, cleanly isolating the representation effect while holding the best-performing profile and aggregation fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: It tests the most impactful untested design variable (encoder) in the context of our strongest configuration. If scvi_n200 matches or beats PCA, it validates learned representations and opens the door to scgpt and multimodal extensions. If it underperforms, it tells us PCA is surprisingly competitive and we should focus budget on other axes (image, fusion). Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about which encoder to build further upon, making this the highest-information-per-experiment choice under budget constraints.

Evidence: The jump from PCA to SCVI (config_002→config_005: 0.591→0.650) and the multiprofile+avgpool gain for PCA (config_001→config_002: 0.485→0.591) both contributed to the current best result, but we cannot yet disentangle how much of the SCVI gain comes from the encoder representation itself versus the multiprofile+avgpool pipeline. Uncertainty: Is SCVI a fundamentally stronger encoder, or does it primarily benefit from being paired with multiprofile+avgpool? This experiment (config_004: scvi_n200, singleprofile) isolates the encoder by removing the multiprofile/aggregation component while keeping SCVI fixed. If config_004 performs near 0.65, the encoder is the key driver and the pipeline can be simplified; if it drops toward ~0.48–0.52, the multiprofile+avgpool interaction is essential and remaining budget should focus on optimizing within that framework (e.g., SCGPT+avgpool). This single-variable ablation is the highest-information next step under the limited budget because it clarifies which design axis (encoder vs. profile/aggregation) should receive further exploration.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration so far is config_005 (scVI n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, clearly outperforming PCA (0.591) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The encoder choice (scVI vs PCA) and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) are both well-supported. However, scGPT is an entirely untested encoder, and we have no evidence about whether it could surpass scVI. Question: config_008 (scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the encoder effect by holding profile setting and aggregation fixed at their best-performing values, enabling a direct A/B comparison against config_005. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, identifying whether a superior encoder exists is the highest-leverage uncertainty to resolve. If scGPT matches or beats scVI, it opens a new design axis; if it underperforms, we can confidently commit to scVI and shift exploration toward fusion or image-encoder questions. This single experiment reduces uncertainty about the most important remaining design choice on the RNA side without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc. For pca_n2000, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different learned latent representation where attention-based aggregation could interact differently. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the aggregation choice matters for the best-performing encoder, or whether avgpool is simply a safe default. This experiment (config_006: scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, isolating the aggregation effect for the top encoder. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends the strongest evidence, answers a concrete design question that will guide whether to invest in transformer-based pipelines, and avoids the confound of simultaneously introducing a new modality.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer (config_006, acc 0.653) is the clear best so far, and image-only resnet50 is very weak (config_010, acc 0.208). The critical open question is whether adding image information via fusion provides any complementary signal beyond the strong RNA baseline, or whether the image modality is simply uninformative for this task. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) directly tests that question by adding the image branch to the exact best RNA configuration while keeping all other settings identical. Using concat (simplest fusion) and resnet50 (already characterized) limits confounding variables. If performance stays near 0.653, image adds no value and we can deprioritize multimodal configs; if it improves, we know the image carries complementary signal and should then explore ViT and weighted fusion. Under a tight budget, this single experiment most efficiently resolves whether the entire multimodal branch of the search space is worth further investment.

The best result so far (config_032, 0.6878 acc) uses scvi_n200 + ResNet50 in a multimodal setting, while the image-only ResNet50 baseline was very weak (0.2079 acc). This leaves a critical uncertainty: is the image modality contributing meaningfully, or is it limited by a weak encoder? Config_038 upgrades the image encoder to ViT-L (ImageNet-pretrained) while holding all other settings identical to config_032 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer, concat), giving a clean single-variable comparison. If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it confirms the image modality has untapped potential and justifies further image-encoder exploration; if it does not, it tells us the image signal is inherently limited and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side improvements or fusion. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves whether the second modality is a meaningful design axis at all, which governs the direction of all subsequent experiments.

With no prior evidence, the most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: RNA-only, single profile, PCA (n=2000). This establishes a performance floor and a reference point against which all other design choices (richer encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion) can be judged. If this minimal configuration already performs competitively, it challenges the assumption that complex encoders or multimodality are necessary, saving budget. If it underperforms, it identifies which dimension (representation, profile, modality) to explore next. Choosing the most parsimonious configuration first avoids conflating the effects of multiple design changes and gives the clearest signal for subsequent experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the evidence is extremely sparse and the performance is near chance. The most critical uncertainty is whether the low performance is specific to the RNA modality/encoding or reflects a broader task difficulty. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) tests the simplest image-only configuration with a well-established pretrained encoder, providing a clean baseline for the image modality. This is the most informative next step because: (1) it isolates the effect of modality (image vs RNA) while keeping the profile setting (singleprofile) and complexity (no aggregation/fusion) minimal, (2) it establishes whether image features carry useful signal for this classification task, which directly informs whether any multimodal configuration is worth pursuing, and (3) it broadens our understanding of the design space before committing to deeper exploration within one modality. If image performs substantially better, the bottleneck is RNA encoding; if it also performs poorly, the task or data may be the limiting factor. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty for all subsequent decisions.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant modality, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is very weak at 20.8%. The key uncertainty is whether moving from a single profile to multiple profiles with aggregation can improve the RNA signal, since this structural choice gates a large portion of the remaining search space (all multiprofile and multimodal configs). Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the minimal change from config_001—same encoder, same modality—adding only multiprofile with a simple avgpool aggregation. This cleanly isolates the effect of profile setting/aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: if multiprofile+avgpool improves over singleprofile, it validates the multiprofile branch and justifies investing in aggregation variants (transformer) and learned encoders on top of it; if it does not help, we can prune the multiprofile branch and focus budget on encoder choice (scvi, scgpt) or better image encoders. This single experiment reduces the most consequential uncertainty in the search tree with a low-risk, well-controlled comparison.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is our best result at 0.591 acc, substantially outperforming config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming multiprofile aggregation adds significant value. However, we have not yet tested whether the aggregation mechanism itself (avgpool vs transformer) matters. Question: config_003 isolates a single variable—aggregation (transformer vs avgpool)—holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (multiprofile), and modality (rna_only) constant. This directly tests whether a learned, attention-based aggregation of multiple profiles captures inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the cleanest single-variable comparison to our strongest result, reducing confounding; (2) the aggregation choice is a foundational design decision that will propagate to all future multimodal experiments, so resolving it early saves budget; (3) if transformer aggregation yields a meaningful gain over avgpool, it justifies investing in transformer-based configs for subsequent encoder and fusion tests; if not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion questions. This balances exploitation (building on the best config) with targeted exploration of an important, untested design axis.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, and it clearly outperforms single-profile (config_001, 0.485) and transformer aggregation (config_003, 0.519). Image-only is very weak (0.208). The only RNA encoder tested so far is PCA n2000, leaving a major uncertainty: does a learned nonlinear encoder (scvi) improve over linear PCA when the profile and aggregation are held at their best-performing settings? Question: config_005 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 while keeping multi-profile + avgpool (the winning combination from config_002), isolating the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single-variable comparison against our current best, directly tests a fundamental representation choice that could shift the ceiling for all downstream multimodal experiments, and avoids prematurely committing budget to multimodal fusion when the RNA backbone itself may not yet be optimized. If scvi matches or beats PCA, we gain confidence in the encoder direction; if it underperforms, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can pivot to multimodal or scgpt with clearer rationale.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (config_005, acc=0.650) is the best result so far, and for PCA-based encoders, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (config_002: 0.591 vs config_003: 0.519). However, scvi produces a learned 200-dim representation that may interact differently with aggregation than linear PCA. Question: Does transformer aggregation help, hurt, or match avgpool when paired with the scvi encoder? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005). Why this is the best next step: The answer directly determines whether we should invest subsequent experiments in transformer-based multimodal configs (e.g., config_032/033) or avgpool-based ones (config_030/031), making it a high-leverage decision for the remaining budget. It also confirms whether the avgpool>transformer preference is a general principle or encoder-specific.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.653) massively outperform the single image-only test (config_010, resnet50, 0.208). The image modality appears very weak, but we cannot yet tell whether this is because the image modality carries no useful signal or because resnet50 is a poor encoder for this task. Question: config_013 (image_only, ViT-L, singleprofile) isolates the image-encoder variable by swapping resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l while keeping everything else identical to config_010. If ViT-L also yields ~0.2 accuracy, the image modality is fundamentally uninformative and multimodal fusion is unlikely to add value, freeing budget for RNA-encoder refinement (e.g., scgpt). If ViT-L substantially improves, the image modality has recoverable signal and multimodal experiments become a high-priority direction. This single-variable comparison is the most informative use of the next experiment because it resolves the critical uncertainty about whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal fusion or to focus exclusively on optimizing the RNA pathway.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.48–0.65) vastly outperform image-only models (0.21–0.23), and the best RNA setup is scvi_n200 + multiprofile (config_005/006, ~0.65). However, no multimodal configuration has been tested yet, leaving a critical uncertainty: does fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal help or hurt? Question: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) isolates the effect of adding image features via simple concatenation to the best-known RNA pipeline. If accuracy drops below 0.65, image is net noise and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-only encoder/aggregation refinements (e.g., scgpt). If it matches or exceeds 0.65, multimodal fusion is viable and justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and ViT backbones. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single, clean extension of the top RNA-only result (only change: add resnet50 image + concat fusion), directly resolves the go/no-go question for the entire multimodal branch, and prevents wasting limited budget on 20+ multimodal configs if image contributes no useful signal.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile+avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is the strongest RNA-only result, and adding image (config_030, acc 0.632) actually underperforms it, confirming image is a weak/negative contributor. The scgpt encoder has not been tested in any experiment, leaving a critical gap in our understanding of which RNA representation is best. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as a single-cell RNA encoder under identical conditions (multiprofile, avgpool)? config_008 is directly comparable to config_005, isolating only the encoder variable. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving which RNA encoder is superior is the highest-leverage decision because it determines the backbone for all future multimodal and aggregation experiments. A single-variable comparison against a known result (config_005) gives clean evidence without confounding, and the outcome will either reveal a new best encoder to exploit or confirm scvi_n200 as the ceiling, letting us redirect remaining budget toward aggregation/fusion refinements.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool/transformer) achieves ~0.650-0.653 accuracy, while the only multimodal test (config_030: scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored 0.632, slightly below RNA-only. Image-only models are very weak (0.21-0.23), raising the question of whether the image modality is fundamentally unhelpful or whether the concat fusion is simply the wrong strategy. Question: config_031 is identical to config_030 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, providing a clean single-variable comparison. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only baseline (~0.650), it shows that fusion strategy is critical and multimodal is a viable direction worth further exploration. If it also underperforms, it strongly indicates the image modality (at least resnet50) is not contributing useful signal, allowing us to redirect budget toward RNA-only refinement. Why best under limited budget: This is the highest-information next step because it directly resolves the key uncertainty (is multimodal salvageable with better fusion?) with a minimal, controlled change, and the answer will determine whether subsequent experiments should target multimodal variants or focus on RNA-only optimization.

With no prior experiments, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a clear, low-cost baseline to anchor all future comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: it uses a standard, well-understood linear encoder (PCA to 2000 dims) on a single RNA profile, avoiding confounds from multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders, image processing, or fusion. This gives a fast, reliable reference for RNA-only performance. Subsequent experiments can then isolate the marginal contribution of each design axis (multiprofile + aggregation, alternative RNA encoders, image modality, multimodal fusion) by holding other factors constant relative to this baseline. Choosing the simplest baseline first maximizes information per experiment because every later result can be interpreted as a delta from this reference, and it is computationally cheap, preserving budget for more complex configurations later.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical uncertainty for a multimodal study is whether image data carries useful signal for this task at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the image-only baseline under the same profile setting as config_001, allowing a clean modality comparison. If image-only substantially outperforms or underperforms RNA-only, it immediately tells us whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and which modality dominates. If performance is similar, it suggests complementary signals that fusion could exploit. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty (is image informative?) before committing budget to the many multimodal configurations, making it the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether multiprofile aggregation improves the RNA signal, which is the most fundamental architectural question before investing in multimodal fusion or more complex encoders. This experiment (config_002) tests whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation helps the already-dominant RNA modality, using the same pca_n2000 encoder as config_001 for a clean, single-factor comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the answer directly determines whether to pursue transformer aggregation, better RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion in subsequent experiments—if multiprofile doesn't help RNA, the search space simplifies dramatically; if it does, it justifies further investment in aggregation and fusion design.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a substantial +10.6% improvement over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is a major performance lever. However, we only have one data point for aggregation (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unclear whether transformer-based aggregation captures inter-profile structure more effectively than simple averaging, which would be critical for all downstream multiprofile and multimodal experiments. This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly one variable—aggregation method (transformer vs avgpool)—while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and RNA encoder constant. It directly extends the strongest result and resolves a design choice that will inform every subsequent multiprofile configuration. Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison is the most informative next step: it either confirms avgpool is sufficient (simplifying the search space) or reveals that transformer aggregation unlocks further gains (justifying its use in multimodal settings).

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly dominate (0.485–0.591) over image-only ResNet50 (0.208), and within RNA, multi-profile with avgpool aggregation (config_002, acc 0.591) is the best setting so far, outperforming both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Uncertainty: PCA n2000 is the only RNA encoder tested; it is a linear dimensionality reduction and may leave substantial signal on the table. Question: Does replacing the linear PCA encoder with the learned scvi_n200 VAE encoder improve performance in the already-best RNA configuration (multi-profile, avgpool)? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA is the dominant signal, so improving its representation is the highest-leverage design decision before committing budget to multimodal fusion. If scvi_n200 lifts accuracy meaningfully over PCA, it validates learned encoders and directly informs which RNA encoder to pair with image in later multimodal runs. If it does not help, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can focus budget on fusion/image questions. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about a core design axis.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.650) over image-only (0.208). Within RNA, the encoder choice is the largest source of variation: scvi_n200 (0.650) clearly beats pca_n2000 (0.591) under the same multiprofile+avgpool setting, and avgpool consistently outperforms transformer. The current best is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650). Question: Does the third available encoder, scgpt, outperform scvi_n200 under the same multiprofile+avgpool conditions? This is a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the encoder effect. Why this experiment: Before investing in multimodal or more complex fusion experiments, it is critical to identify the best RNA encoder so that any multimodal test uses the strongest unimodal baseline. config_008 directly answers whether scgpt is a better or worse representation than scvi_n200, reducing uncertainty about the most impactful design choice (encoder) with minimal confounds, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, and we know avgpool beat transformer for pca_n2000 (0.591 vs 0.519 in configs 002/003). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different learned representation than PCA, so the aggregation interaction may differ. Uncertainty: whether transformer aggregation could outperform avgpool when paired with scvi_n200's richer, non-linear features. This experiment (config_006) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding everything else constant (scvi_n200, multiprofile, rna_only), giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. This is the best next step because it finalizes the optimal RNA pipeline (encoder + aggregation) before committing budget to multimodal fusion experiments, which all depend on this choice. A clear result here will directly inform which aggregation to pair with scvi_n200 in any subsequent multimodal configuration.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool/transformer) achieves ~0.65 acc, while image-only with resnet50 is near chance (0.208). The critical unanswered question is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal via concat fusion yields any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_005 (RNA-only, same encoder/profile/aggregation, acc=0.650): the only added factor is the image branch and concat fusion. If accuracy stays near or below 0.65, it strongly suggests the image modality (with resnet50) adds no value and budget should focus on RNA-only refinement. If it improves, it justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and image encoders. This is the most informative next step because it directly resolves the central multimodality question before committing budget to more complex fusion or image-encoder variants.

The most striking finding from the completed experiments is that the multimodal config (config_030: scvi_n200 + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat, acc=0.632) underperforms the RNA-only scvi_n200 configs (config_005: 0.650, config_006: 0.653), and image-only ResNet50 is very weak (0.208). This raises a critical question: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task, or is ResNet50 simply a poor encoder? Config_036 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + avgpool + concat) changes only the image encoder relative to config_030, cleanly isolating whether a stronger visual representation can contribute complementary signal. If config_036 approaches or exceeds the RNA-only ceiling (~0.653), it validates the multimodal direction and justifies further fusion/aggregation exploration. If it remains at or below RNA-only levels, it strongly indicates the image modality adds no value, allowing us to redirect the remaining budget toward RNA-only refinement (e.g., scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation, or scgpt comparisons). This is the highest-information single-variable experiment available under the budget constraint.

The current best configuration (config_036: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.715 accuracy, a substantial jump over RNA-only scvi_n200 (0.653) and over multimodal with resnet50 (0.632). This is the highest-information single-variable test available: it directly exploits the strongest configuration while probing an entirely unexplored design choice, making it the best use of the next experiment under a limited budget.

No experiments have been completed, so the critical first question is: what is the performance floor of the simplest possible model? config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA n2000) is the most minimal configuration in the search space—it uses a linear projection, a single profile (no aggregation), and no image or fusion components. Running this first establishes the baseline RNA signal strength with minimal assumptions, which is essential for interpreting all subsequent experiments. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty with the least risk of confounding, since no design choice is 'turned on' simultaneously.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides the cleanest possible comparison to the existing baseline: same profile setting (singleprofile), same simplicity level (no aggregation, no fusion), differing only in modality. If image_only approaches or exceeds 0.485, it confirms image features are informative and justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion. This single experiment resolves the largest structural design question (modality value) while keeping the comparison maximally controlled, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant signal. Evidence: scvi_n200 is our best RNA encoder (0.520 acc) vs pca_n2000 (0.485), and image alone (resnet50) is very weak (0.208). Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile, 0.520), confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. Evidence: Multiprofile RNA models with scvi_n200 (config_005/006) achieve ~0.65 acc, far outperforming singleprofile and image-only baselines. Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.721 acc, substantially above RNA-only best (0.653) and image-only (0.208), confirming that fusion of a strong RNA encoder with a strong image encoder is highly beneficial. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile (multiple profiles per cell) provides additional discriminative signal for RNA, and this is a fundamental design axis that affects a large portion of the remaining search space. This experiment (config_002) isolates the effect of multiprofile + avgpool aggregation on the already-best modality and encoder (PCA n2000), changing only profile_setting and adding a simple aggregation relative to config_001. If multiprofile helps, it validates the entire multiprofile branch and motivates testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not, we can deprioritize multiprofile configurations and focus on encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt). Under a tight budget, this single-variable extension of the current best result maximally reduces uncertainty about a high-impact design choice.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a +10.6pp gain over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile representation is highly beneficial. However, we only have one data point for multiprofile aggregation (avgpool). The key uncertainty is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further exploit the multi-profile structure, or whether simple averaging already captures most of the signal. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all else constant (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000), giving a clean A/B comparison against config_002. This is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it isolates a single design variable, (2) the answer directly determines whether transformer aggregation is worth the added complexity in all future multiprofile configurations (including multimodal ones), and (3) it builds on the strongest baseline we currently have, maximizing the chance of finding an improvement while still being informative if it does not.

Evidence: RNA-only with multiprofile + avgpool + PCA (config_002, 0.591) is the best result so far, substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and image-only (0.208). Aggregation choice matters (avgpool > transformer by ~7 pts). However, PCA n2000 is the only RNA encoder tested, leaving a major uncertainty: whether a learned nonlinear representation (scvi_n200) captures more biologically meaningful structure than linear PCA. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and aggregation at their best-known values, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: it tests the single most important untested design axis (representation quality) in the strongest-performing regime, and the result will determine whether to invest remaining budget in learned encoders or pivot toward multimodal fusion with the PCA baseline.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, showing that (a) multiprofile + avgpool is a strong combination and (b) scvi_n200 outperforms PCA_n2000 by ~0.059 under identical settings. However, we have no data on scgpt, a third learned encoder, and it is unclear whether it can match or exceed scvi_n200. Question tested: config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) holds profile setting and aggregation constant while swapping the encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next: Under a limited budget, establishing which RNA encoder is superior before committing to multimodal experiments (which are more complex and expensive) is the highest-information-value step. A clean A/B encoder comparison under the best-known profile/aggregation settings will either reveal a new best encoder to exploit in subsequent multimodal trials or confirm scvi_n200 as the optimal backbone, reducing uncertainty about the most impactful design axis before we add fusion complexity.

Evidence: RNA-only models (especially scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool at 0.650) dominate, while the only image test (resnet50, singleprofile) scored just 0.208, suggesting image features may be uninformative. However, this single data point conflates modality value with encoder quality. Uncertainty: We cannot yet tell whether images are fundamentally uninformative for this task or whether resnet50 is simply a poor image encoder for cellular profiles. This experiment tests imagenet_vit_l (a much stronger, pretrained vision transformer) in the simplest possible image-only setting, isolating the image encoder quality question without confounding effects from fusion, aggregation, or profile settings. Why this is the best next step: Before investing limited budget in any of the 36 multimodal configurations, we must resolve whether the image modality can contribute meaningful signal at all. If ViT-L also yields low accuracy, we can confidently rule out image/multimodal directions and focus remaining experiments on RNA-only refinements. If ViT-L performs substantially better, multimodal fusion becomes a high-value exploration target. This single experiment gates an entire branch of the search space and is therefore the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.485–0.650) dramatically outperform image-only models (0.208–0.227), and the best configuration so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. The critical unresolved question is whether the image modality, despite its very weak standalone performance, provides any complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation. This experiment tests that question in the most controlled way: it pairs the best-performing RNA setup (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool) with the simpler image encoder (resnet50) and simplest fusion (concat), changing only the addition of the image branch relative to config_005. If config_030 fails to beat 0.650, it strongly indicates that image features are uninformative for this task, allowing us to eliminate all 36 multimodal configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinements. If it does improve, it confirms complementary signal and justifies further exploration of fusion strategies and image encoders. This is the highest-information single experiment under the limited budget because it resolves the largest remaining design uncertainty (is multimodality worth pursuing at all?) with a minimal, interpretable change.

Evidence: The best RNA-only model (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.632 acc—a slight drop. Image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23), so the image branch may be adding noise. Question: Does weighted fusion (config_031) mitigate the small performance loss from adding the weak image modality, potentially allowing multimodal to match or exceed the RNA-only baseline? This is a single-variable change (concat→weighted) from config_030, isolating the fusion strategy. Why best next: It directly tests whether the multimodal direction is salvageable with the best RNA encoder, and if weighted fusion recovers the ~2-point gap, it justifies further multimodal exploration; if not, it confirms RNA-only is the better path and saves budget from pursuing a dead end.

Evidence: The current best is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678). RNA is the dominant modality, and image-only models perform poorly (~0.21-0.23), suggesting limited image signal. However, we have only tested resnet50 as the image encoder in the multimodal setting. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l (a stronger pretrained encoder) improve the multimodal fusion result, or is the image contribution inherently limited regardless of encoder quality? This experiment (config_037) changes exactly one variable—image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l—relative to the current best, isolating the image representation effect. Why best next step: It is a clean single-variable comparison that directly informs whether further investment in image-side improvements is worthwhile or whether the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., RNA encoder, aggregation). If ViT-L helps, it opens a promising direction; if not, it confirms the image modality's ceiling and redirects budget toward RNA-side or fusion refinements. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (config_033), where RNA-only evidence already strongly favors avgpool.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit. The most informative first experiment is to establish a minimal baseline: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 (config_001). This configuration has the fewest design decisions (no aggregation, no fusion, no image encoder), making it a clean reference point. It tests the fundamental question: how well does a simple PCA-reduced RNA representation perform on this task? From this baseline, subsequent experiments can isolate the marginal contribution of each added complexity—multiprofile/aggregation (config_002/003), alternative RNA encoders (config_004/007), image modality (config_010), and multimodal fusion (config_016/017). Starting with the simplest configuration avoids conflating multiple design choices and ensures that any later performance gains can be attributed to specific additions rather than to an unknown interaction of several untested components simultaneously.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), giving us essentially no information about whether the image modality contributes predictive signal or whether multimodal fusion is beneficial. The central question for this multimodal cellular profiling study is whether combining image with RNA improves over RNA alone. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal, clean extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), the same profile setting (singleprofile), and adds only the image modality with a standard ResNet50 and simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding the image modality. If config_016 substantially outperforms 0.485, it justifies investing further in multimodal configurations and image encoder/aggregation choices; if it does not, it redirects the search toward RNA-only improvements (better encoders, multiprofile aggregation). This is the highest-information-gain experiment given the near-total absence of evidence about the image modality's contribution.

We have only two data points: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 0.485 acc and multimodal (pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat, singleprofile) at 0.527 acc. The ~4% gain from adding the image is meaningful, but we cannot yet determine whether this gain reflects genuine complementary information from fusion or simply that the image features are a stronger predictor on their own. Testing config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the image-only baseline, directly isolating the image modality's independent contribution. This is the single most informative missing piece: if image-only is near 0.52, the multimodal gain is modest and fusion strategy matters less; if image-only is well below 0.48, the multimodal model is extracting real complementary signal and fusion/aggregation choices become high-value next questions. Under a tight budget with sparse evidence, reducing uncertainty about this fundamental modality-contribution question is more valuable than prematurely optimizing fusion type or profile setting, which would be harder to interpret without the image baseline.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) improves to 0.527, confirming that adding image helps. However, the multiprofile axis (with aggregation) remains entirely untested. Question: Does using multiple profiles with avgpool aggregation improve over the single-profile baseline for the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000)? This directly compares to config_001, changing only the profile/aggregation setting while holding model setting and RNA encoder fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: The multiprofile decision is the most consequential unexplored axis—if it provides a meaningful gain in the simpler rna_only setting, it is very likely to compound in multimodal configurations (configs 018–051), and we should prioritize those; if it does not help, we can safely focus remaining budget on singleprofile configurations and other axes (RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion). Testing this in rna_only isolates the aggregation effect without the confound of multimodal fusion, making the result maximally interpretable under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc, showing multiprofile aggregation is a major gain over singleprofile (0.485). Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, concat) showed that adding resnet50 image features to RNA provides a modest but consistent boost (+0.042 over config_001). Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the image modality's benefit transfers to the multiprofile setting, or whether the stronger RNA signal in multiprofile makes the weak image contribution redundant. Config_018 tests exactly this: it keeps the proven multiprofile+avgpool+pca_n2000 backbone from config_002 and adds resnet50 with concat fusion (the same fusion that worked in config_016), changing only the modality composition. This is the most informative next step because (a) it directly extends the two strongest findings, (b) it isolates the effect of adding image to the multiprofile context, and (c) the result will clarify whether further multimodal experiments (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, ViT) are worth pursuing or whether the multiprofile RNA signal is already near its ceiling.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, and multiprofile + avgpool was the single largest improvement observed (config_001→002: +0.106 RNA-only; config_016→018: +0.092 multimodal). However, we have zero information on whether transformer aggregation could further improve profile integration. Question: config_020 is identical to config_018 except aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer, giving a clean single-variable A/B test of the aggregation mechanism in the strongest known setting. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly exploits our strongest evidence with the minimal change needed to resolve whether the current avgpool is near-optimal or whether a sequence-aware aggregator captures inter-profile interactions that matter for the dominant RNA signal. The result immediately informs whether all future multiprofile configurations should default to transformer or avgpool, reducing uncertainty across the entire remaining search space.

Evidence: Our best result is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1. All completed experiments use concat fusion; we have zero data on weighted fusion. The key uncertainty is whether the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) meaningfully affects how the RNA and image signals combine, which is a fundamental architectural choice. Question: config_019 is identical to config_018 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, giving a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates the fusion effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) Fusion is a completely untested design axis, so any result reduces uncertainty on a core decision. (2) The answer generalizes across all future multimodal configurations—if weighted fusion helps, we adopt it everywhere; if not, we confirm concat suffices and can pivot to RNA encoder or image encoder exploration. (3) It is the most budget-efficient choice: one experiment resolves a binary architectural question with no confounds, rather than testing a new RNA encoder (e.g., scvi) which, while also informative, is a second-order question relative to how the two modalities are combined.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant signal (rna_only 0.485 vs image_only 0.208), and our best result (config_019, acc 0.639) uses PCA as the RNA encoder. The RNA encoder is the most important unexplored design axis—we have zero evidence on whether a learned encoder (scvi_n200) could improve upon PCA. Question: Does replacing pca_n2000 with scvi_n200 in the multimodal multiprofile pipeline (keeping resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion fixed) improve performance? This is a single-variable change from our current best (config_019), cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect in the setting most likely to yield the highest accuracy. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests the highest-impact unexplored axis in the configuration regime where we expect the best results, and the outcome (improvement or not) will guide all subsequent encoder choices across the remaining search space.

The current best (config_031: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.678) establishes a clear winning direction. However, the image encoder dimension is completely unexplored—only resnet50 has been tested. Config_037 changes exactly one variable (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) while holding all other settings at their proven-best values (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This cleanly isolates the image encoder effect: if accuracy improves, the image modality is a bottleneck and a stronger visual representation unlocks further gains; if it does not, resnet50 is sufficient and the image contribution has plateaued. This is the highest-value single-variable test because it extends the current best along an untested axis, maintains the exploitation of the strong scvi+weighted+avgpool evidence, and directly informs whether further investment in the image branch is warranted under the limited budget.

The current best (config_037, acc=0.706) uses scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, but scgpt has never been tested in any experiment.
