The progression from pca→scvi yielded a meaningful +0.039 gain (config_019→config_031), and the image encoder upgrade (resnet50→ViT-L) added another +0.028 (config_031→config_037). The RNA encoder is the single most impactful design axis, and we have only tested 2 of 3 options. Config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from config_037, isolating the effect of the RNA encoder in the best overall setting. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can focus remaining budget on finer-tuning (e.g., aggregation or fusion). This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space with a direct A/B comparison against the current best.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most informative. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most 'null' RNA configuration. It establishes the baseline performance of RNA data with a standard, non-learned dimensionality reduction (PCA) and the simplest profile setting. This gives a clear reference point to later isolate the effect of learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, image modality, and fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first experiment should be fast, interpretable, and maximally informative as a reference. PCA is computationally cheap and introduces no learned-representation confound, singleprofile eliminates the aggregation variable, and rna_only isolates the RNA signal. A strong result confirms RNA carries useful signal and sets a floor; a weak result immediately redirects attention toward image or multimodal configurations. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty per unit of compute and provides the anchor against which every subsequent comparison (encoder choice, profile setting, modality, fusion) can be measured.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the highest-priority uncertainty is whether the image modality adds complementary signal to RNA. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the most direct extension of config_001: it keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical and adds only the image branch with a simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding image information with minimal confounds. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 48.5%, it confirms multimodal fusion is worth further exploration (better image encoders, fusion strategies, multiprofile). If it does not improve, it tells me the image modality (at least via resnet50) is not complementary to this RNA representation, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder quality or multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most impactful design-axis question (model setting) before committing budget to deeper sub-axes like aggregation or fusion method.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc, a +4.2 pp gain. However, we cannot yet decompose whether this gain comes from the image modality alone or from a genuine synergistic combination. Uncertainty: We lack an image-only baseline with the same resnet50 encoder, so we cannot attribute the multimodal improvement to either modality or to interaction. This experiment (config_010: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the image contribution by holding the image encoder and profile setting constant while removing RNA. It is the best next step because it directly decomposes the multimodal gain, informs whether further multimodal complexity (fusion variants, multiprofile aggregation) is warranted, and is a single-variable comparison to both prior experiments—maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 52.66% acc / 51.04% F1, outperforming RNA alone (config_001: 48.49%) by ~4.2 points, confirming that the weak image modality (config_010: 20.79%) still adds complementary signal. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining the asymmetrically-contributing RNA and image representations? config_017 is identical to config_016 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, making this a clean single-variable A/B test. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends our strongest configuration, isolates exactly one design decision (fusion method), and the answer will inform the fusion choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments (multiprofile, alternative encoders). Under a limited budget, resolving whether fusion strategy matters before scaling to more complex settings (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, different encoders) avoids wasting experiments on a suboptimal fusion baseline.

Evidence: The current best (config_016, multimodal/singleprofile/pca/resnet50/concat, acc 0.527) shows that RNA is the dominant signal and adding ResNet50 image features gives a modest ~4% boost over RNA-only. However, the profile axis (single vs. multi) is completely unexplored across all four experiments, representing the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space. Question: config_018 extends config_016 by switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) constant. Because aggregation is a necessary consequence of multiprofile, this isolates a single design decision—whether multiple profiles improve the representation. Why best next experiment: If multiprofile helps, it opens the aggregation axis (avgpool vs. transformer) and confirms a promising direction for further exploitation. If it does not, we can eliminate ~30 multiprofile configurations and refocus on RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt) or image encoder (ViT-L) variations. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental axis is more informative than testing a secondary encoder swap that might be confounded by an unexplored profile/aggregation interaction.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best result (acc 0.619, F1 0.610), showing a large ~9% gain over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (config_016, acc 0.527). However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. In the singleprofile comparison, concat vs weighted fusion made almost no difference (0.527 vs 0.523), suggesting fusion is a lower-priority axis. The aggregation mechanism is a more fundamental design choice: avgpool simply averages profile representations, while a transformer can model interactions between profiles. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when combining multiple profiles in a multimodal model, holding fusion=concat constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_020 changes exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool→transformer) relative to our current best (config_018), giving a clean isolation of the aggregation effect. If transformer helps substantially, it reveals that profile interactions are informative and justifies further investment in richer aggregation; if it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder choices. This is the highest-information single experiment available under the limited budget.

The strongest result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 0.619), which jumps ~9 points over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (0.527). However, we cannot yet decompose whether this multiprofile gain is driven primarily by better RNA aggregation (avgpool over multiple profiles) or by a synergistic interaction between multiprofile RNA and the image branch. Image-only performance is very weak (0.208), suggesting the image signal is limited, but we have no direct evidence for its marginal contribution in the multiprofile regime. config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean ablation that removes only the image branch while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical to config_018. If rna_only multiprofile approaches 0.58–0.60, the image adds little and future budget should target RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt); if it stays near 0.50, the image still contributes meaningfully and image-encoder upgrades become worthwhile. This single experiment resolves the most important architectural uncertainty and will efficiently direct all subsequent choices under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result at 0.619 acc, and RNA signal is the dominant driver (RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reaches 0.591, while image-only is only 0.208). The only RNA encoder tested so far is the simple linear PCA (pca_n2000). Question: Does a learned nonlinear RNA representation (SCVI) improve over PCA in the strongest configuration, holding all other design choices (multiprofile, avgpool, resnet50, concat) constant? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates the RNA encoder effect in the highest-performing regime without changing multiple variables simultaneously. If SCVI improves performance, it identifies the RNA representation as a key lever for further gains; if it does not, it tells us PCA already captures the relevant variance and we should look elsewhere (e.g., image encoder or fusion). This is more informative than testing weighted fusion (config_019), where the singleprofile evidence (0.527 vs 0.523) suggests only a marginal difference, or testing a new image encoder when image-only performance is so weak that the image contribution appears limited.

Evidence: The current best config (030, multimodal/multiprofile/scvi_n200/resnet50/avgpool/concat, acc=0.632) outperforms its pca_n2000 counterpart (config_018, acc=0.619) by ~0.013, suggesting scvi_n200 may be a superior RNA encoder. However, this comparison conflates encoder quality with potential RNA-image interaction effects. Uncertainty: We lack a clean RNA-only comparison to determine whether scvi_n200 is genuinely a better representation or whether its small edge is specific to the multimodal context. Question tested: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly contrasts with config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, acc=0.591) as a single-variable ablation of RNA encoder. Why best next experiment: This is the cleanest available isolation of the RNA encoder variable with all other factors held constant. The result will (a) confirm or refute scvi_n200 as a generally better encoder, guiding all future multimodal experiments, and (b) quantify the RNA-only ceiling so we can better attribute gains in multimodal settings to image contribution vs. encoder quality. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational variable before further exploring image encoders or fusion strategies is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The current best configuration is rna_only + scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (0.650). Strikingly, adding resnet50 image in multimodal mode actually *hurts* performance (config_030: 0.632 vs config_005: 0.650). However, resnet50 is a weak encoder (image_only accuracy is only 0.208), so it is unclear whether the image modality is fundamentally unhelpful or whether a stronger encoder would provide complementary signal. 2) What this tests: config_036 is a clean single-variable change from config_030 (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), holding model_setting=multimodal, profile=multiprofile, rna_encoder=scvi_n200, aggregation=avgpool, and fusion=concat constant. It directly asks whether a much stronger visual encoder can make the image modality additive with the best RNA encoder. 3) Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether image has any value with scvi_n200 is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact question. A positive result opens the multimodal+ViT-L direction for further optimization; a negative result lets us confidently discard the image modality and focus remaining experiments on RNA encoder/aggregation improvements. No other single experiment reduces as much decision-relevant uncertainty.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no prior evidence to exploit. The most critical first step is to establish a simple, well-understood performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest RNA-based configuration: PCA is a standard, parameter-free encoder, singleprofile avoids aggregation confounds, and rna_only avoids fusion confounds. This experiment (1) provides a performance floor against which all other RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), profile settings (multiprofile), and multimodal configurations can be compared; (2) is the most computationally inexpensive option, preserving budget for subsequent informative experiments; and (3) isolates the contribution of the RNA modality in its most basic form, which is essential context before testing whether more complex encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or image fusion actually add value. Without this baseline, any later performance differences would be uninterpretable.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this question: it matches config_001 on profile setting (singleprofile) and model simplicity, changing only the modality. This isolates the 'does image information help?' question without confounding with fusion strategy, aggregation, or multiprofile complexity. The result will directly inform whether to invest subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion (if image is strong) or in RNA encoder/profile improvements (if image is weak), making it the highest-information-value use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is only 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant modality. The only RNA encoder tested so far is PCA (a linear method), so we have no evidence about whether a learned nonlinear representation (e.g., scVI) could improve RNA-based classification. Question: config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates exactly one variable—the RNA encoder—against config_001, cleanly testing whether a learned latent representation outperforms PCA in the same single-profile, RNA-only setting. Why this is best: With a limited budget, the highest-leverage question is whether we can improve the dominant modality's representation before investing in multiprofile aggregation, alternative image encoders, or multimodal fusion. A clean encoder comparison (scvi_n200 vs. pca_n2000, all else held constant) reduces the most important uncertainty with a single experiment, and the result will directly inform whether to pursue learned encoders in subsequent multiprofile or multimodal configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.5203 acc) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.4849) as the RNA encoder in singleprofile, and image-only is very weak (0.2079), confirming RNA dominates the signal. Uncertainty: we have zero data on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves over singleprofile, a choice that gates many downstream multimodal experiments. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a minimal single-variable extension of the best existing config (config_004), isolating the effect of multiprofile with average-pool aggregation on the strongest RNA representation. If it improves over 0.5203, it validates the multiprofile direction and justifies further aggregation/fusion exploration; if it does not, it efficiently prunes a large portion of the search space (configs 002,003,006,008,009,011,012,014,015,018-027,030-039,042-051) under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.650, F1 0.628), a large jump over singleprofile scvi_n200 (0.520). This confirms multiprofile + avgpool is highly beneficial. However, we have no data on whether transformer aggregation could further improve upon avgpool in this setting. Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation method (avgpool → transformer) while keeping the same encoder (scvi_n200), profile setting (multiprofile), and modality (rna_only), isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next step: It is a single-variable extension of our strongest result, directly testing whether a more expressive aggregation can push performance higher. The answer will inform the aggregation choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 018-051), making it highly informative for the remaining search. It balances exploitation (building on the best config) with exploration (testing an untested aggregation in the multiprofile regime).

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile+transformer achieves 0.653, a large gain over its single-profile counterpart (0.520), while pca_n2000 single-profile is 0.485. The aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference (0.650 vs 0.653), so it is not the key lever. Uncertainty: We do not know whether the ~0.13 multiprofile gain is specific to scvi's learned representation or a general property of multi-profile aggregation. Question: config_003 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer) directly compares against config_006 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) with only the RNA encoder changed, isolating the encoder effect in the multiprofile regime. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison that tells us whether the multiprofile benefit is encoder-agnostic (suggesting we should focus on aggregation/fusion next) or encoder-specific (suggesting scvi's latent structure is critical). This knowledge shapes all subsequent decisions about whether to invest in scgpt, multimodal fusion, or further RNA encoder variants, making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_006: scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieves 0.653 acc. The largest single gain came from multiprofile + scvi_n200 (0.520→0.653), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) showed negligible difference (0.650 vs 0.653). However, the scgpt RNA encoder has never been tested, leaving a major uncertainty about whether an alternative learned RNA representation could surpass scvi_n200. Question: config_009 (scgpt, multiprofile, transformer) isolates the encoder effect by changing only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding profile (multiprofile) and aggregation (transformer) constant, enabling a direct head-to-head comparison with config_006. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether scgpt is competitive with or superior to scvi_n200 is the highest-value uncertainty. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new branch of multimodal experiments; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can redirect budget toward multimodal fusion or image-encoder upgrades with confidence in the RNA side.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is clearly the strongest signal (acc ~0.65), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (acc 0.208). However, we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50); ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet is substantially more expressive and may extract meaningful cellular morphology signal. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether the image modality contributes any useful information at all, or whether the poor resnet50 result reflects a fundamental lack of signal in the images. This experiment (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the effect of a stronger image encoder while keeping the setting minimal (no aggregation, no fusion), directly comparable to config_010. Why this is the best next step: before investing budget in any of the 36 multimodal configurations, we need to know whether the image channel has any predictive value. If ViT-L image is still near-chance, multimodal fusion is unlikely to help and remaining budget should focus on RNA-only refinements (e.g., scvi_n200 multiprofile with different aggregation). If ViT-L image is competitive, it justifies exploring multimodal fusion with the proven scvi_n200 multiprofile backbone. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (whether to include image at all) at minimal cost.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 and transformer aggregation (config_006, acc=0.653) is the clear best so far, while image-only models (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227) are very weak in isolation. The critical open question is whether the weak image modality provides complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA modality, or whether it adds only noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_006—the only difference is the addition of the image branch with simple concat fusion. If it fails to beat 0.653, we can confidently deprioritize all multimodal configs and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinements. If it does help, it opens the fusion-method and image-encoder dimensions for further exploration. Choosing concat over weighted keeps the fusion assumption minimal, and resnet50 (already characterized) over ViT-L avoids introducing two new variables at once.

The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, which beats the best RNA-only (config_006, 0.653) by ~3.5%. The key open question is whether the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) meaningfully affects performance, since we only have one multimodal data point. Config_033 is a clean single-variable A/B comparison with config_032 (only fusion changes from concat to weighted). If weighted fusion improves accuracy, it reveals that modality importance is asymmetric and learnable, guiding future fusion design. If it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and directs budget toward other levers (e.g., image encoder choice or aggregation). This is the most informative next step because it isolates one design decision at the current best-performing operating point, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit; the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest standard configuration: PCA is the most widely used and reproducible RNA dimensionality reduction, single-profile avoids confounding from aggregation, and RNA-only avoids confounding from fusion. This experiment establishes (1) whether the RNA signal alone is informative for the task, (2) a performance floor against which all image-only, multimodal, and alternative-encoder configurations can be compared, and (3) a reference for how much value the more complex design choices (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile, image, fusion) actually add. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with the most standard, low-risk baseline maximizes the interpretability of every subsequent comparison and reduces uncertainty about whether the task is solvable from RNA at all before investing experiments in more complex modalities or encoders.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), evidence is extremely sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries independent predictive signal. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-axis comparison to config_001 that isolates modality: it keeps the same profile setting and simplicity level (no aggregation, no fusion) while swapping RNA for image. If image_only performs comparably or better, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion; if it performs poorly, it signals that image adds little and we should focus budget on RNA encoder or profile improvements. Answering this foundational question before investing in any multimodal or multiprofile configuration maximizes information per experiment and prevents misattributing performance gains/losses in later fusion experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc / 0.464 F1, while config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) was much weaker at 0.208 acc / 0.172 F1. RNA is clearly the dominant modality, but we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA). Uncertainty: whether a learned, biologically-informed encoder (scVI) substantially outperforms linear PCA for downstream classification. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) makes the minimal single-variable change from our best baseline—swapping only the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and all other hyperparameters constant. It cleanly isolates the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it directly answers whether representation quality is a major performance lever, which would inform every subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiment; (2) if scVI is markedly better, we gain a stronger RNA backbone to build on; if similar, PCA suffices and we can focus budget on profile/aggregation/fusion axes; (3) it avoids conflating multiple design choices, keeping the comparison interpretable under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly dominate (0.485–0.520) over image-only (0.208), and among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) in singleprofile rna_only settings. However, scgpt remains untested, leaving uncertainty about which RNA representation is best. Question: config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) provides a clean, single-variable comparison against config_001 (pca) and config_004 (scvi), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and modality constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Resolving the encoder question before investing in multiprofile or multimodal configurations avoids committing the remaining budget to a suboptimal representation. If scgpt is substantially better, it reshapes the entire search; if it is comparable or worse, we can confidently build forward with scvi_n200. This is the highest-information experiment given the current sparse evidence.

Evidence: All four completed experiments are singleprofile. The best result is config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) at 0.520 acc, establishing scvi_n200 as the strongest RNA encoder. Image-only (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), reducing the urgency of multimodal tests. The largest remaining uncertainty is whether multiprofile aggregation provides meaningful gains over singleprofile. Question: Does multiprofile with the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve validation accuracy over the 0.520 singleprofile baseline? config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the profile-setting effect while using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), avoiding confounding from a more complex transformer. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly tests the most impactful unexplored design axis (profile setting) with the best-known encoder, and the result will inform whether to invest further in multiprofile variants or pivot to other axes.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.520), making it the clear best configuration so far. The dominant design axis is now RNA encoder + multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: we have not tested whether transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool under this strong setting. This experiment (config_006) isolates the aggregation choice (transformer vs avgpool) while holding rna_only, scvi_n200, and multiprofile fixed—a clean single-variable comparison directly extending our strongest result. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it exploits the most promising direction with a minimal, interpretable change, and the answer (whether transformer adds value over simple averaging) will guide all subsequent multiprofile and multimodal experiments that involve aggregation.

Evidence: The largest effect observed so far is the multiprofile boost for scvi_n200 (0.520 single → 0.650/0.653 multi, ~+13 pts), while singleprofile RNA encoders rank scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt. Image-only (resnet50) is essentially at chance (0.208). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the multiprofile gain is a general property of seeing multiple profiles or is specific to scvi's learned latent representation. Question: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly tests this by changing only the profile setting from config_001 (pca, single: 0.485). If pca also jumps substantially, multiprofile is a universal design lever; if it stays near 0.485, the gain is tied to scvi's learned representation. This is the best next experiment because it isolates one variable (profile setting) against an already-completed baseline, reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision before committing budget to multimodal or additional encoder combinations, and the aggregation choice (avgpool) is already shown to be near-equivalent to transformer, so it does not confound the comparison.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) achieves 0.653 accuracy, while the only image-only test (resnet50, singleprofile) scored a very weak 0.208. This single data point is insufficient to conclude the image modality carries no signal—resnet50 may simply be a poor encoder for this task. Uncertainty: Before investing budget in any multimodal fusion configuration, we need to know whether a stronger image encoder (ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L) can extract meaningful cellular signal. This experiment tests exactly that: image-only with ViT-L in a clean singleprofile setting, isolating the encoder choice. Why this is the best next step: If ViT-L also performs poorly, we can confidently redirect remaining budget to RNA-only optimization (e.g., exploring scgpt+multi or confirming aggregation effects). If ViT-L performs substantially better than resnet50, it justifies the next experiments in multimodal fusion with the best RNA encoder. This single experiment resolves the largest open design question—whether the image modality is worth pursuing at all—without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the strongest configuration (0.653 acc / 0.628 F1, config_006), and image-only models are very weak (best: ViT-L at 0.227 acc, config_013). The single biggest design lever identified is multiprofile (+13 pts over single-profile), and scvi_n200 is the best RNA encoder. The critical remaining uncertainty is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal adds any value. This experiment (config_039) pairs the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200), best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), multiprofile, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion—directly testing whether weighted multimodal fusion can improve on the 0.653 RNA-only baseline. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can learn to downweight a weak modality, making it the most informative test: if even weighted fusion fails to beat the RNA-only result, it provides strong evidence that image contributes little and further multimodal exploration is not worthwhile under a limited budget. This single experiment resolves the highest-impact open design question before committing additional budget to the 20+ remaining multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_039 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted fusion) achieved 0.725 acc, the best result so far, a substantial jump over the best RNA-only multiprofile (0.653, config_006). However, we have only one multimodal data point, so we cannot yet tell whether the weighted fusion specifically drives this gain or whether any fusion would work. Question: config_038 is identical to config_039 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, cleanly isolating the fusion-method effect. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a minimal, single-variable comparison that directly tests whether the fusion strategy is a critical design decision or interchangeable. If concat performs similarly, the fusion choice is a low-priority axis and we can focus budget on image-encoder or aggregation effects. If concat is substantially worse, it confirms weighted fusion as a necessary component and guides all future multimodal experiments. This is more informative than testing a second image encoder or aggregation variant, because fusion is the mechanism by which the two modalities interact and we have zero prior evidence on it.

With no prior experiments completed, there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. The most informative first step is to establish a simple, fast baseline that anchors all future comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: it uses a non-learned linear encoder (PCA), avoids aggregation and fusion complexity, and isolates the contribution of RNA data alone. This gives us (1) a performance floor, (2) a reference to judge whether more complex encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion actually add value, and (3) a fast-to-run experiment that conserves budget for later, more targeted comparisons. Establishing this baseline before testing any image-only or multimodal variant ensures we can attribute performance gains to specific design decisions rather than confounding multiple factors.

Only one experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, acc=0.485) is completed, so evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical unresolved question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality to the RNA baseline provides any benefit. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder and profile setting, and only adds the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This directly isolates the effect of the image modality against the existing baseline. If it outperforms 0.485, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies further exploration of fusion/aggregation/encoder choices; if it does not, it saves budget from pursuing the 36 multimodal configs. Testing image_only (config_010) would be less efficient because it would still require a subsequent multimodal experiment to answer the same core question, consuming an extra budget slot.

We have two data points: RNA-only (config_001, acc 0.485) and multimodal with PCA+ResNet50 concat (config_016, acc 0.527). The ~4% multimodal gain is promising but we cannot yet decompose it: we do not know how much of the performance comes from the image modality alone versus the combination. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the exact image-only counterpart to config_016, differing only in model_setting. This completes a clean three-way comparison (RNA-only / image-only / both) holding profile setting and image encoder constant, isolating each modality's contribution. If image-only is near 0.52, RNA adds little and we should focus on image encoder or profile improvements; if image-only is substantially lower (e.g., ~0.40), the combination is genuinely synergistic and investing in more complex multimodal configs (multiprofile, better fusion, ViT) is justified. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis (modality contribution) before spending budget on more complex configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only (config_001, acc=0.485) is the dominant signal, image-only is weak (config_010, acc=0.208), and adding image via concat gives a modest boost (config_016, acc=0.527). All three completed experiments use singleprofile, so the effect of multiprofile is entirely untested. Question: Does multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve RNA representation over singleprofile? Config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a direct, minimal-change comparison to config_001, isolating the profile-setting effect on the dominant modality. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) Multiprofile is the largest unexplored design axis and affects ~2/3 of remaining configs; a negative result here would efficiently prune that branch. (2) Since RNA drives most of the signal, any multiprofile benefit should be most visible in the RNA-only setting, making the result highly interpretable. (3) It avoids conflating the profile-setting change with fusion or image-encoder changes, per the principle of isolating one design decision. The outcome directly informs whether to invest subsequent budget in multiprofile multimodal configurations (configs 018–051) or to focus on encoder/fusion variations within singleprofile.

Evidence: The two strongest findings so far are (1) multiprofile + avgpool aggregation boosts RNA-only accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591 (config_002 vs config_001), and (2) adding image (resnet50, concat) to singleprofile RNA improves accuracy from 0.485 to 0.527 (config_016 vs config_001). However, we have not yet tested whether these two gains are additive. Question: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly combines the two proven design choices—multiprofile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion with resnet50—changing only the addition of the image modality relative to config_002. This isolates the marginal contribution of image in the multiprofile setting. Why best next: It is the most logical exploitation of the two strongest signals, uses a single-variable change from the current best (config_002), and will clarify whether the weak image-only signal (0.208) can still contribute meaningfully when paired with a strong multiprofile RNA backbone. The result will guide whether further budget should go toward better image encoders (ViT-L), alternative aggregation (transformer), or alternative fusion (weighted) in the multimodal+multiprofile regime.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc, and multiprofile with avgpool aggregation was the single largest gain observed (config_002 vs config_001: +0.106). However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) and one fusion strategy (concat), leaving uncertainty about whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can better exploit the multiprofile structure. Question: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion (concat) identical to config_018, cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next step: multiprofile is the dominant performance driver, so how profiles are combined is the highest-leverage unresolved design choice. A single-variable comparison against our current best gives the clearest signal per experiment, and the result directly informs whether to invest further in aggregation (or pivot to RNA encoder / fusion / image encoder) under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at acc=0.619/F1=0.610. We know multiprofile+avgpool is the dominant recipe, and image adds a modest ~0.03 boost over RNA-only. However, we have only tested concat fusion; the relative weighting of the two modalities is unexplored. Question: config_019 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while holding every other factor identical to config_018, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next: (1) It directly exploits the strongest evidence by testing the simplest possible improvement to the best configuration. (2) It isolates the fusion mechanism's contribution without confounding with encoder, aggregation, or profile changes. (3) If weighted fusion helps, it reveals that modality balance matters and opens a clear optimization axis; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward the next most uncertain dimension (e.g., image encoder strength or RNA encoder choice). This is the highest information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. Key findings: multiprofile > single (+0.106 for RNA), weighted > concat fusion (+0.020), avgpool > transformer aggregation (+0.040), and image contributes modestly (+0.028 over RNA alone). The RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA (linear, 2000-dim); scVI and scGPT are completely unexplored. Since RNA is the dominant modality (0.591 alone vs 0.208 for image), the quality of the RNA representation is likely the highest-leverage untested design choice. Question: Does a learned nonlinear encoder (scVI) improve over linear PCA in the best-performing multimodal setup? This experiment changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI while holding all other settings (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at their empirically best values, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It tests the single most impactful unexplored axis (RNA representation) in the current best configuration, providing a direct comparison that will tell us whether investing in richer RNA encoders is worthwhile before exploring image encoder upgrades or other combinations.

Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200, multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.678 vs config_019 (pca_n2000, same other settings) at 0.639, a +0.039 gain. However, we cannot yet tell whether scvi_n200 improves the RNA representation in general or only benefits from richer interaction with image features during fusion. Question: Does scvi_n200 outperform pca_n2000 in the RNA-only multiprofile setting? Config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002 (same but pca_n2000, acc=0.591). If scvi_n200 also lifts RNA-only performance, the gain is in the RNA representation itself and we should expect similar improvements when upgrading the image encoder next. If it does not, the scvi benefit is fusion-specific, redirecting our strategy toward image-side improvements. This is the best use of the next experiment because it isolates one critical design axis (RNA encoder quality) with a controlled comparison, reducing uncertainty that directly informs whether to prioritize RNA or image encoder upgrades in subsequent trials.

Evidence: RNA encoder has been the single largest performance lever (PCA→SCVI gave ~6 pts in RNA-only, ~4 pts in multimodal), and the current best config_031 (scvi, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.678. However, we have zero evidence about scgpt, the third available RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA representation, or is scvi already near-optimal? This experiment (config_043) changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding the proven-best settings (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_031. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) RNA encoder quality has historically produced the largest gains, so resolving whether scgpt could push performance above 0.678 is the highest-impact open question; (2) it reduces uncertainty on a completely unexplored dimension with no prior data; (3) if scgpt underperforms, it confirms scvi as optimal and redirects budget toward image-encoder upgrades (ViT-L); if it outperforms, it opens a new promising direction. This is more informative than testing a better image encoder (ViT-L) because the image contribution is already known to be modest (~3 pts), whereas the RNA encoder lever has shown much larger effects.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most effective. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) establishes the simplest possible baseline—a single-modality, single-profile model with a standard linear dimensionality reduction. It answers the foundational question: how well does a minimal RNA-only model perform, and what is the floor of the search space? 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With no prior evidence, the most efficient use of the first experiment is to anchor the search with a fast, interpretable, low-complexity baseline. This gives a clear reference point against which all subsequent experiments (other encoders, multiprofile, image-only, multimodal, different aggregations/fusions) can be meaningfully compared. It also trains quickly, reducing the risk that the first experiment is uninformative or fails. Starting here avoids the trap of jumping to a complex multimodal configuration whose performance cannot be attributed to any specific design choice without a simple reference.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), leaving almost all design dimensions unexplored. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest unimodal baseline for the image side, structurally parallel to config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion). If image-only performs competitively with or above the RNA baseline, it justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion and aggregation. If it performs poorly, we can redirect the budget toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This experiment isolates the image modality's standalone contribution without confounding it with fusion strategy or multiprofile complexity, making it the highest-information-gain choice under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, single profile, PCA n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (Image, single profile, ResNet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant signal and leaving large uncertainty about whether multiprofile aggregation can improve the RNA baseline. Question: config_002 directly extends config_001 by switching from single to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA n2000 encoder, cleanly isolating the effect of profile multiplicity and aggregation on RNA performance. Why this is the best next experiment: With only two data points, the highest-value question is whether the multiprofile design axis adds value over the current best single-profile setup. A positive result would justify investing further in multiprofile + aggregation variants (and ultimately multimodal multiprofile configs); a negative or neutral result would redirect effort toward encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion with single profiles. This experiment changes only the profile/aggregation dimension relative to the current best, making it the cleanest and most informative next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large jump over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles—this is the key mechanism enabling the multiprofile gain. This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly one variable (aggregation: transformer vs avgpool) while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (multiprofile) constant, giving a clean comparison against config_002. If transformer substantially exceeds avgpool, it tells us the aggregation architecture is a high-leverage knob to exploit in later multimodal experiments; if not, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices. Under a tight budget, this single-variable test on the strongest-performing branch is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool (config_002, PCA n2000) is the best result so far (0.591 acc), substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and image-only ResNet50 (0.208). Avgpool clearly beats transformer for aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). However, only PCA n2000 has been tested as an RNA encoder, leaving a major uncertainty: does a learned representation (scVI) improve on the linear PCA baseline in the best-performing multi-profile + avgpool setting? Question: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates the RNA encoder as the single variable changed relative to config_002, directly testing whether a nonlinear learned embedding outperforms PCA. Why this is the best next experiment: Before committing budget to multimodal fusion (which adds image encoder, fusion strategy, and more hyperparameters), we need to know whether the RNA backbone can be improved. If scvi substantially beats PCA here, it reshapes which multimodal configs to prioritize; if it does not, PCA remains the efficient choice and we can focus budget on fusion design. This is a clean, single-variable comparison that maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 vs config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.591, suggesting scvi improves performance by ~0.06. However, this comparison is confounded because both use multiprofile+avgpool. The singleprofile PCA baseline (config_001) is 0.485. Uncertainty: Is the scvi improvement driven by the encoder itself or by an interaction with multiprofile? config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) directly isolates the encoder effect by changing only the RNA encoder relative to config_001. If scvi-singleprofile substantially exceeds 0.485, the encoder matters independently and we should prioritize encoder choice in multimodal designs. If it remains near 0.485, the gain is profile-interaction-driven, shifting focus to aggregation. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about a core design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc, while image_only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). We have strong evidence that RNA dominates and that scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool is the optimal RNA pipeline. The key remaining uncertainty is whether adding the image modality via fusion provides any complementary signal beyond the already-strong RNA representation. Question tested: config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly compares against config_005 by adding only the image branch and a simple concat fusion, isolating the marginal contribution of image. Why best next: It uses the already-validated best RNA settings so any performance change is attributable to the image modality and fusion. If it improves, it justifies further investment in multimodal and stronger image encoders; if it does not, it efficiently rules out multimodal as a direction and lets us focus remaining budget on RNA encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt) or aggregation refinements. This is a single-variable change from the current best, making it the most informative use of one experiment.

Evidence: The best rna_only config (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA settings + resnet50, concat fusion) scores 0.632 — slightly worse. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), suggesting resnet50 features may be noisy or uninformative. The key uncertainty is whether the small multimodal deficit is due to the concat fusion failing to handle modality imbalance, or whether the resnet50 image features are simply unhelpful. This experiment (config_031) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, holding all other settings identical to config_030. If weighted fusion recovers the gap to ~0.650+, it shows the image carries marginal signal that concat was diluting; if it does not, it strongly indicates the resnet50 image features are not useful and we should pivot to testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or focus further on RNA-only improvements. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to isolate the fusion effect before committing further budget to multimodal variants.

The current best configuration is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678). The only aggregation tested with scvi_n200 in the multimodal setting is avgpool. For pca_n2000, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), but scvi_n200 produces a learned latent representation that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. Config_033 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) relative to the current best, cleanly isolating this design choice. If transformer improves performance, it identifies a new best and a promising direction; if it does not, it confirms avgpool is optimal for scvi and frees subsequent experiments to probe the image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder (scgpt) as the next lever. This is the highest-information single-variable test available under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc. Within the same family, avgpool+concat (0.6315) → avgpool+weighted (0.6776) shows a ~4.6pp gain from weighted fusion. However, we have not yet tested whether this fusion advantage persists when aggregation is switched to transformer. Question: config_032 (identical to config_033 except fusion=concat) isolates the single variable of fusion method under transformer aggregation. If concat ≈ weighted, then fusion choice is secondary to aggregation and we can simplify the design; if concat << weighted, it confirms weighted fusion is essential regardless of aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-variable comparison against the current best, has the highest expected performance among untested configs, and directly reduces uncertainty about whether the weighted-fusion gain seen with avgpool generalizes to transformer—information that determines which fusion strategy to lock in before exploring other axes (e.g., scgpt encoder or ViT-L image backbone).

No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence and maximal uncertainty across all design dimensions (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion). The most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: rna_only, singleprofile, PCA (2000 dims). This establishes the performance floor for the RNA modality with a linear, interpretable encoder and no added architectural complexity. Every other configuration in the search space adds one or more layers of complexity (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, image modality, fusion) on top of this baseline, so knowing its accuracy and F1 is essential to calibrate whether those added components actually contribute. It also trains quickly and reliably, reducing the risk of a wasted experiment due to training instability. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with this minimal reference point maximizes the interpretive value of all subsequent experiments.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) with a very low validation accuracy of 48.5%, leaving almost no evidence about which modality or representation carries signal for this task. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether image features alone are informative. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) tests this directly with the simplest image configuration, providing a clean cross-modality comparison to config_001. If image accuracy is substantially higher, it identifies image as the key signal and justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion; if it is similarly low, it indicates the task is intrinsically difficult and we should prioritize better RNA representations or multiprofile aggregation; if it is lower, RNA is the stronger modality. This single experiment resolves the most consequential unknown for the entire search and is the highest-information next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is at chance level (~20.8%), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation adds meaningful value over the single-profile baseline, or whether the single PCA profile already captures sufficient signal. This experiment (config_002) directly compares to config_001 with only the profile setting and aggregation changed, isolating the effect of multiprofile+avgpool on the stronger modality. It is the best next step because: (1) it targets the modality that actually carries signal, (2) it is a minimal, clean comparison that isolates one design axis, (3) the result will inform whether aggregation mechanisms are worth the added complexity before investing in multimodal fusion experiments, and (4) under a limited budget, confirming or rejecting the value of the aggregation pipeline on the dominant modality reduces uncertainty for all downstream decisions.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 accuracy, a substantial +10.6% improvement over config_001 (same encoder, singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is a high-impact design choice. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) and do not yet know whether a more expressive transformer aggregation can further improve performance. Question: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and encoder identical to config_002, giving a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the effect of aggregation architecture. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly exploits the strongest signal found so far (multiprofile RNA) and tests a logical extension before moving to more complex multimodal settings. (2) The result will tell us whether transformer aggregation is worth the added complexity, which will inform aggregation choices in all future multimodal experiments. (3) It remains in the RNA-only space where signal is strongest, avoiding confounding with the weak image modality (config_010 at 0.208). (4) Under a limited budget, resolving the aggregation question early prevents wasting experiments on suboptimal aggregation in multimodal settings later.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and image-only (0.208). Within multi-profile, avgpool (0.591) clearly beats transformer (0.519), establishing avgpool as the preferred aggregation. Uncertainty: we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA n2000). Whether a learned representation (scvi_n200) can outperform a linear one is an open and important question. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multi-profile, avgpool) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_002, cleanly isolating the effect of representation quality while holding the best-known profile and aggregation settings fixed. If scvi_n200 improves, it signals that encoder choice is a high-leverage axis worth further exploration (e.g., scgpt); if it does not, PCA is likely sufficient and budget is better spent investigating multimodal fusion or other axes. Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison maximizes information gained per experiment.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.650 acc, and we know avgpool beat transformer for pca_n2000 (0.591 vs 0.519). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different low-dimensional (200-d) latent representation, so the aggregation preference may not transfer. Question: Does transformer aggregation still underperform avgpool when paired with the scvi_n200 encoder? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005). Why best next: It directly extends our strongest result while resolving uncertainty about an important design choice (aggregation) that will affect all future multimodal experiments. If avgpool remains superior, we can confidently fix that choice and spend remaining budget on encoder comparison or multimodal fusion; if transformer catches up or surpasses, it changes the aggregation strategy for downstream configs.

Evidence: The current best RNA-only model uses scvi_n200 (config_005: 0.650 acc, config_006: 0.653 acc), and multiprofile+avgpool is the strongest combination. However, we have no data on the scgpt encoder, leaving a key representation question unresolved. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a direct single-variable comparison to config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether a different RNA representation can beat our current best (0.650), which would reshape all subsequent multimodal and encoder choices. If scgpt underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can confidently proceed to test whether adding image signal (even with a stronger ViT-L encoder) provides any marginal gain over the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. This is more informative than jumping to multimodal configs (which add two new variables at once) or testing image-only ViT-L (which, given resnet50's 0.208, may not change the strategic picture as directly as knowing our best RNA encoder).

Evidence: RNA-only models with scvi_n200 + multiprofile reach ~0.65, while image-only resnet50 (singleprofile, config_010) is very weak at 0.208. The multiprofile + aggregation strategy was the single largest improvement for RNA (pca: 0.485→0.591; scvi: baseline→0.65). Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the image modality can benefit from multiprofile aggregation, or whether it is fundamentally uninformative for this task. This experiment (config_011: image_only, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is a controlled comparison against config_010, changing only the profile/aggregation strategy while holding the encoder fixed. If image accuracy remains near 0.2, it strongly indicates the image signal is too weak to contribute meaningfully in multimodal fusion, allowing us to deprioritize many multimodal configurations. If it improves, it establishes a better image baseline and justifies investing in multimodal experiments. This is the most informative single experiment before committing budget to complex multimodal fusion, as it isolates one key design variable (profile/aggregation) on the image modality.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is clearly the strongest direction (~0.65 acc), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.21 single, 0.33 multi). The image modality's potential is the largest remaining uncertainty before committing budget to multimodal configurations. Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010 (resnet50), isolating the effect of a stronger, pretrained ViT-L encoder on image performance. Why this is the best next experiment: If ViT-L substantially raises image accuracy, it justifies investing in multimodal configs (e.g., config_030/036 with scvi_n200 + ViT-L). If image remains weak even with ViT-L, it confirms we should focus remaining budget on refining the RNA-only pipeline rather than exploring 30+ multimodal combinations. This single experiment efficiently gates a large portion of the search space under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: scvi_n200 + multiprofile at ~0.65 acc), while image-only models are weak (best: resnet50 + multiprofile at ~0.33 acc). The critical open question is whether the image modality, despite its weak standalone performance, provides complementary information (e.g., morphology) that improves predictions when fused with the strong RNA signal. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests that question by adding image to the best-known RNA configuration (config_005, acc 0.650) while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical. Using concat (simpler than weighted) and resnet50 (already characterized) keeps the comparison clean. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 0.650, image adds value and we should explore the multimodal space; if it does not, we can eliminate the majority of remaining multimodal configs and focus on refining the RNA-only pipeline. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) under the limited budget.

No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence to exploit and maximum uncertainty across all design axes. The most informative first experiment is a minimal, well-understood baseline that establishes a reference performance level. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: PCA is a standard, low-risk dimensionality reduction; singleprofile avoids aggregation complexity; and no image or fusion components are involved. This gives a clean RNA-only reference that will be essential for later determining whether (a) learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) add value, (b) multiprofile aggregation helps, and (c) multimodal fusion actually improves over the single-modality baseline. Starting here reduces the risk of confounding implementation issues with design effects and anchors all subsequent comparisons.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 at 48.5% accuracy), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any discriminative signal for this task. The very low baseline suggests either the task is inherently difficult or PCA on 2000 dims is an inadequate representation. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest image-only configuration: it tests a fundamentally different information source (visual cellular morphology via a pretrained deep encoder) against the RNA-only baseline. This single experiment answers the highest-level design question—does the image modality provide useful signal at all?—before committing budget to the 30+ multimodal or more complex RNA-encoder variants. If image_only performs substantially better, it justifies investing in multimodal fusion and ViT variants; if it performs similarly poorly, the search should focus on improving RNA representations (scvi, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation. This is the most informative single experiment because it partitions the remaining configuration space into two very different strategic directions.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, single profile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (resnet50) is weak at 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. The key uncertainty is whether leveraging multiple cellular profiles with aggregation can improve the RNA baseline beyond the single-profile PCA result. This experiment (config_002) tests multiprofile + avgpool with the same pca_n2000 encoder, providing a clean, near-single-variable comparison to config_001 (only the profile/aggregation structure changes). It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it isolates the effect of profile multiplicity and aggregation without confounding encoder choice, (2) avgpool is a low-risk, simple aggregator that is less likely to fail than a transformer with limited data, and (3) the result directly informs whether the multiprofile axis is worth further exploration (e.g., with scvi/scgpt encoders) or whether we should instead invest in encoder quality or multimodal fusion next.

Evidence: Multiprofile RNA with avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms singleprofile RNA (config_001, acc=0.485), confirming that profile ordering and aggregation matter. Image-only resnet50 (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak, so RNA remains the primary signal. Question: Does transformer aggregation further improve over avgpool in the multiprofile RNA setting? This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation method from avgpool to transformer while holding rna_only, multiprofile, and pca_n2000 fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. Why this is the best next step: It directly tests whether the ordering of multiple profiles carries additional signal beyond their mean, which determines whether we should invest further in more complex aggregation for downstream multimodal experiments. If transformer helps, it justifies transformer-based fusion in multimodal configs; if not, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder choice or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.591 acc, showing that multiprofile+avgpool is a strong setting and that RNA dominates image (0.591 vs 0.208). The only RNA encoder tested is pca_n2000, leaving significant uncertainty about whether a learned encoder (scvi_n200) captures biological structure better than linear PCA. This experiment (config_005) changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding multiprofile+avgpool fixed, directly isolating the encoder effect against the known baseline of 0.591. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information single-variable test: if scvi_n200 improves, it justifies investing in learned encoders for multimodal configs; if it does not, PCA is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget toward fusion/image questions with confidence.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (image_only resnet50: 0.208 vs rna_only: 0.485-0.650). Within RNA, multiprofile+avgpool is the best profile/aggregation setting (pca: 0.591 vs singleprofile: 0.485; avgpool: 0.591 vs transformer: 0.519), and scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000 under identical settings (0.650 vs 0.591). This establishes a clear encoder ranking: scvi_n200 > pca_n2000. Question: Does scgpt, the third available RNA encoder, further improve on scvi_n200, or has encoder quality plateaued? config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) holds profile setting and aggregation at their known-best values, isolating the encoder effect. This is the best use of the next experiment because it directly extends the strongest evidence (encoder choice drives the largest observed gap), requires no new assumptions about aggregation or profile interactions, and will determine whether to invest remaining budget in encoder exploration or pivot toward testing image/multimodal contributions.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: scVI/multi/avgpool at 0.650), while the sole image test (ResNet50, single-profile) yielded only 0.208 accuracy, suggesting the image modality may carry little signal. However, ResNet50 is a relatively weak encoder; ViT-L (ImageNet-pretrained) is substantially more expressive and could extract features that ResNet50 missed. Uncertainty: We cannot yet determine whether the image modality is fundamentally uninformative for this task or simply poorly encoded. This experiment (config_014: image_only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) isolates the image encoder quality question while holding profile setting and aggregation at their known-best values (multiprofile + avgpool), avoiding confounds. If ViT-L still yields very low accuracy, we can confidently rule out the image modality and focus remaining budget on RNA-only optimization or fusion strategy. If it yields a meaningful signal, it justifies investing in multimodal experiments. This is the highest-information experiment available because it resolves a binary design question (is image useful at all?) that gates an entire family of ~36 multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (best: scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool at 0.650 acc), while image-only models are weak (best: ViT-L multiprofile at 0.332). Within RNA, scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt, multiprofile > singleprofile, and avgpool > transformer. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether adding image features to the best RNA configuration provides any complementary signal or merely adds noise. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) directly tests whether the simplest fusion (concat) of the best RNA setup with a modest image encoder improves over the 0.650 RNA-only baseline. It is the best next step because it extends the strongest known configuration along the single most important untested axis (fusion), uses the simplest fusion rule to isolate the effect of adding image information, and avoids changing multiple design choices simultaneously. If it fails to beat 0.650, it strongly argues against further multimodal exploration; if it succeeds, it justifies deeper fusion and image-encoder experiments.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200/multiprofile/avgpool (config_005) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA settings + resnet50/concat) drops to 0.632, suggesting the weak resnet50 image signal (image-only acc 0.208) adds noise rather than information. Meanwhile, imagenet_vit_l as image encoder yields substantially better image-only performance (0.332 vs 0.208). Question: Does a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) allow the multimodal model to match or exceed the RNA-only baseline? This experiment (config_036) is a clean single-variable comparison with config_030, changing only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, and concat fusion constant. Why best next: It directly tests whether the image modality can contribute useful signal at all, which determines whether further multimodal exploration (fusion methods, transformer aggregation) is worthwhile or whether the budget should be redirected to RNA-only refinements. Under a limited budget, resolving whether multimodal is a viable direction is more informative than tuning fusion or aggregation within a likely unproductive regime.

The current best result is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc=0.715). All multimodal experiments tested so far used concat fusion, so the effect of fusion strategy is completely unexplored. Config_037 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, holding all other settings identical to config_036. This is a clean single-variable experiment that directly tests whether a learned weighted combination of modalities can outperform simple concatenation. Given that the image modality alone is weak (best 0.33) while RNA is strong (0.65), the optimal weighting between modalities may differ substantially from an equal-weight concat, making this a high-information experiment. If weighted fusion improves performance, it confirms that modality importance is asymmetric and guides further tuning; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., transformer aggregation with scvi in multimodal).

With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a clean performance floor. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: no image branch, no aggregation, no fusion, and a standard linear encoder. It isolates the RNA modality under the least confounded settings, giving a well-defined baseline against which every other design axis (image modality, multiprofile aggregation, learned encoders like scVI/scGPT, and fusion strategy) can later be evaluated as a controlled increment. Choosing this first experiment maximizes the interpretability of all subsequent comparisons and avoids committing to any complex design choice before we know the unimodal, single-profile reference performance.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single profile, PCA → ~48.5% accuracy), so uncertainty is high across all design axes. The most fundamental open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests this while keeping the profile setting identical to config_001 (singleprofile), making the comparison as clean as possible across modalities. Knowing the image-only ceiling is essential before investing budget in multimodal fusion experiments: if image alone performs poorly, multimodal gains are unlikely and we should instead focus on improving the RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. Conversely, if image alone is competitive or strong, it justifies prioritizing multimodal configurations. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty in the search space and is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is weak at 20.8%, making RNA the dominant modality and the primary target for improvement. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the multiprofile structure (multiple profiles per cell) plus aggregation carries meaningful signal beyond a single profile. This experiment (config_002) isolates that question by changing only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, keeping the same pca_n2000 encoder as config_001. If accuracy improves, it confirms that profile structure matters and motivates testing transformer aggregation (config_003) and multiprofile with better encoders. If it does not improve, we learn that the bottleneck is encoder quality rather than profile structure, redirecting effort toward scvi/scgpt encoders. This is the most informative single-variable extension of our best result under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large +10.6 pt gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc), confirming that multiprofile structure carries substantial signal. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether a transformer-based aggregation, which can model cell-to-cell relationships within a profile, can further exploit the multiprofile structure beyond simple averaging.
