This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly one variable—aggregation (transformer vs avgpool)—while holding model setting, profile setting, and RNA encoder (pca_n2000) constant, making it a clean comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends our strongest result with a single, well-motivated change; if transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool, it identifies a high-value design axis to build on, and if it does not, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can redirect effort toward encoder choice or multimodal fusion without having wasted an experiment on a confounded comparison.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, and we've established that multi-profile + avgpool is the strongest RNA-only setting. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA n2000), leaving uncertainty about whether a learned representation could further improve performance. Question: config_005 (RNA, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_002, cleanly isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether the linear PCA representation is a bottleneck or whether a non-linear learned embedding (scVI) captures additional biological signal. If scvi outperforms PCA, it justifies investing further in learned encoders (including scgpt) and multimodal fusion with richer RNA features. If it underperforms, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward fusion strategy or image modality questions. This single-variable comparison maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile+avgpool is the best profile/aggregation combination (avgpool beats transformer by 0.072 for PCA; multiprofile beats singleprofile by 0.106). However, the RNA encoder dimension is only partially explored: PCA (0.591) and scvi_n200 (0.650) are tested, but scgpt is completely untested. Question: Does scgpt, with its pretrained single-cell generative architecture, produce a better or worse representation than scvi_n200 under the same multiprofile+avgpool setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. Why this is the best next experiment: The aggregation question (avgpool vs transformer) is relatively well-answered with a large margin, while the encoder choice is a high-impact, under-explored dimension. Testing scgpt at the best-known profile/aggregation settings isolates the encoder effect and could reveal whether a third encoder option outperforms scvi_n200, which would significantly change the search direction for subsequent multimodal experiments.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1. Image-only with resnet50 was very weak (0.208), but we have not yet tested whether adding image features to the strong RNA signal via fusion can provide complementary information. The key uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion improves over the best unimodal model, which is the central question of this study. Config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the minimal, logical extension of config_005: it keeps every RNA-side setting at its best-known value and adds only the image modality with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the effect of adding image information to the strongest RNA pipeline. If it improves, we have a new best and a clear direction for exploring fusion type and image encoder. If it does not, we learn that resnet50 image features do not complement scvi RNA representations, redirecting effort toward either a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA-only refinements. Under the limited budget, this single experiment directly answers the highest-value question—does multimodal fusion help?—using the most validated component settings available.

Evidence: config_005 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, while config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) dropped to 0.632 acc—adding the image modality with simple concatenation actually hurt performance. This is the most surprising and consequential finding so far. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted, keeping all other settings identical to config_030. This isolates whether the performance drop is due to the fusion mechanism (concat forcing equal-weight combination of a strong RNA signal with a weak ResNet50 signal) or due to the image features themselves being uninformative/noisy. Why best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable A/B comparison against config_030, directly addressing the key open question of whether the image modality can contribute value under proper integration. If weighted fusion recovers to ≥0.650, it reveals the image carries signal that needs gating; if it stays near 0.632, it strongly indicates ResNet50 features are not useful for this task, redirecting effort toward RNA-only optimization or a stronger image encoder (ViT-L). No other available configuration answers this question with fewer confounds.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc, only modestly above RNA-only scvi_n200 (config_005, 0.650). ResNet50 alone is very weak (0.208), raising the question of whether the image modality has meaningful additional signal that ResNet50 simply cannot extract. Question: config_037 swaps the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L while holding all other settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) identical to config_031. This isolates the image-encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly testing whether the modest +0.028 gain from adding ResNet50 reflects a ceiling in the image encoder or a true ceiling in the image modality's complementary signal. (2) If ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, it identifies a promising direction for further multimodal optimization; if it does not, it tells us the image modality contributes little beyond RNA and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side improvements. (3) Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image channel is worth further investment is more consequential than confirming the already-suggested avgpool>transformer aggregation preference.

The best configuration so far is config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.7062 acc. The only untested dimension in this top-performing setup is aggregation: we have strong evidence that avgpool > transformer for pca_n2000 RNA (config_002: 0.5907 vs config_003: 0.5191), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different (lower-dimensional, learned) representation where transformer aggregation might interact differently. Config_039 changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other factors at their best-known values (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_037 that will clarify whether aggregation is a meaningful design axis in the best multimodal regime. If it improves, we identify a new best; if it does not, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can redirect budget to other unexplored dimensions (e.g., scgpt encoders or image-only multiprofile baselines) with confidence that aggregation is settled.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or fusion strategy is effective. The entire configuration space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA-2000, single-profile) is the simplest possible configuration in the search space. It establishes the performance floor and confirms that the pipeline runs correctly end-to-end. It also gives a reference accuracy/F1 against which every added complexity (deeper encoders, multiprofile, image modality, fusion) can be measured. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With a limited budget, the highest-value first step is a fast, low-risk baseline that reduces the most uncertainty per unit of compute. PCA is a linear, well-understood encoder that runs quickly, single-profile avoids aggregation confounds, and RNA-only isolates one modality. This single result immediately tells us whether the task is solvable at a basic level and anchors all subsequent comparisons (e.g., does scVI or scGPT help over PCA? does adding image modality help? does multiprofile help?). Choosing a more complex configuration first would conflate multiple design decisions and make it impossible to attribute performance to any single factor.

We have only one data point (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), so the dominant uncertainty is whether adding image modality provides complementary signal. Config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the minimal logical extension of config_001: it keeps the same RNA encoder and profile setting and adds only the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This cleanly isolates the effect of multimodality. If accuracy improves meaningfully, subsequent budget can be directed at image encoder choice and fusion strategy; if it does not, we learn that image adds little and can focus on RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt) and multiprofile aggregation instead. No other single experiment answers this highest-impact design question with fewer confounds.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, PCA, single profile) achieved 0.485 acc, while config_016 (multimodal, PCA + ResNet50, concat, single profile) improved to 0.527 acc. The +4.2% gain could come from the image modality itself or from synergistic fusion. Uncertainty: We have no data point for image-only performance, so we cannot attribute the improvement to the image encoder versus the multimodal fusion. Question tested: config_010 (image_only, single profile, ResNet50) is a clean ablation that removes only the RNA branch from config_016, isolating the image modality's standalone contribution. Why best next step: With only two completed experiments, the single largest unknown is whether the image is the primary signal carrier or whether RNA+image fusion is genuinely synergistic. Resolving this determines the entire subsequent search strategy—if image alone matches the multimodal result, we should prioritize image encoder choices (ViT-L) and multiprofile aggregation; if image alone is substantially lower, fusion strategy and RNA encoder quality become the key levers. This is a single-variable change from config_016, making the result interpretable, and it maximally reduces uncertainty under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000) achieves 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA n2000+ResNet50, concat) improves to 0.527, confirming RNA is the dominant signal and image adds a modest boost. However, we have no evidence yet on whether multiprofile with aggregation improves over single-profile—a fundamental architectural choice that halves the remaining configuration space. Question: config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_001, isolating the effect of multiprofile+avgpool aggregation while holding the RNA encoder constant. Why this is best: It is the simplest, cheapest experiment that directly answers whether the multiprofile/aggregation axis is worth pursuing. If it improves over config_001, we gain confidence to extend multiprofile into the multimodal setting (e.g., config_018/020). If it does not help, we can deprioritize all multiprofile variants and focus budget on RNA encoder or image encoder choices in the single-profile regime. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

The strongest evidence so far is that multi-profile RNA (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms single-profile RNA (config_001, acc=0.485), and that adding ResNet50 image to single-profile RNA gives a modest gain (config_016, acc=0.527 vs 0.485). The key open question is whether these two gains—multi-profile aggregation and image fusion—are additive or sub-additive. Config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends our best result (config_002) by adding the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder and aggregation, allowing a clean comparison: config_018 vs config_002 isolates the image contribution given multi-profile, and config_018 vs config_016 isolates the multi-profile contribution given image. This is the highest-information next step because it tests the most promising direction (our best config + the one other modality that showed positive contribution) with only one new variable changed, and the answer will determine whether further budget should go toward improving the image side (ViT-L, transformer aggregation) or the RNA side (scVI, scGPT encoders).

Evidence: Multi-profile with avgpool clearly outperforms single-profile (config_002: 0.591 vs config_001: 0.485), and the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multi-profile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc. However, aggregation method is completely untested beyond avgpool—transformer aggregation has never been evaluated. Question: Does transformer aggregation over profiles yield a meaningful improvement over simple average pooling in the strongest multimodal multi-profile setting? This is a single-variable change from config_018 (only avgpool→transformer), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is the mechanism that determines how multi-profile information is combined, and since multi-profile was the single largest gain observed (~0.10 over single-profile), the aggregation strategy is a critical design axis with high uncertainty. If transformer helps, it unlocks a higher performance ceiling across many configurations; if it does not, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices without wasting experiments on transformer variants.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result at 0.619 acc, and RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.485 vs image_only 0.208). However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA, a linear method), leaving high uncertainty about whether a learned nonlinear representation would improve the RNA branch. Question: Does scvi_n200 (a learned variational representation) outperform PCA in the best-performing architecture? This is a single-variable change from config_018, isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the highest-impact remaining design axis because RNA drives most of the signal. Resolving whether a learned encoder beats PCA either unlocks a major performance gain or eliminates an entire branch of the search space, making it more informative than testing fusion (a likely smaller effect) or image encoder (image signal is weak). It directly extends our strongest evidence with a minimal, interpretable change.

The current best configuration (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.632) has only been tested with 'concat' fusion. No experiment has yet explored 'weighted' fusion, which is a fundamental design dimension left untested. Given the large signal asymmetry between modalities (RNA-only acc≈0.485 vs image-only acc≈0.208), weighted fusion could allow the model to down-weight the weaker image branch, potentially improving over the fixed equal-weighting implied by concat. Config_031 is a clean single-variable change (concat→weighted) from the current best, isolating the fusion mechanism while holding all other settings constant. This is the most efficient next step: it either yields a new best (exploiting a promising direction) or confirms that fusion strategy is not a major lever (reducing uncertainty and freeing future experiments to focus on other dimensions like scgpt or ViT-L). Under a limited budget, this low-risk, high-information comparison is preferable to jumping to a wholly new encoder (scgpt) or image backbone (ViT-L) that would change multiple untested variables at once.

Evidence: The largest single improvement observed was switching from concat to weighted fusion (+4.6pp, config_030→031), but this was only tested with scvi_n200. We also know scvi_n200 gives a modest +1.3pp over pca_n2000 under concat (config_018→030). Question: Does weighted fusion provide a comparable benefit with pca_n2000, or is the gain specific to the scvi latent representation? Config_019 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable change from both config_018 (concat→weighted) and config_031 (scvi→pca), isolating the fusion×encoder interaction. Why best: If pca+weighted approaches scvi+weighted (~0.67), it confirms weighted fusion as a robust, encoder-agnostic improvement and directs future effort toward other axes (image encoder, scgpt). If it lags substantially, it reveals that the scvi representation is specifically enabling effective weighted fusion, making RNA encoder selection the critical lever. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about which design axis to exploit next under the limited budget.

The current best (config_031: scvi_n200, multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, acc=0.678) outperforms the best RNA-only baseline (config_002: pca_n2000, rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool, acc=0.591) by 0.087, but this gap conflates three factors: RNA encoder upgrade (pca→scvi), image modality addition, and weighted fusion. We lack a direct RNA-only scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool baseline. Config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable change from config_002, isolating the RNA encoder effect. Critically, comparing config_005 to config_031 will quantify how much the image modality (resnet50 + weighted fusion) actually contributes on top of the best RNA representation. If config_005 approaches ~0.63, the image adds only ~0.05 and further image-encoder investment (e.g., ViT-L) is low-priority; if it stays near 0.59, the image contributes substantially and upgrading the image encoder (config_037) becomes the clear next step. Under a limited budget, this single experiment resolves the most important open question—whether the image modality is worth further investment—while also providing the RNA encoder comparison we lack.

With no prior experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, minimal baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: a single RNA profile encoded with PCA (2000 dims), no aggregation, no image modality, no fusion. This minimizes implementation risk and confounding factors. It directly enables the next set of high-value comparisons: (a) does multiprofile + aggregation help? (compare to config_002/003), (b) do learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) improve over PCA? (compare to config_004/007), and (c) does adding an image modality via concat fusion help? (compare to config_016). Without this reference, we cannot attribute performance gains to any specific design choice. Starting with the simplest modality and encoder is the most information-efficient first experiment under a limited budget.

The only completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA) yielded a weak ~48.5% accuracy, giving us almost no information about the broader design space. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. If it does not, the 36 multimodal configurations become low-priority and the search should focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile strategies; if it does, image becomes the primary modality to optimize and multimodal fusion becomes the key question. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-modality probe with a standard, well-understood encoder that isolates the question 'does image signal exist?' without confounding changes to profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. This is the highest-information-gain experiment available: its outcome partitions the entire remaining search space into two very different strategic directions, making it the best use of the next limited-budget trial.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc, far outperforming image (resnet50, singleprofile) at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA data point, so we cannot yet tell whether multiprofile aggregation improves the RNA signal. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve RNA performance while keeping the same pca_n2000 encoder? This isolates the profile/aggregation axis as the only change from config_001. Why best next: It is the minimal logical extension of our best result, directly tests a design axis (profile setting + aggregation) that gates ~half the remaining configuration space, and its outcome will inform whether to invest subsequent budget in multiprofile variants or focus on encoder choice. A single-variable change keeps the comparison clean and interpretable under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a substantial +10.6% gain over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile representation is highly beneficial. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) and do not know whether a more expressive transformer aggregation can further improve profile combination. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform simple average pooling for combining multiple RNA profiles, holding encoder and modality fixed? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly extends the current best configuration by changing only the aggregation mechanism, isolating that effect. The answer informs whether we should invest in transformer-based aggregation for all subsequent multimodal experiments (where aggregation becomes even more critical for combining profiles across modalities), or whether avgpool is sufficient and we should instead focus budget on RNA encoder upgrades (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational design choice before adding further complexity (new encoders, multimodal fusion) is the most information-efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 accuracy, and the key findings are (a) multi-profile + avgpool strongly outperforms single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519), and (b) image-only is very weak (0.208). Uncertainty: We have only tested PCA as the RNA encoder. It is unclear whether a learned, biologically-informed representation (scvi) can capture structure that a linear 2000-dim PCA projection misses, or whether PCA already saturates the useful signal. This experiment (config_005: RNA, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates exactly one variable — the RNA encoder — against the established best config_002, making the comparison clean and interpretable. If scvi_n200 improves on 0.591, it justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal experiments with learned encoders; if it does not, it tells us PCA is sufficient and we should pivot budget toward multimodal fusion or other levers. Under a limited budget, this single-variable test maximally reduces uncertainty about the representation design choice before committing to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.650 acc, and we have strong evidence that multiprofile+avgpool is the right aggregation regime. However, we have zero data on the scgpt encoder. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, which is a major design axis. This experiment (config_008: scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares scgpt vs scvi_n200 under identical profile and aggregation settings, isolating the encoder effect. If scgpt is substantially better, it redirects exploitation toward scgpt-based multimodal configs; if it is comparable or worse, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and lets us focus remaining budget on multimodal fusion. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about the encoder dimension before committing to multimodal experiments.

Evidence: RNA-only models range from 0.48–0.65 while the sole image-only test (resnet50, singleprofile) scored only 0.208, suggesting image may be fundamentally weak for this task. However, we have only one image data point and cannot distinguish between 'image is uninformative' and 'resnet50 is an inadequate encoder.' This experiment (imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010, isolating the effect of image representation quality. If ViT-L also performs poorly, we can confidently deprioritize all ~40 multimodal configs and concentrate remaining budget on RNA optimization (e.g., scvi+transformer in config_006). If ViT-L substantially improves, it validates image as a viable modality and justifies multimodal exploration. Resolving this high-impact uncertainty with one experiment is the most budget-efficient choice before committing to complex multimodal combinations.

Evidence: The best RNA-only config so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. We know multiprofile substantially helped pca_n2000 (config_002: 0.591 vs config_001: 0.485), but we have no data on whether the multiprofile advantage holds for the learned scvi_n200 representation. Image modality is very weak standalone (~0.22), making RNA-side design decisions the highest-priority question. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile, no aggregation) isolates the profile-setting effect for the best encoder by changing only profile_setting relative to config_005. If config_004 approaches 0.650, the learned latent is robust to profile aggregation and the simpler singleprofile model suffices; if it drops substantially, multiprofile aggregation is confirmed as essential regardless of encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-variable comparison with the current best, directly tests an important and still-uncertain design axis (profile setting) for the strongest encoder, and avoids prematurely committing budget to multimodal fusion when the image branch is so weak. It reduces uncertainty about whether we can simplify the pipeline before investing in more complex multimodal combinations.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy. Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), raising the question of whether adding image features to the strong RNA signal will help or merely inject noise. Uncertainty: We have no multimodal result yet, so we cannot tell whether fusion adds complementary information or degrades the RNA signal. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends the best RNA configuration by adding the image modality while keeping all other settings (encoder, profile, aggregation) identical to config_005. It isolates the effect of adding image + concat fusion. If accuracy improves over 0.650, it confirms multimodal value and guides further fusion/image-encoder exploration; if it does not, it tells us to focus budget on RNA-only refinements rather than testing all 24 multimodal variants. This is the highest-information single experiment under the limited budget because it answers the central design question (does image help?) with the fewest new variables introduced.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (config_005: scvi_n200, multi-profile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 accuracy, while the only multimodal test (config_030: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored 0.632—slightly *worse* than RNA alone. Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), suggesting the image signal is noisy. However, one data point with concat fusion is insufficient to conclude that multimodal fusion is inherently unhelpful; concat may simply overweight the weak image features. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted (keeping scvi_n200, resnet50, multi-profile, avgpool identical to config_030), directly testing whether a learned/rebalanced fusion can recover or exceed the RNA-only baseline. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of the most recent multimodal result, resolving the critical design question of whether the image modality adds any value under a more flexible fusion. If weighted fusion still fails to beat 0.650, we gain strong evidence to abandon multimodal paths and focus remaining budget on RNA-only optimization (e.g., testing transformer aggregation with scvi_n200). If it does help, it identifies fusion as a key lever and justifies further multimodal exploration. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice given the current uncertainty.

With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: a single modality, the simplest profile setting, and a standard linear encoder with no learned parameters. This gives a well-defined reference performance against which all subsequent experiments (multiprofile aggregation, alternative RNA encoders, image-only, and multimodal fusion) can be meaningfully compared. If multimodal or multiprofile models later fail to exceed this simple baseline, that is a critical finding about where added complexity is unhelpful. Starting here minimizes confounding (no aggregation, no fusion, no image) and reduces uncertainty about whether the basic RNA signal is informative at all, making it the most efficient first use of the experiment budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000, acc≈0.485), the largest source of uncertainty is whether image features carry any useful signal for this task. Testing image_only with a standard resnet50 encoder and singleprofile (config_010) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the RNA baseline: it isolates the modality question without confounding by aggregation, fusion, or encoder complexity. If image_only performs comparably or better, it justifies investing subsequent budget in multimodal fusion strategies; if it performs poorly, it redirects effort toward improving RNA representations (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This is the highest-information experiment under the current sparse evidence because it resolves the most fundamental design decision before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether the RNA representation itself can be improved—pca_n2000 is a simple linear projection, and it is unclear whether a learned, biologically-informed encoder (scvi_n200) would capture more discriminative structure. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_001, providing a clean one-variable comparison. It will clarify whether representation quality is a bottleneck: if scvi_n200 substantially improves accuracy, it justifies investing further in learned encoders and multimodal combinations built on them; if it does not, PCA-level representations may suffice and we can redirect budget toward profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational question about the strongest modality's representation is the highest-information next step before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520 acc) clearly outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485 acc) in singleprofile RNA-only settings, and image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), indicating RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have no data yet on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves over singleprofile, and whether the benefit (if any) depends on the RNA encoder. This experiment (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) to isolate the effect of multiprofile with simple average-pool aggregation while holding the encoder fixed. Choosing avgpool over transformer first is the more conservative, interpretable step: if simple averaging does not help, it questions the value of multiprofile broadly; if it does, it motivates testing transformer aggregation next. This is the highest-information single experiment under budget because it extends the best-performing configuration along one new design axis without introducing confounds (no new encoder, no image modality, no fusion).

Evidence: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 accuracy, a dramatic ~13-point jump over its single-profile counterpart (config_004, 0.520), establishing that multi-profile representation with scVI is the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) meaningfully affects performance in this multi-profile setting. Question tested: config_006 is identical to config_005 except it replaces avgpool with transformer aggregation, cleanly isolating the effect of the aggregation strategy. Why best next experiment: This is a single-variable, directly comparable follow-up to the best result, so the outcome will tell us whether the simpler avgpool is sufficient or whether a learned transformer aggregation unlocks further gains. That answer will propagate to every subsequent multimodal configuration (configs 018-051 all include an aggregation choice), making this the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the strongest configuration so far (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1), a large jump over singleprofile scvi_n200 (0.520). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference (~0.003). The encoder effect is moderate: scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 by ~3.5 points in singleprofile. However, scgpt—a fundamentally different pre-trained single-cell model—has not been tested at all. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting, or is scvi_n200 the ceiling for RNA encoders? config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the encoder effect in the highest-performing regime. Why this is the best next step: It directly tests whether a different encoder architecture can push beyond the current 0.65 ceiling, using the same profile and aggregation as our best result. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we gain a new direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 is the best encoder and can redirect budget toward multimodal fusion or other dimensions with greater confidence.

Evidence: RNA-only with scVI n200 and multi-profile achieves ~0.65 accuracy, while image-only with ResNet50 is very weak (0.21). The single image data point (config_010) leaves major uncertainty about whether the image modality can contribute meaningfully. Question: Does a stronger image encoder (ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet) produce a competitive image representation, or is the image modality fundamentally weak for this task? This experiment isolates the image-encoder variable by comparing directly to config_010 (same image-only, single-profile setup, only the encoder changes). Why this is the best next step: Before investing limited budget in complex multimodal fusion configurations (configs 028-051), we need to know whether the image branch can produce a useful signal at all. If ViT-L image-only remains weak (<0.35), multimodal fusion is unlikely to help and we should focus on refining the RNA-only pipeline. If it is competitive (>0.5), multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction. This single experiment resolves a critical uncertainty that gates many downstream decisions, making it the most information-dense use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer (config_006, acc=0.653) is the clear best configuration, far exceeding image-only models (≤0.227). The multiprofile setting and scvi_n200 encoder are strongly validated. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether adding the image modality (very weak alone) provides complementary signal to the already-strong RNA representation, or whether it introduces noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the direct multimodal extension of config_006, changing only the addition of image + concat fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality against the best known RNA baseline. It is the most informative next step because it answers the central question—does multimodal fusion improve upon the strong RNA-only result—before committing budget to further multimodal variants (weighted fusion, ViT, scgpt). If it fails to beat 0.653, it saves many downstream multimodal experiments; if it succeeds, it justifies exploring fusion type and image encoder.

The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc, which outperforms the best RNA-only multiprofile (config_006, 0.653 acc) by ~3.5 pp, suggesting the image modality adds modest but real value. However, we have only one multimodal data point and have not yet isolated the effect of the fusion strategy. Config_033 is identical to config_032 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, making it a clean single-variable A/B comparison. This tells us whether the way modalities are combined is a meaningful design lever or whether concat is already near-optimal. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step: it either confirms concat is sufficient (freeing us to explore image encoder quality or aggregation next) or reveals that weighted fusion meaningfully improves multimodal performance, guiding subsequent experiments toward better fusion-aware configurations.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc, showing that multimodal fusion with weighted combination provides a substantial boost over RNA-only multiprofile (0.6530). However, the only image encoder tested in multimodal is resnet50, which alone achieves only 0.208 acc. The stronger imagenet_vit_l (0.227 alone) has not been tested in the multimodal setting. Question: Does a higher-capacity image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) improve multimodal fusion performance when all other design choices are held at their best-known values? This is a clean single-variable comparison (image encoder only) against the current best, isolating the effect of image representation quality on fusion. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image modality's contribution is encoder-dependent or encoder-agnostic is critical. If vit_l helps, it justifies further investment in image quality; if it doesn't, it confirms the image signal is inherently limited and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side or fusion refinements. This single experiment reduces the most important remaining uncertainty about the multimodal architecture.

With zero completed experiments, the highest-priority need is to establish a performance floor. Config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: a single modality, a single profile, and a linear PCA encoder with no aggregation or fusion. Running this first gives a clean, interpretable baseline that every subsequent experiment (adding image modality, switching to learned encoders like scVI/scGPT, moving to multiprofile, or introducing fusion) can be directly compared against to isolate the marginal contribution of each design axis. It also avoids the risk of over-investing in a complex multimodal model before knowing whether a simple RNA signal is already sufficient or whether the image modality adds meaningful information. This is the most uncertainty-reducing first step under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) establishes the image-only baseline under the same singleprofile, no-aggregation simplicity as config_001, enabling a direct modality comparison. If image accuracy substantially exceeds 48.5%, the search should pivot toward multimodal fusion and image-encoder selection; if it falls well below, RNA-focused improvements (multiprofile, learned encoders) become the priority. This single experiment resolves the highest-level design question—whether to invest in the image branch—before committing budget to more granular choices like aggregation, fusion strategy, or encoder variants, making it the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant modality over image (20.8% for resnet50). With only two completed experiments, we have high uncertainty about whether the RNA encoder choice matters. Question: config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) changes only the RNA encoder from PCA (linear) to scvi (learned), keeping profile setting identical to config_001. This isolates the effect of representation learning. Why this is best: It is a single-variable comparison directly against config_001, making the result cleanly interpretable. If scvi substantially improves over PCA, it tells us representation learning is a high-leverage design axis and justifies further investment in scgpt and multimodal variants. If it does not, we can deprioritize encoder complexity and focus budget on profile/aggregation or fusion questions. This reduces the most critical uncertainty before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (config_004, acc=0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (config_001, acc=0.485) as the RNA encoder in singleprofile mode, establishing scvi_n200 as the current best representation. Image-only (resnet50) is very weak (acc=0.208), so the immediate priority is understanding the RNA-side design space before investing in multimodal fusion. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile + aggregation adds value over singleprofile. This experiment (config_005: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly extends the best-performing configuration by changing only the profile/aggregation dimension, giving a clean comparison against config_004. If multiprofile+avgpool improves accuracy, it validates the multiprofile axis and justifies further aggregation comparisons (transformer) and multimodal multiprofile tests. If it does not, we can confidently focus budget on singleprofile and encoder/fusion decisions. This is the highest-information next step because the answer gates an entire branch of the configuration space.

Evidence: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI n200, avgpool) achieved the best performance so far (Acc 0.650, F1 0.628), a large jump over its single-profile counterpart config_004 (Acc 0.520). This confirms multi-profile is the dominant design lever. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multi-profile setting. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses? config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding encoder (scVI n200) and profile setting (multi) constant, giving a clean A/B comparison against config_005. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a fundamental architectural choice that affects every multi-profile configuration downstream. If transformer aggregation provides a meaningful gain, it signals that profile-order/interaction information is exploitable and should be carried into all subsequent multi-profile and multimodal experiments. If it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward encoder comparison (e.g., scGPT) or multimodal fusion. This single experiment reduces the most impactful uncertainty with minimal confounding.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.653) while image-only is very weak (0.208). The largest single gain so far is multiprofile with scvi_n200 (0.520→0.650, +13 pts), and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) makes negligible difference. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the multiprofile gain is a general property of multi-profile representations or is specific to the learned scvi encoder. Config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) completes a clean 2×2 comparison: it shares the encoder with config_001 (singleprofile, pca, 0.485) to isolate the multiprofile effect, and shares the profile+aggregation with config_005 (scvi, multiprofile, avgpool, 0.650) to isolate the encoder effect under multiprofile. This single experiment simultaneously clarifies whether multiprofile is a universal win and how much of the current performance is attributable to encoder choice vs. profile setting, which directly informs whether to invest further in scgpt encoders, multimodal fusion, or profile/aggregation refinements.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA-only setup (config_005/006, ~0.65), and scvi_n200 consistently beats pca_n2000 (~0.06 gap). Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the immediate priority is maximizing the RNA branch before investing in multimodal fusion. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested scgpt, a distinct RNA foundation-model encoder, so we do not know whether it outperforms scvi_n200. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) differs from config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) only in the RNA encoder, giving a clean isolation of encoder quality in the best-performing profile setting. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly answers whether a different encoder family can push past the current 0.65 ceiling, which would reshape the entire search strategy. (2) avgpool is used because transformer ≈ avgpool (config_006 vs 005), so we avoid a redundant axis. (3) If scgpt is superior, we immediately know the best RNA-only baseline before any multimodal comparison; if it is not, we confirm scvi_n200 as the encoder of choice and can pivot to testing whether multimodal fusion adds value over this strong RNA-only baseline.

Evidence: The best RNA-only model (config_006, scvi_n200 multiprofile transformer) achieves 0.653 acc, while image_only with resnet50 (config_010) is near-random at 0.208. This raises a critical uncertainty: does the image modality carry any useful signal at all, or is the resnet50 encoder simply too weak? Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the effect of image encoder quality by swapping only the encoder from resnet50 to a much stronger ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet, keeping profile_setting and all other factors identical to config_010. Why this is the best next step: Before investing limited budget in any of the 22 multimodal configurations (which add fusion complexity), we must first determine whether the image modality contributes any discriminative signal. If ViT-L also performs near-randomly, the image channel is likely uninformative and multimodal fusion is unlikely to help; we can then focus remaining budget on refining RNA-only designs. If ViT-L substantially improves, it justifies exploring multimodal fusion with a known-good image backbone. This single-variable comparison is the most informative gate for all downstream multimodal decisions.

Evidence: RNA multiprofile with scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation is the strongest configuration found (config_006, acc 0.653), while image-only models are very weak (best: imagenet_vit_l at 0.227). No multimodal configuration has been tested yet, so it is entirely unclear whether adding the weak image signal to the strong RNA signal helps, is neutral, or is harmful. Question: config_038 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) directly isolates the effect of adding the image modality to the best-known RNA setup, using the slightly stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l > resnet50) and the simpler concat fusion as a baseline. Comparing config_038 to config_006 (0.653) tells us whether multimodal fusion adds value at all. Why this is the best next experiment: it answers the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question (should we include image data?) while keeping all other choices at their best-supported settings, making the comparison clean and interpretable under a limited budget.

The best result so far is config_038 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) at 0.7207 acc, which substantially outperforms the best RNA-only result (config_006, 0.6530 acc) and confirms that the image modality provides complementary signal despite its very low standalone accuracy (~0.23). The key remaining uncertainty is whether the fusion strategy matters: concat simply appends modality features, while weighted fusion lets the model learn adaptive modality importance. Config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, giving a clean single-variable A/B comparison. This is the most informative next step because it directly exploits the strongest evidence, isolates the effect of one design decision (fusion), and will clarify whether the image modality's contribution is best captured by fixed concatenation or learned weighting—information that will guide all subsequent multimodal experiments.

With no prior evidence, the most informative first step is to establish a minimal, well-understood baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the space: a standard PCA encoder, a single profile, no image branch, no aggregation, and no fusion. It isolates the contribution of the RNA modality under the most straightforward settings, giving a reference accuracy/F1 against which every subsequent experiment (image-only, multimodal, alternative encoders, multiprofile, different aggregation/fusion) can be meaningfully compared. Running this first also minimizes computational cost, preserving budget for the more complex configurations that will follow. It does not assume any particular modality will dominate; it simply anchors the search.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests this by holding profile_setting constant and using a standard encoder, enabling a clean cross-modal comparison against the RNA baseline. If image accuracy is substantially higher, the search should pivot toward image-centric or multimodal configurations; if it is similarly low, the bottleneck likely lies in data quality or task difficulty, and we should focus on RNA representation improvements or multimodal fusion. This single experiment reduces the largest source of strategic uncertainty and will most efficiently guide all subsequent choices under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 20.8% acc—essentially at chance level for a 5-class task. This raises a critical uncertainty: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task, or is resnet50 simply a poor encoder? Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the effect of image encoder quality by changing only the encoder from resnet50 to a stronger pretrained ViT-L, keeping model_setting and profile_setting identical to config_010. Why this is the best next experiment: The answer determines whether the entire multimodal branch (configs 016–051) is worth pursuing or whether budget should be redirected to optimizing the RNA pipeline. If ViT-L also yields near-chance performance, we can confidently deprioritize image-dependent experiments and focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices. If it substantially improves, multimodal fusion becomes a viable and promising direction. This single experiment resolves a high-level design uncertainty that gates many downstream decisions, making it the most budget-efficient choice given only two completed experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 0.485 acc, while both image-only configs (0.208–0.227) are far weaker, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA data point and PCA is a linear, unlearned projection. Question: Does a learned, biologically-informed RNA encoder (scvi_n200) produce a meaningfully better representation than PCA for the same singleprofile, rna_only setting? This is a clean one-variable comparison against config_001 (only the encoder changes). Why this is the best next step: The encoder choice is the most fundamental design axis—if a learned encoder substantially improves over PCA, it validates investing in scvi/scgpt across profile settings and multimodal fusion; if it does not, PCA suffices and we should pivot to multiprofile/aggregation or multimodal experiments. Resolving this uncertainty before testing aggregation or fusion avoids spending budget on downstream combinations built on a suboptimal representation.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.48–0.52) vastly outperform image-only models (0.21–0.23), and among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 (0.5203) beats pca_n2000 (0.4849) by ~3.5 pts, indicating learned representations matter. However, we have zero evidence on whether the multiprofile setting with aggregation improves over singleprofile. Question: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile) to isolate the effect of multiprofile + simple aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: it uses the strongest known encoder, tests the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to establish a lower bound on multiprofile benefit, and provides a clean single-variable comparison. If avgpool helps, transformer aggregation becomes a justified follow-up; if it does not, we avoid spending budget on more complex aggregation schemes. This resolves a fundamental architectural question (single vs. multi-profile) before committing to multimodal fusion experiments, which would change multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.650, F1=0.628), a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (acc=0.520). This strongly indicates multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design axis. However, the aggregation method itself is untested beyond avgpool—config_005 is the only multiprofile experiment completed. Question: Does transformer aggregation (config_006) outperform simple avgpool for combining multiple scvi_n200 profiles? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005), directly isolating whether learning inter-profile interactions adds value over uniform averaging. Why best next: It exploits the strongest promising direction while reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice (aggregation) before committing budget to more complex multimodal or alternative-encoder configurations. If transformer helps, it justifies further investment in sophisticated aggregation; if not, avgpool suffices and budget can shift to testing scgpt or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile + scvi_n200 (config_005/006) achieves ~0.65 accuracy, far above singleprofile RNA (~0.52) and all image-only models (~0.21-0.23). Within the multiprofile regime, avgpool and transformer aggregation are essentially equivalent (0.650 vs 0.653). The key untested variable in this high-performing regime is the RNA encoder: we have shown scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 for singleprofile, but scgpt (a distinct generative-model-based encoder) has never been tested. Question: Does scgpt match or exceed scvi_n200 when combined with multiprofile aggregation, and if so, by how much? This isolates the encoder choice while holding profile setting (multiprofile) and aggregation (avgpool, the simpler of the two equivalent options) constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly probes whether a different learned representation can push past the current ~0.65 ceiling in the most promising regime, without introducing confounds from modality fusion or a second new variable. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, it reshapes the best configuration; if it is comparable, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and lets us move on to testing multimodal fusion with confidence in the RNA backbone.

1) Evidence: RNA multiprofile with scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation is the clear best configuration so far (acc 0.653, F1 0.628), while both image-only models are very weak (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227). We have strong evidence that multiprofile scvi_n200 dominates, but zero evidence yet on whether adding the image modality via fusion improves on this RNA-only baseline. 2) This experiment tests whether concat-fusing the stronger image encoder (ViT-L) into the best RNA multiprofile configuration (scvi_n200, transformer aggregation) yields any gain over the 0.653 RNA-only baseline. It isolates the fusion question by holding the RNA side at its known-best setting and adding only the image branch. 3) Under a limited budget, this is the highest-value next step: the study's core question is whether multimodal profiling outperforms unimodal, and we should answer that before spending further experiments on other multimodal variants (different encoders, fusion types, or aggregations). If it fails to beat 0.653, it saves many downstream multimodal experiments; if it helps, it identifies a productive direction to refine.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.721 acc, a ~7-point jump over the best RNA-only (config_006, 0.653). Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), so the multimodal gain likely comes from complementary rather than independently predictive image features. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the concat fusion in config_038 is optimal or whether a weighted fusion would better balance the strong RNA signal against the weak image signal. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion=weighted vs concat, isolating the fusion strategy as the single variable. Why best next experiment: it is a clean one-parameter A/B against our current best, directly testing whether the fusion mechanism is a critical design lever. If weighted substantially outperforms concat, it tells us the weaker image modality should be down-weighted and reshapes all future multimodal choices; if the two are comparable, it tells us fusion method is not a key factor and we should pivot to testing image encoder or aggregation. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_039: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725) shows that adding image to multi-profile RNA yields a substantial gain (~0.65→0.72). However, we have only tested one image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) in the multimodal setting. Image-only experiments show a small but present encoder effect (resnet50=0.208 vs imagenet_vit_l=0.227). Config_033 changes only the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l→resnet50) while keeping all other settings identical to config_039, cleanly isolating whether image encoder quality matters when the image is a secondary modality. If performance is similar, the image contributes a complementary signal regardless of encoder sophistication, and we can redirect budget to other variables (e.g., aggregation or RNA encoder in the multimodal context). If resnet50 degrades notably, it confirms the image encoder is a bottleneck and justifies prioritizing the stronger encoder. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about the image modality's contribution mechanism under the limited budget.

With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a reliable performance baseline to anchor all future comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: it uses a linear PCA reduction with no learned encoder, no multi-profile aggregation, and no fusion. Running this first gives us (1) a floor performance estimate for the RNA signal under minimal modeling assumptions, (2) a fast and cheap experiment (PCA requires no training), and (3) a clean reference point against which every subsequent change—learned RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), multi-profile aggregation, image modality, and fusion strategies—can be measured. This maximizes the information gained per experiment by isolating the raw data signal before introducing any additional complexity.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, PCA-2000, single profile → 48.5% acc, 46.4% F1). We have zero information about whether the image modality carries any useful signal for this task, which is the most fundamental design question in a multimodal profiling study. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50) is the direct single-modality counterpart to config_001, isolating the effect of switching from RNA to image as the sole input while keeping the profile setting (single) and using a standard, well-established encoder (ResNet50). This tells us the standalone image baseline and lets us compare which modality is stronger. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: With only one data point, the highest-value uncertainty to reduce is whether the image modality is informative at all. If image performance is comparable to or exceeds RNA, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If image is very weak, it redirects effort toward improving the RNA representation (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This is the simplest, cleanest single-variable comparison available and avoids conflating modality, fusion, and aggregation effects simultaneously.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 0.485 accuracy, while config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieves only 0.208, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have no information on whether the RNA representation itself can be improved. Question: config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) changes only the RNA encoder from a linear PCA projection to a learned deep generative representation (scVI), keeping profile setting and all other factors identical to config_001. This cleanly isolates the effect of representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: With only two data points, the most uncertain and consequential design axis is whether a simple linear projection is sufficient or whether a learned encoder captures biologically meaningful structure that PCA misses. The answer determines whether subsequent experiments should prioritize encoder choice (scgpt, deeper models) or other axes (multiprofile aggregation, multimodal fusion). A single-variable comparison to our current best (config_001) maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: scVI n200 (config_004, acc 0.520) outperforms PCA n2000 (config_001, acc 0.485) for single-profile RNA, and image-only (config_010, acc 0.208) is very weak. All completed experiments use single-profile; the multiprofile axis is entirely untested. Question: Does moving from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve performance when paired with the best RNA encoder (scVI n200)? This isolates the structural effect of multiprofile + aggregation as a single design decision (aggregation is a necessary consequence of multiprofile). Why this is the best next experiment: The multiprofile decision gates roughly half the remaining search space (configs 002-003, 005-006, 008-009, 011-012, 014-015, 018-027, 030-039, 042-051). If multiprofile+avgpool with scVI does not beat single-profile scVI, we can deprioritize all multiprofile variants and focus on encoder choice and fusion. If it does help, we gain a strong prior for investing in multiprofile+transformer and multimodal multiprofile configurations. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential unexplored design axis.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a large jump over config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile) at 0.520, confirming that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is highly beneficial for scvi-encoded RNA. However, the aggregation choice within the multiprofile setting remains untested. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when paired with scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes from config_005). Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest positive signal in the search so far, isolates the aggregation design decision, and will either (a) yield a stronger RNA baseline for subsequent multimodal experiments or (b) confirm that simple avgpool is sufficient, redirecting budget toward other design axes (encoder choice, multimodal fusion) with greater confidence.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the strongest configuration so far (0.650–0.653), a large jump over singleprofile (0.520), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has negligible effect. RNA encoders showed a meaningful gap in singleprofile (scvi_n200 0.520 > pca_n2000 0.485), but scgpt has never been tested. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable swap from config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the RNA encoder effect in the highest-performing regime. Why best next: (1) It directly tests whether a stronger/different pre-trained encoder can push past the current 0.65 ceiling, or whether scvi_n200 is already near-optimal for multiprofile RNA. (2) It keeps all other variables fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, rna_only), making the comparison interpretable. (3) Establishing the best RNA-only multiprofile baseline before investing in multimodal fusion is prudent given that image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), so we need to know the RNA ceiling before asking whether adding image helps. (4) If scgpt substantially beats scvi_n200 here, it changes the encoder choice for all downstream multimodal experiments; if it does not, we confirm scvi_n200 as the default and can pivot to multimodal exploration with confidence.

Evidence: The current best result is RNA-only multiprofile scvi_n200 (config_006, acc 0.653), while the only image-only test (config_010, resnet50) scored very poorly (0.208). This raises a critical uncertainty: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative, or was resnet50 simply an inadequate encoder? Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the effect of upgrading the image encoder from a small CNN to a large pretrained ViT, directly comparable to config_010. Why this is the best next experiment: Before committing limited budget to any of the 36 multimodal configurations, we need to know whether a stronger image encoder can produce a viable image representation. If imagenet_vit_l image-only is still very weak (<0.35), multimodal fusion is unlikely to beat the 0.653 RNA-only baseline and remaining budget should focus on RNA-only refinements. If it reaches ~0.5+, multimodal fusion becomes a high-value direction. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (unimodal vs. multimodal) before any fusion experiments are run.

Evidence: The strongest result so far is RNA-only multi-profile with scVI n200 + transformer aggregation (config_006, acc=0.653), showing that multi-profile representation is the dominant design lever (~13pt gain over single-profile). Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) is nearly irrelevant. The critical remaining uncertainty is whether fusing the image modality into the already-strong RNA multi-profile pipeline adds any value. This experiment (config_038) tests exactly that: it pairs the best proven RNA setup (scVI n200, multiprofile, transformer) with the slightly stronger image encoder (ViT-L) and a simple concat fusion, changing only the model setting from rna_only to multimodal. This is the highest-information next step because it directly answers whether multimodal fusion is worth the added complexity, and the result will gate whether further multimodal experiments (fusion type, image encoder, aggregation) are warranted under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_038 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + concat) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.7207), a clear jump over the best RNA-only result (0.6530). However, the fusion strategy has never been varied in any completed experiment—concat is the only fusion tested. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of the fusion mechanism while holding all other design choices (encoder, profile, aggregation, image encoder) at their best-evidenced settings. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison that directly exploits the strongest evidence while reducing uncertainty about a completely untested design axis. If weighted fusion improves on concat, it reveals a new optimization direction; if it is comparable or worse, we can confidently fix fusion=concat and redirect budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., aggregation in multimodal or image encoder choice). Under a limited budget, this targeted test is more informative than simultaneously changing multiple variables or revisiting dimensions already well-characterized (e.g., transformer vs avgpool, which showed a negligible gap in RNA-only).

The current best (config_039: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725) shows a strong multimodal result, but we have no evidence yet about whether the RNA encoder choice still matters when image information is present. In RNA-only, scvi_n200 clearly outperforms PCA (0.520 vs 0.485 single-profile; the gap likely persists in multi-profile), yet image-only models are very weak (~0.22). Config_027 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted) is a clean single-variable swap of only the RNA encoder relative to config_039, isolating the contribution of the learned RNA representation in the multimodal setting. If PCA + image approaches scvi + image, the image modality is carrying most of the signal and we can simplify the RNA pipeline; if it falls well short, the scvi representation remains critical even with image fusion. This is the highest-information next step because it directly tests whether the most expensive design choice (RNA encoder) is still necessary, and the result will guide whether subsequent experiments should focus on image-encoder quality, fusion strategy, or other axes.

With no prior experiments, the most informative first step is to establish a minimal baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest RNA configuration with the most standard encoder, providing a clear performance anchor. This baseline will allow subsequent experiments to isolate the effect of (a) richer RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), (b) multiprofile aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer), (c) adding the image modality (image_only or multimodal), and (d) fusion strategy. Starting from the simplest, lowest-risk configuration avoids confounding multiple design choices at once and gives a reference point against which every added complexity can be evaluated, making it the most efficient use of the first experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), giving a minimal baseline. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all. Question: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet-50) provides a clean, single-variable contrast to config_001—same profile setting (singleprofile), no aggregation or fusion—so the comparison isolates the effect of modality. Why this is the best next experiment: In a multimodal study, knowing the relative strength of each modality in isolation is the foundational decision that shapes every subsequent choice (which encoder to prioritize, whether fusion is worthwhile, whether multiprofile aggregation is needed). If image-only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, it justifies investing budget in multimodal fusion configurations; if it is much weaker, it redirects attention toward improving the RNA side (better encoders, multiprofile). This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty with a single clean comparison, avoiding the confound of simultaneously introducing a new modality, a new fusion strategy, and a new profile setting.

Evidence: With only two completed experiments, RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the PCA representation is near-optimal or whether a learned biological encoder (scVI) can substantially improve RNA signal quality. This experiment (config_004: RNA, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, changing only the RNA encoder while holding modality and profile setting constant. It directly tests whether a learned, lower-dimensional (200-d) representation can match or exceed a high-dimensional (2000-d) linear one. This is the best next step because the answer determines whether to invest remaining budget in scvi/scgpt-based configurations or to focus on aggregation and fusion strategies with PCA; it reduces uncertainty about a fundamental representation choice that gates many downstream decisions.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (config_004, acc=0.520) is our best RNA encoder, clearly outperforming pca_n2000 (config_001, acc=0.485). Image alone (config_010, acc=0.208) is very weak, so the RNA modality is the primary driver. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile for the best encoder. This is a fundamental design axis that will determine the strategy for all downstream multimodal experiments. Question: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly extends our best singleprofile result by adding multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), isolating whether multiple profiles carry complementary signal. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a minimal, clean change from our strongest configuration (only profile_setting and the required aggregation differ), it tests a design decision that propagates to every multimodal config, and using avgpool (rather than transformer) keeps the experiment simple so we can attribute any change to the multiprofile representation itself. If multiprofile helps, subsequent experiments should prioritize multiprofile multimodal configs; if not, we can focus budget on singleprofile multimodal or better image encoders.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.6501 acc, a large +0.13 jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.5203), making multiprofile+scvi the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is sufficient or whether a transformer aggregator can further exploit the multi-profile structure. This experiment (config_006) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding encoder (scvi_n200) and profile setting (multiprofile) fixed, giving a clean isolated comparison against config_005. This is the best next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence (the multiprofile+scvi direction) while resolving a critical design choice—aggregation strategy—that will govern all subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiments. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it signals that the multiprofile benefit is underexploited and justifies more complex aggregation; if they are comparable, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion questions.

Evidence: The largest gain so far comes from switching to multiprofile with scvi_n200 (0.520 → 0.650, +0.13), while avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly equivalent (~0.65). We also know scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in the singleprofile setting (0.520 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multiprofile benefit is encoder-agnostic or specific to scvi_n200's learned latent space. This experiment (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly isolates the RNA encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant, enabling a clean comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool). If pca_n2000 also benefits substantially from multiprofile, the profile setting is the dominant driver and we can broaden our search; if not, the scvi_n200 + multiprofile interaction is critical and we should prioritize that encoder for further exploration (e.g., scgpt or multimodal fusion). This single-variable test is the most informative next step before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.48-0.65 vs image 0.21), multi-profile with scVI is the current best (0.650-0.653), and scVI clearly outperforms PCA in both single and multi-profile settings. The aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) appears negligible (0.650 vs 0.653). Key uncertainty: whether scGPT, the third available RNA encoder, can improve on scVI in the multi-profile setting where the largest gains have been observed. This experiment (config_008: scGPT, multi-profile, avgpool) is a clean A/B comparison against config_005 (scVI, multi-profile, avgpool = 0.650), isolating the encoder effect while holding profile setting and aggregation constant.
